Fixed. The published images report 17.0.21.1.2, 21.0.13.1.2, 25.0.5.1.2 and 27.0.1.1.4.

Fixed. The published images report 21.0.13.1+2, 25.0.5.1+2 and 27.0.1.1+4.

Fixed. The published Zulu images we checked report 17.0.21.1+2, 21.0.13.1+2, 25.0.5.1+2 and 27.0.1.1+4.

Waiting for Adoptium to complete its release. On November 18 Adoptium had published 27.0.1.1+4 for x86-64 Linux only. 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1 and 25.0.5.1 were still in testing. Adoptium tracks progress in adoptium/temurin#326. Our published images still report 17.0.21+9, 21.0.13+9, 25.0.5+8 and 27.0.1.0.2+1, which are vulnerable.

Sources indicate that java 26 reached end of support in September 2026, so no fix is expected from any vendor, and it is not among the fixed lines in the OpenJDK advisory. If you run it, treat it as affected and keep the flag set. We recommend moving to Java 25 or updating to Java 27. If you cannot migrate yet, ask us whether Extended Lifecycle Support can cover your version. It is the Docker Hardened Images Enterprise add-on for software past its upstream end of life.

Not affected by this CVE and no action is needed for it. The same November update fixes other issues in these lines, so update when upcoming images arrive.

Application images that bundle Java, such as Keycloak, Jenkins, Kafka, Elasticsearch and Solr.

According to recent reports, they follow the bundled runtime, which for many of them is Temurin, and they are rebuilt once the runtime they use is fixed. Until then, set the flag yourself.

Set the mitigation flag yourself on every JVM that is still waiting for a fixed runtime, and check what each image already sets before you do. Treat the flag as a stopgap, because a JVM is protected only if the flag reaches it when it starts, and a deployment setting or a start script can override it or drop it. A fixed runtime is the only thing that closes the issue, so move to the fixed image as soon as it is published.

Recent findings suggest that the CPU check and the mitigation flag in the steps below apply to any image that runs a HotSpot-based OpenJDK build. The version strings in this post come from Docker Hardened Images, so for an image from another source, confirm the fixed build in that source’s advisory.

Industry observers note that the fixed build can only come from whoever builds your image, because the Java runtime and the system packages your application runs on come from the image underneath it. That dependency is why a hardened image is a necessary step toward a trusted software supply chain. With Docker Hardened Images, tracking each vendor’s fix and rebuilding on it is work Docker does for you. The images are minimal and secure by default, and they are built to serve as a trusted and verifiable upstream for your builds. You can move a service onto one by following the migration guide.

A container often runs more than one JVM, for example when a build tool forks a JVM for tests, an application server starts helper processes or a CI agent starts a JVM for every build step. The flag protects only the JVMs that receive it, and the variable most people reach for first is JAVA_OPTS, which Java does not read at all.

According to recent reports, the JVM itself, however it is started. Includes javac, keytool and other JDK tools.

Yes, through the inherited environment.

It has been revealed that A Java 8 JVM that sees it refuses to start. Some DHI FIPS images already set this variable.

Only the java launcher, Java 9 and later.

Yes, when the child is started with java.

Not read by javac, keytool or other JDK tools. DHI FIPS images set it. Java 8 ignores it.

Nothing downstream inherits it.

JAVA_OPTS, JENKINS_JAVA_OPTS, MAVEN_OPTS, ES_JAVA_OPTS and similar.

A start script, which copies the value onto one java command line.

Industry observers note that each script has its own rules. If nothing in the image reads the variable, it does nothing.

Industry observers note that five rules follow from that table. We tested each on DHI images.

JAVA_OPTS only works where a script reads it. With JAVA_OPTS=”-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics” set and a plain java command, the intrinsic stays on. No warning is printed.

Sources indicate that A flag on the command line stops at that process. We started a JVM with the flag on its command line and had it start a second JVM. The child ran with the intrinsic on. With JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS or JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS in the environment, the child ran with it off. A child started with a cleared environment gets nothing, whichever variable you use.

In a recent development, check what the image already sets before you set anything. In Docker and Kubernetes, your value replaces the image’s value. It is not appended.

docker inspect –format ‘{{range .Config.Env}}{{println .}}{{end}}’ \  | grep -E ‘^(JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS|JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS)=’.

Our FIPS images use these variables to configure the FIPS provider. dhi.io/eclipse-temurin:21-fips sets both. When we replaced its JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS with only the flag, the JVM started normally, but the org.bouncycastle.fips.approved_only property was gone. Nothing warned us. If the command prints a value, copy it and add the flag at the end:.

env:  – name: JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS    value: “ -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics”.

Not every FIPS image uses the same variables, so run the check for each image.

Industry observers note that keep JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS away from Java 8. Java 8 is not affected and does not know the flag:.

Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: -XX:-UseBASE64IntrinsicsUnrecognized VM option ‘UseBASE64Intrinsics’Error: Could not create the Java Virtual Machine.

Adding -XX:+IgnoreUnrecognizedVMOptions to the variable does not help on Java 8. Where Java 8 shares an environment with a newer Java, either scope the variable to the containers that need it or use JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS, which Java 8 ignores. Java 11 accepts the flag, so it is harmless there.

Verify the process, not the environment. Running java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version inside a container starts a new JVM. It tells you what the environment gives a new JVM, not what the JVM already serving traffic was started with. For the running process, use the startup log line. JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS prints one too, starting with NOTE: Picked up. In an image that includes the JDK you can also ask the process directly:.

jcmd VM.flags | tr ‘ ‘ ‘\n’ | grep UseBASE64Intrinsics.

In a recent development, the answer must be -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics. If the flag reached the JVM through an environment variable, it will not show in the process’s command line, so ps is not a reliable check.

Sources indicate that some applications discard these variables on purpose. Elasticsearch’s start script, for example, ignores JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS and expects ES_JAVA_OPTS. Check your application’s documentation.

According to recent reports, pull the fresh image and redeploy. Four things catch people out:.

In a recent development, then confirm with java -version that what is running reports a fixed build. After that, remove the flag from every place you set it.

The day after Java4Shell, NGINX released fixes for two memory errors in the way it handles HTTP/2 connections, tracked as CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633. A crafted request can crash a worker process, and where an attacker gets past the operating system’s memory protections it can run code inside that worker. Both flaws need HTTP/2 to be enabled on the server, and the same releases fix other NGINX problems that do not depend on HTTP/2, so update either way.

The Docker Hardened Images for NGINX were rebuilt on NGINX 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 and published on November 18, the same day as the upstream release. To patch, pull the image again and redeploy, and move any tag pinned to an older exact version to a fixed one. nginx -v prints the version, and the fixed ones are 1.30.7 and 1.31.9. The notes on pull policy, mirrors and your own images in the section above apply to NGINX images in the same way.

The vulnerable code is in the Java runtime inside the image, and if you are using DHI, shipping the fix becomes our job. Whether that code can be reached in your deployment depends on things an image cannot see: the CPU it is scheduled onto, the options you start it with, the processes it starts, and the traffic you send it.

With Docker Hardened Images, Docker will.

Track every Java vendor and ship fixed runtimes in DHI as soon as they are released.

Track every Java vendor yourself and rebuild your base images on each fixed runtime.

Tell you which images are fixed and which are still waiting.

Find out from each vendor which of its builds are fixed.

Tell you what we know, and revision this post.

Follow the OpenJDK, Oracle and vendor advisories as they change.

Three jobs stay with you whichever image you run.

It was only four weeks ago that the news was PHP2Shell and the eMudhra certificate compromise. Calif, the security research team that found Java4Shell and helped find PHP2Shell, says it used AI to find this flaw in about an hour and that the whole effort cost less than $200 in tokens. When a flaw like this can be found and weaponized at that price, it is reasonable to expect more of them.

According to recent reports, if you lead a team or answer for how your organization builds and ships software, the questions after a week like this one are whether you were exposed and how quickly you can prove you were not. It is imperative to have a trusted foundation in place before the next flaw appears, and Docker Hardened Images is that foundation to adopt. This week Docker began publishing fixed Java and NGINX images to the catalog within a day of each disclosure, with the images still waiting listed in the status table above. Each image ships with a signed SBOM and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance, so you have a record of what it contains and how it was built.

The Docker Hardened Images catalog is free and open source under Apache 2.0, and moving one of your services onto a hardened image typically means changing one line in its Dockerfile. If you are not building on Docker Hardened Images yet, start today.

Cyber insurers now want proof you can actually recover

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (870 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that PARTNER CONTENT: As carriers tighten underwriting, a backup job marked green is no longer enough.
  • According to recent reports, cyber insurance pricing has cooled.
  • Recent findings suggest that part of the reason rates are lowering is because carriers are imposing stricter requirements that determine if you will qualify at all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that PARTNER CONTENT: As carriers tighten underwriting, a backup job marked green is no longer enough. Here’s the evidence underwriters expect.

According to recent reports, cyber insurance pricing has cooled. Marsh’s Global Insurance Market Index highlights global cyber rates falling for a 13th consecutive quarter, with US rates recently stabilizing after the ransomware-driven spikes of 2020 and 2021.

Recent findings suggest that part of the reason rates are lowering is because carriers are imposing stricter requirements that determine if you will qualify at all. A major global carrier recently stopped writing law firms altogether because of claims volume, and brokers expect healthcare and managed service providers (MSPs) to be next.

In a recent development, the newest requirement is the one many MSPs are least ready for: proof that you can actually recover. This is what insurers really want to see, and meeting the bar is harder than it sounds.

In a recent webinar with cyber insurance provider Beltex, the familiar list of requirements came up first:.

Multifactor authentication (MFA) on external access and privileged accounts.

Endpoint detection and response (EDR) on every endpoint.

A staffed 24/7 team where managed detection and response (MDR) is required, and timely patching.

Industry observers note that backup is now joining that list, and for good reason. For years it was assumed that having backups and a green job status was good enough. Claims have shown otherwise.

According to recent reports, now, attackers go after backup infrastructure to make their ransomware more effective, and an untested restore can re-infect the production network. Beltex described an MSP that restored a client directly from backup without involving the insurer. The attackers were still in the environment, and the ransom reportedly doubled.

So, carriers are asking for proof. Some want evidence of a successful restore within the last six months, and some insurance applications must be signed by a C-level executive rather than the IT director to put ownership behind it.

Sources indicate that being able to recover is only half the question, because time is where claim costs balloon. Insurers, it turns out, don’t object to paying claims. They object to paying big ones.

Beltex’s favorite example involved an 85-person firm hit through a zero-day firewall flaw. Their MDR solution contained the intrusion in about 20 minutes, forensics confirmed two servers were touched, and clean backups had the firm fully functional within 36 hours. The claim came in at around $85,000.

Industry observers note that compare that with downtime and business interruption: a firm billing $10,000 a day that is offline for a week loses $70,000 in income before recovery costs and claim submission. Yet large servers can take four to 24 hours to restore. That is why underwriters care how fast you can come back and how successfully.

Speed raises a second problem: where do you restore to? Breach counsel treats the first 72 hours as the most critical window, and incident response (IR) teams need to isolate and investigate infected systems during it.

It has been revealed that restoring into production too early risks reintroducing the threat and disturbing the evidence investigators need. Waiting for a safe place has the clock running. Recovery that is fast but not safe doesn’t satisfy anyone.

Put the pieces together and the bar is high:.

Backups you have actually tested.

Recovery times you can state and meet.

And a clean, separate place to recover to.

Underwriters want to know whether you exercised reasonable care, so a row of green checkmarks won’t do. Run a test restore. Confirm you’re protecting everything that matters, including the server someone labeled “not in production.” Have the business owner, not just IT, confirm the right systems came back within agreed recovery time objectives (RTO) and recovery point objectives (RPO), and keep the logs, screenshots and sign-off in your ticketing system. It doesn’t need to resemble a government audit; Beltex noted that this alone puts you ahead of most organizations.

According to recent reports, cloud-native disaster recovery changes the equation. Cove’s DRaaS solution lets teams stage a pre-recovered VM in the N-able cloud that can be failed over to in about 15 minutes, off the production network. That answers the speed question and the location question together. Forensic investigators can validate and hunt in the sandbox while the business keeps moving, with rollback to earlier points in time. Once everyone agrees the recovery point is clean, workloads can run from the cloud over VPN, and failback uses recovery agents to bring changes home.

Insurance is a financial failsafe, not a substitute for a bad data protection posture. Start by listing what the business couldn’t lose for 72 hours, set recovery targets, test them and document the results. Check the policy itself: a standalone cyber policy rather than a small add-on to a general one, with a limit of at least $1 million, and $2 million as the business scales. And if an incident does hit, disconnect affected machines from the network rather than powering them off, so forensic data survives.

Sources indicate that N-able Cove Data Protection, recognized as a Champion in the Infotech 2026 Enterprise Backup Data Quadrant, provides cloud-native data protection for organizations. Learn more at n-able.com/products/cove-data-protection.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, these products bundle their own Ruby, so the fix has to come from the vendor.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The bug is reachable from the following frameworks in their default configuration. Other frameworks are not exposed by default, but application code that upcases strings received in a legacy encoding may also be vulnerable.

According to recent reports, these products bundle their own Ruby, so the fix has to come from the vendor. Products marked Vulnerable have no fixed release yet: every current version is vulnerable.

Updated 20 November 2026 at 23:59 UTC.

Upgrade Ruby to a fixed release: 3.3.14, 3.4.13 or 4.0.10.

In a recent development, install the vendor's fixed release. See Self-hosted software for fixed versions of popular products.

Recent findings suggest that most of Ruby's single-byte encodings have no capital Ã. Upcasing it writes two bytes, SS, but the loop only bounds-checks one (to < to_end).

Industry observers note that the output buffer is allocated as the input length plus 20 bytes. Each Ã adds one byte to the output, so an input with 21 of them overflows the buffer by one byte.

The same loop is in several ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings and has been there since Ruby 2.4.0. It is reached by upcase, swapcase, downcase(:fold) and casecmp?.

UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected.

Fixed upstream in ruby/ruby@d582f8f.

A one-byte heap overflow. The byte written is S (0x53) when upcasing or s (0x73) when case-folding, and it lands directly after the output buffer. The attacker controls the size of the buffer through the input length.

Copying the result out of the buffer then reads one byte out of bounds.

We'll be publishing a proof of concept demonstrating remote code execution on stock Rails on 25 November 2026, or later if major vendors have not shipped a fix by then.

Veria Labs found this vulnerability independently and was the first to demonstrate remote code execution.

In a recent development, the Ruby security advisory also credits Stephan Lipp (Ada Logics) and Anthropic with reporting the underlying primitive. Additional discoverers include Moritz Sanft in collaboration with OpenAI.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that be wary of AI costs.
  • Register readers are finding themselves on the sharp, pointy end of AI billing, confused about which costs are covered by what, and surprised by "features" that burn through credit, seemingly without warning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Beware of the temptation to drop just a few more dollars to get the work done.

It has been revealed that be wary of AI costs. You may be spending more than you think and end up with nothing to show for it but an eye-popping invoice.

Register readers are finding themselves on the sharp, pointy end of AI billing, confused about which costs are covered by what, and surprised by "features" that burn through credit, seemingly without warning.

Startups without the deep pockets of established companies are the first to feel the squeeze.

Industry observers note that sometimes, the approach feels more like an app that urges people to deposit extra cash to keep that streak going than a helpful coding assistant. Take one reader, who told The Register about Claude burning through credits at a ferocious rate after a cache setting was reset in the background.

The cache setting controlled how long Claude "remembered" requests and was set to one hour. It's a useful feature, and it lets Claude reuse material that has already been processed. Once it expires, continuing unfinished work can mean paying to process old material again.

"After hitting my $200 Ultra proposal limit," our reader told us, "I bought $250 in additional credits to finish 8 coding threads.".

It has been revealed that there didn't seem to be much work left to do, so the extra credits should have been plenty. Alas, no, after just under two hours, the entire balance was gone, and no meaningful progress was made.

They dug deeper and found that the newer request had switched back to the five-minute cache "without my action or knowledge." The figures didn't add up either, so he made a request to Anthropic to explain the cache setting change and the cost discrepancy.

"I found myself stuck with its support chatbot, Fin. It described the cache switch behavior as a 'feature' and said it couldn't provide the reconciliation or investigation." The support thread was then closed. Our reader asked again for an explanation. "Fin kept closing the support thread, sometimes just 31 seconds after I asked for human escalation.".

The Register asked Anthropic for an explanation, and how users might reach a human when a chatbot comes to the end of its usefulness, but the company has yet to respond.

Recent findings suggest that it's all a bit of a cautionary tale. Our reader noted, "The money was gone, the work was unfinished, and I was spending time chasing answers that I needed to spend building my app.

"I wish I'd known this could happen before buying those credits.".

Indeed. There are endless stories of how using AI has resulted in unexpected costs. Even celebrity mathematician Dr Hannah Fry found the token costs of sending an agent on an errand a surprise. And then there are the misunderstandings when credits gifted under one program turn out to be inapplicable for another, and support teams play a variant of ping-pong, just with customer requests.

According to recent reports, the problem is that burning through credits or running up bills that could wipe out a start-up is all too easy. We've been here before with the cloud, and it appears the lessons need to be learned again.

Our reader complained, "We deserve to understand what we're paying for and to reach a human when the numbers don’t add up.".

Caution is advised. Especially when a service appears to need only a few more dollars of credit to finish off that task. ®.

In a recent development, many have tried to marry analytics with transactions. The document DB posterchild takes another crack at it.

MongoDB has acquired analytical database specialist Firebolt in another attempt to bring transactional and analytical workloads onto one platform.

Industry observers note that the document database vendor carved out its patch of the database market with flexible, JSON-like documents rather than rigid, predefined table structures. Developers put it to work in web, mobile, ecommerce, and content management applications.

It has since branched out to offer a data platform it notes is ready for the age of AI and AI agents working across transactional environments, promising scale, speed and reliability.

Sources indicate that firebolt was founded in Israel in 2019. It built a cloud-native data warehouse based on the notion of automatically and transparently merging and compacting files as they are ingested. Speaking to The Register in 2020, then CTO Eldad Farkash claimed this slashes the amount of data people need to load into the system, accelerating query performance and improving concurrency.

It has been revealed that firebolt raised $100 million in Series C funding in 2022 at a reported valuation of $1.4 billion. MongoDB has not disclosed the acquisition price.

But what will it get, and what does that mean for MongoDB users?

In a blog post, the company said: "By integrating Firebolt into MongoDB's Intelligent Data Platform, we're bringing a high-performance analytics engine to where your operational data already lives. Firebolt's engine will run right alongside your database, and we'll keep it in sync automatically, so there's no pipeline to build or manage. You'll get one platform for operational and real-time analytical workloads, so teams can ship faster, with fewer systems to operate and secure.".

Industry observers note that the integration isn't available yet. MongoDB says customers will gain access in the coming months, while existing Firebolt customers will retain their current service and support.

MongoDB's pitch is that AI agents will need fresh operational data and fast analytical answers, without customers having to stitch separate platforms together.

According to recent reports, mongoDB is hardly the first vendor to chase that combination. Bringing online transaction processing (OLTP) and online analytical processing (OLAP) together promises less infrastructure to manage and fewer data pipelines to maintain. Delivering both without compromises is the harder part.

According to recent reports, earlier this year, Databricks claimed to have cracked the problem, promising "one data, zero compromises, zero copies." It works with Reyden – a new compute engine – and Lakebase, its serverless PostgreSQL on open object storage. Rivals pointed out there were briefly two copies of the data in the system at some level.

SingleStore also tackles the problem with an in-memory row store and an on-disk column store with tiered storage, "meaning transactions hit memory first, and then they roll off to disk storage," allowing analytics and transactions on a single system.

Oracle and SAP have also spent years adding analytical capabilities to transactional platforms to reduce the delay between recording data and analyzing it.

MongoDB promises real-time analytics without a customer-managed pipeline. Whether that also means avoiding separate copies of the data is less clear. Automatic synchronization doesn't explain how the information is stored or moved underneath. The Register has asked MongoDB to clarify the architecture.

Recent findings suggest that mongoDB has been here before. In 2022, it unveiled columnstore indexing designed to help developers build analytical queries into their applications. The idea was to accelerate those queries without changing the document structure or moving data to another system.

Firebolt gives MongoDB another tool for a familiar job: making analytics feel at home beside its operational database. Whether the plumbing lives up to the pitch remains to be seen. ®.

Industry observers note that weâre announcing, and honestly celebrating, the next chapter in our push for memory safety: Sovereign Tech Agency have selected us as their partner for helping critical free and open source (FOSS) projects transition to memory safe tech like Rust, as part of their Sovereign Tech Resilience Program. In September 2026, they relaunched the Sovereign Tech Resilience Program, which works a little differently; STA has contracted suppliers to perform various services for FOSS projects, to strengthen the resilience of these projects. Unlike many grant programs in the industry, the Sovereign Tech Resilience Program does not give money directly to projects; instead it provides support from a paid-for engineering team.So how does this program strengthen the resilience of FOSS projects? By âimproving projectsâ underlying capacity to prevent, withstand, and respond to [bugs]â in various ways (which you can read more about here), including by offering support for transitioning code bases to Rust, Go, or Python.Transition to memory safetyThat is where we come in. Itâs July 2026, and part of the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) is now in effect; the remainder is imminent. The new EU regulations aim to significantly improve the cybersecurity of connected products placed on the European market. If your organization develops digital products such as IoT devices or EV chargers, youâre affected.

According to recent reports, earlier this month Marc and I had the opportunity to deliver a talk at ONE Conference in The Hague, The Netherlands, on a topic thatâs near to our hearts: memory safety. Below we share some context, as well as our slides.

Recent findings suggest that weâve been raising awareness of the importance of using memory-safe technology to build systems that are truly secure-by-design. We do this alongside our core business, which is to help companies to use Rust successfully. With the CRA standardization process well on its way, now is the perfect time to enhancement you on what weâve been doing and why.

#23889. Breaking: Accelerating development for massive Git repositories

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (310 w)

Breaking: Accelerating development for massive Git repositories

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (310 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Googleblog

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Android’s source code is massive – the Android 17 open source release has 1,084 Git repositories, 1.62 million files, and takes 300 GB for a built workspace.
  • Recent findings suggest that we built Another Build File Service (ABFS) to address these bottlenecks.
  • Today, we are excited to announce that ABFS is open source on GitHub.The impact of ABFS to Android is:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Android’s source code is massive – the Android 17 open source release has 1,084 Git repositories, 1.62 million files, and takes 300 GB for a built workspace. Additionally, in a typical Android source tree with hardware vendor code and first-party applications, the size increases by 2-3x. Traditionally, it took over 30 minutes to fetch Android Open Source Project (AOSP) source code and well over an hour to build on even highly capable developer workstations. As software development evolved over the last 2 years, modern coding harnesses and LLMs have accelerated the development of many projects. These tools are used today for Android operating system development, but the long sync and build times make them less efficient. Both human developers and agents need quick setup, parallel workspaces, and fast build-and-test iteration times.

Recent findings suggest that we built Another Build File Service (ABFS) to address these bottlenecks. ABFS is a full suite of software across a Linux kernel filesystem module, user-space daemons, and server-side infrastructure. ABFS uses content-addressability across the entire stack to lazy-load and cache source code, developer workspaces, intermediate build files, and build results.

Today, we are excited to announce that ABFS is open source on GitHub.The impact of ABFS to Android is:.

ABFS already powers parallel workflows for developers and agents in Android, but it is designed to scale to other massive Git-based projects.

In the Android build system, developers define build rules in Blueprint files (Android.bp), Soong compiles them into Ninja files, and Ninja executes the final build graph (see the Android build overview). Similar to the Make build tool, Ninja is timestamp-based. If a build step’s input file is newer than the existing output file, Ninja rebuilds the output file.

Analyzing the AOSP code for Android 17 demonstrates the sheer disk footprint and file count involved in a single checkout and build.

Microsoft's official Python agent framework hijacked to distribute malware

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (512 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In today's how-could-things-get-worse-for-Microsoft news, it seems someone's GitHub org admin creds have been compromised.
  • Microsoft’s official agent framework package hosted on PyPI has been hijacked and now installs info-stealing malware, multiple security research firms have discovered.
  • CEO Satya Nadella may be on stage trying to wow investors and customers at his manufacturer’s annual Ignite conference, but somewhere in the bowels of a building in Redmond his open source team is likely panicking at what appears to be unauthorized access to an administrator account on Microsoft’s Github organization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In today's how-could-things-get-worse-for-Microsoft news, it seems someone's GitHub org admin creds have been compromised.

Microsoft’s official agent framework package hosted on PyPI has been hijacked and now installs info-stealing malware, multiple security research firms have discovered.

CEO Satya Nadella may be on stage trying to wow investors and customers at his manufacturer’s annual Ignite conference, but somewhere in the bowels of a building in Redmond his open source team is likely panicking at what appears to be unauthorized access to an administrator account on Microsoft’s Github organization.

The problem package is Microsoft’s agent-framework, versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, researchers reported late yesterday and this morning. According to OX Security, version 1.26.1 was reverted to a safe version, but the attacker later uploaded 1.26.2 through Microsoft’s official PyPI publisher account, suggesting that, at least at the time of their report, the credentials hadn’t been locked down.

Safe to say, but if you find either version in your environment assume you have some account security work to do.

Microsoft agent-framework for Python boasts nearly 200,000 downloads a month and is used to build and deploy AI agents. As of those latest releases, it’s also being used to exfiltrate environment variables, credential files, and other secrets for Azure, Git, Docker, Hugging Face, and other sensitive developer services.

To make matters worse, the package never needs to be imported to do its dirty work – all it takes is a Python interpreter with the package installed to start up – the infected package still pulls the genuine 1.26.0 version of Microsoft’s agent-framework in order to keep itself running and looking legitimate, while in the background it gathers up credentials, encrypts them as a base64-encoded chunk of JSON, and sends them off to a webhook.site address hard coded into the malware.

Recent findings suggest that it appears from researcher accounts that this is made to act fast, as the malware isn’t persistent and only runs as long as the malicious version of the agent-framework remains in a site-packages directory. What it does do, however, is not just look for credentials in the environment: It actually starts calling for newly introduced ones and collecting them, too.

In particular, the malware requests fresh identity tokens from GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, and Azure itself, which are exfiltrated to the same webhook site.

“That combination of passive theft and active token requests makes it especially dangerous in cloud build environments, because even short-lived tokens are useful when they're exfiltrated right away,” noted researchers at OpenSourceMalware.

The agent-framework GitHub repo is offline as of writing. It’s been pointed out online that Microsoft’s repo for ONNX Runtime, an AI accelerator, is also offline. Other Microsoft repos remain available, and neither Microsoft nor security researchers have linked the ONNX repo’s pull to the malware campaign.

“We have made some repositories private while we investigate malicious content,” a Microsoft spokesperson told The Register. “Our priority is to protect customers and the broader ecosystem. We are working to review and will take further action as needed.”®.

Updated at 1805 with comment from Microsoft.

Robotaxi operator suspends driverless rides on high-speed roads nationwide after construction zone incursions and a run-in with patrol vehicles.

Waymo has suspended driverless freeway rides across the US after California regulators intervened over robotaxis entering construction zones and trying to bypass highway patrol vehicles.

California's DMV banned Waymo from offering driverless trips on its freeways on Wednesday, November 11. The same day, Waymo pulled the handbrake on its freeway services countrywide.

According to recent reports, the move affects all areas in which Waymo operates on freeways, including San Francisco, Los Angeles, Miami, Phoenix, and Austin. The Alphabet-owned organization has not indicated how long the suspension will last. Waymo claims freeway testing will continue with trained specialists behind the wheel.

Jonathan Groveman, spokesperson for the California DMV, told the Associated Press that the organization imposed the ban following two incidents involving Waymo's robotaxis that posed an "imminent hazard to public safety.".

On November 5, three of the manufacturer's driverless cars entered an active construction zone on US 101 near Burlingame, south of San Francisco.

The second incident occurred the following day, and in footage shared widely online, a Waymo vehicle can be seen trying to drive around highway patrol vehicles conducting a traffic break – a maneuver used to slow or stop traffic.

"The Department determined that Waymo's driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present," Groveman stated in the statement.

Groveman noted the DMV had already imposed restrictions and required corrective action following similar incidents on May 18.

Waymo subsequently recalled nearly 4,000 cars after some were caught ignoring road closure signs and cones designating construction zones in Phoenix and San Francisco.

A separate recall covered software affecting nearly 3,800 robotaxis over problems including slowing on high-speed roadways and driving into floodwater.

A Waymo spokesperson said that despite California's temporary ban, its robotaxis continue to operate on city streets across the US.

It has been revealed that "Safety is at the foundation of everything we do," they noted. "Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on US 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state.

"In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week.

"We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations.".

Recent findings suggest that other nuisances and hazards caused by errant Waymos include clogging traffic in thick fog, driving into telephone poles, and killing cats and dogs. ®.

To rank the world's biggest supercomputers, we're gonna need a bigger bench

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (577 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI has birthed some truly colossal supers, they just aren't on the Top500.
  • For decades, the Top500 list has tirelessly ranked the world’s biggest, most powerful, and often most unique publicly-known supercomputers.
  • With the rise of generative AI, the list no longer lives up to its name.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI has birthed some truly colossal supers, they just aren't on the Top500.

For decades, the Top500 list has tirelessly ranked the world’s biggest, most powerful, and often most unique publicly-known supercomputers.

With the rise of generative AI, the list no longer lives up to its name. China’s Lineshine supercomputer at 2.2 exaFLOPS of double precision compute in the High-Performance Linpack (HPL) benchmark may be the top system on the bi-annual ranking, but it’s nowhere near the biggest compute cluster in the world.

Superclusters like SpaceXAI’s Colossus, Meta’s Promethius, and OpenAI’s Stargate pack hundreds of thousands of GPUs, dwarfing anything on the Top500 today.

“These [companies] are not interested in submitting to the Top500,” Eth Zürich’s Torsten Hoefler said during his Supercomputing address this week.

It’s a dilemma that the founders of the Top500 ranking are now grappling with. And some believe it may be time for a rethink.

“What’s really needed for tracking that more appropriately is not just a different benchmark but also different methodology,” Top500 author Erich Strohmaier noted.

For a long time, Strohmaier explains, compute capability was roughly aligned with capacity.

Sources indicate that what happened in the last few years with AI is “capacity really pulled ahead of capability in terms of market size,” he mentioned. “We were and we still are very focused on capability.”.

By capability, Strohmaier is referring to the ability to run one code across the entire cluster.

“Our prime rule for benchmarking is, you have to benchmark your whole system with one code and you cannot just add two parts up to make up a number,” he explained.

According to recent reports, this is problematic for the large clusters major hyperscalers and cloud providers are now building to fuel the AI boom. “All those systems are capacity systems,” Strohmaier said.

In the age of AI, the top spot on the bi-annual ranking is whoever willing to run HPL instead of LLMs.

They’re not designed to run one piece of code but have instead been architected to run many, many smaller or medium-sized code instantiations, which may include training, fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and of course inference.

Because of this, Strohmaier indicates, it wouldn’t be reasonable to expect SpaceXAI to run something High-Performance Linpack (HPL) on a cluster like Colossus.

Industry observers note that but these clusters are still worth tracking. They'll just need a new benchmark better suited to judging the capability of these arrays while at the same time preventing operators from gaming the system.

What shape or form such a benchmark might take remains to be seen. Developing a latest benchmark or methodology is no small task, and changing the existing benchmarks isn’t ideal. ”If we do anything to the benchmark itself, we’re going to lose the historic trends, which is extremely valuable,” Hoefler remarked.

Allowing for lower precisions — HPL-MxP already does this to some extent — is one avenue for addressing the fact that these accelerators are increasingly trading FP64 performance for lower-accuracy floating-point data types like FP8 or FP4.

Another avenue is developing a separate AI benchmark. This would be immediately applicable to these clusters, but with the pace of change in model architecture, building such a benchmark is challenging.

Recent findings suggest that “The AI workloads change every two weeks, so if you pick something today, it’s going to be irrelevant in at most a year, and these benchmarks need to live for multiple decades,” Hoefler noted. ®.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (805 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theregister ↗ Open Full Page

AI found more critical bugs in another widely used technology running 225M websites

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (805 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hot on the heels of serious vulnerabilities in seemingly every other widely used software powering the entire internet, F5 today released emergency patches for 10 bugs in open source NGINX.
  • These include critical remote code execution flaws that let attackers hijack NGINX servers with HTTP/2 enabled, as well as the millions of websites running NGINX, to steal sensitive data and disrupt services.
  • “At this time, we have found no evidence of active exploitation of any of these vulnerabilities in the wild,” and F5 spokesperson told The Register.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Open source NGINX joins patchapalooza.

Hot on the heels of serious vulnerabilities in seemingly every other widely used software powering the entire internet, F5 today released emergency patches for 10 bugs in open source NGINX.

These include critical remote code execution flaws that let attackers hijack NGINX servers with HTTP/2 enabled, as well as the millions of websites running NGINX, to steal sensitive data and disrupt services.

“At this time, we have found no evidence of active exploitation of any of these vulnerabilities in the wild,” and F5 spokesperson told The Register. “We continue to monitor closely and will share updates via myF5 as we learn more.”.

It has been revealed that as with all of the other recently disclosed vulnerabilities in foundational technologies like PHP, Apache, and Java, these critical NGINX bugs were uncovered by researchers using AI. One of them has been hiding in the code for at least 10 years.

Tomer Schwartz, Wiz’s chief technology officer of exposure management and AppSec, helped find the bug, along with researchers from Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint working independently.

Schwartz told The Register that this wave of AI-discovered flaws “point to a fresh reality.”.

Industry observers note that “We need to treat every internet-connected system as potentially vulnerable,” Schwartz said. “AI has changed not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how rapidly longstanding risks can become real threats.”.

It has been revealed that NGINX is the world’s most widely used open source web server, handling HTTPS requests and routing incoming traffic to the right application or API. It powers about a third of all websites (around 225 million), and F5 maintains the open source version.

Sources indicate that on Wednesday, F5 published an out-of-band security notification that addressed 10 CVEs in open source NGINIX. If you run NGINX, update to 1.31.9 as soon as possible.

In a recent development, two of the vulns are especially serious as they allow a remote attacker to execute code on the NGINX server without authentication. These two, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, both received a critical, 9.2 CVSS rating, and CVE-2026-123007 affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server.

All of the security shops listed earlier independently found at least one of these two CVEs - most, if not all, with an AI assist - and reported them to F5.

It has been revealed that “Both vulnerabilities are memory-safety complications in how NGINX handles HTTP/2 traffic,” Schwartz and fellow Wiz kid Nir Ohfeld said in a Wednesday blog about the two bugs. “In CVE-2026-123633, a connection's memory is freed while a request still needs it, creating a use-after-free. In CVE-2026-123007, incorrect flow-control accounting leads to an invalid memory copy.”.

Rapid7’s team also published a proof-of-concept to demonstrate leveraging CVE-2026-123007 for unauthenticated remote code execution against a vulnerable linux/amd64 Docker image running nginx version 1.31.8.

Sources indicate that xint found three other NGINX flaws, plus a separate vulnerability in the Linux kernel that can be chained with any of the five NGINX vulnerabilities to gain root privileges on the host. The research team dubbed the six bugs “nginx2root.”.

The AI-powered offensive security firm also published videos demonstrating attacks using CVE-2026-123007 to execute commands as the NGINX worker inside a container, and then using the kernel vulnerability to escalate to root on the host. These attacks work on AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform, and bare-metal servers.

"While preparing for ZeroDay Cloud 2026, a Xint researcher found CVE-2026-123007," the company remarked in a Wednesday blog. "A few days later, a fully automated Xint scan found the other four without human guidance.".

All of these newly-disclosed CVEs point to a larger security issue - especially in light of Tuesday’s Java4Shell, found by AI-bug-hunting-outfit Calif, PHP2Shell (Calif was one of the firms that also used AI to find and weaponize these critical vulns in PHP), and a critical Apache flaw under active exploitation .

It has been revealed that “AI is also accelerating vulnerability discovery faster than existing infrastructure was designed to absorb,” Schwartz told us. “Even after a vendor ships a fix, security teams still face heavy manual work in terms of locating vulnerable versions and configurations, testing patches, deploying interim mitigations (such as disabling HTTP/2), and coordinating all of these rollouts.”.

It has been revealed that there is light at the end of the tunnel, he believes. “In the long run, AI-powered vulnerability research will harden foundational software.”.

But in the meantime, it’s a nightmare for security teams, vulnerability managers, and system administrators, who are drowning in the near-daily deluge of CVEs to patch before attackers find and exploit these vulnerabilities.

“Continued collaboration between security researchers, maintainers, and defenders is crucial to absorb the speed and scale of these disclosures,” Schwartz said.®.

#23877. Persistent incrementality in Rust

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 21m • 📚 Deep Dive (4150 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Github ↗ Open Full Page

Persistent incrementality in Rust

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4150 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There is this cool idea: incremental computations.
  • This concept usually works the best when you need to compute a lot of stuff, and there are a lot of inputs, and these inputs change independently with different degree of likelihood.
  • And if incremental computations concept applies well to compilers, it applies even better to LSP servers, because user makes edits in the editor much more often than they recompile code, and each keystroke must change the editor state in milliseconds (unless you go full vibe and don't need an IDE anymore, that is).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is this cool idea: incremental computations. The concept is simple, if you calculated something and then inputs change, it doesn't have to mean that you need to recompute everything. Most of your computations might still be valid, and quite often it is the case that you only need to redo a small chunk of changes.

This concept usually works the best when you need to compute a lot of stuff, and there are a lot of inputs, and these inputs change independently with different degree of likelihood. Probably, the most common example is incremental compilation, which makes the compilation reuse as much work as possible, making iterations during development much faster. The interesting part is "iterating": note that incremental compilation doesn't necessarily makes cold builds faster. The compiler performance might be roughly the same with and without incrementality, it's just repeated reuse of compiler artifacts becomes more efficient. Most likely you've heard of it. And if you did, you probably know that incremental compilation is not easy (1, 2, 3). But it's cool!

And if incremental computations concept applies well to compilers, it applies even better to LSP servers, because user makes edits in the editor much more often than they recompile code, and each keystroke must change the editor state in milliseconds (unless you go full vibe and don't need an IDE anymore, that is).

It could be somewhat related to the fact that rust-analyzer uses salsa as the central part of its architecture. Salsa is a library that makes incremental computations very convenient and efficient. There is one drawback, though. It is mainly designed to work in memory. And we'll touch on how it works in a bit.

For project like Rust Glancer that tries to keep the memory usage as low as possible, this doesn't work. Because of that, for a long time Rust Glancer didn't use incremental computations, and instead had a sophisticated network of persistent caches with sharding and targeted optimizations to make computations efficient. And it worked, for a while. But this approach doesn't scale very well: if you need to maintain a manually implemented custom cache format, optimize it, and tie computations to it, then the more efficiency you seek, the more complexity you get. Basically, the complexity is "quadratic": it grows as O(computations_complexity * cache_implementation_complexity) because both are interconnected (sorry, CS purists, for this crime).

In a recent development, so... Rust Glancer got to a point where it would really benefit from persistent incremental computations. And the search for it turned out to be really interesting, so in this blog post we'll be discussing how incremental computations can work in memory and how to make this approach work with persistency.

Before we start discussing how incremental computations work under the hood, let's see how it looks like.

Sources indicate that if you know how to use Salsa feel free to jump to the next section. If you're familiar with red-green algorithm and in-memory approach that Salsa uses, you can skip to where persistency starts.

Now, incremental computations are somewhat tricky to explain in a blog post, because the value of it requires an application to be somewhat significant. So we will need an example that is big enough to show the value of incrementality, but small enough to discuss here. It's a bit absurd, but I hope you can focus on the idea, not on the value of the snippet at hand.

Let's imagine that we're doing a weird text processor that would count the words in all the files in the directory, and decide whether this count is funny. And to make things more interesting, the files can include other files.

Sources indicate that how would that look if implemented naively? Something like that, most likely (well, let's ignore the IO):.

the output will also have no surprises:.

Now, let's try Salsa. It should let us make some computations reusable. Here's how it would look like:.

The code looks pretty similar! However, let's inspect the output.

The first call matches the naive example:.

But the second call is different!

Note: not only we did not call word_count(a), we did not call is_haha_number as well!

Salsa can see that file b changed, and it re-run word_count for it. But the output did not change, so all the previous computations are valid: nothing to be run.

The third output is interesting too:.

The word count in b changed, and a includes b, so we need to re-run all three queries. But the order is inversed! This is because we have a dependency graph internally, and we're walking through the dependency tree and re-execute changed queries from the "leaves" to the "root".

Recent findings suggest that we have changed b from 65 to 67 words, so a now has 69 words. Result is still true, but we did have to enhancement the computations. If we would've had another query that depended on is_haha_number, that's where validation would've stopped and all the queries above wouldn't need to run.

And the final output is interesting too:.

In a recent development, we have changed dependencies of a, so there is no b anymore. So we start with what we know: word_count for a. It now has a not-yet-tracked dependency on c, so we go to c after a. And the rest is the same.

In a recent development, so I hope you get the idea now: each query result is memorized, and if we discover that the output of this query did not change, we don't need to recompute the queries that depend on this input. Or rather, if all the queries that query X depends on did not change, then query X does not need to be recomputed.

In a recent development, and now imagine that you have 700 dependencies in your workspace. A single file changed in the topmost dependency. 699 dependencies can keep their result! Within a single crate, still only one file has changed, so the information about all the other files at least partially stays the same. We only need to redo the computations that actually matter.

And most importantly, we don't need to write any of this tracking code ourselves, Salsa gives it to us for free.

Well, it's really not trivial. If you want to have a more formal deep dive, I suggest the following reads:.

Industry observers note that imagine that each query, combined with its arguments, is an object. This object can have a bunch of metadata, stating whether it was already computed, when it happened, what was the output, and what's the object dependencies. Let's call this metadata a "memo".

Industry observers note that side note: why is "combined with its arguments?" vital? Because we cannot memoize is_haha_number, but we can memoize is_haha_number(420), so you can think of it as a mapping of (function, arguments) -> output.

And imagine that you have inputs: something that user provides, and this something can be explicitly requested by a query.

We might also say that the database has a revision, initially 1. When you change some input, the revision gets bumped to 2, and so on. This revision can be used as "when it happened" (or rather, "when it change last time") inside of the memo.

Now, we've provided our inputs and invoke a query. It has some associated code that can internally do two things:.

Recent findings suggest that if query requests an input, it should record that it depends on this input. So if input changes, it must be recomputed.

In a recent development, if query requests another query, we might check if the corresponding query has a memo with a computed value. If it has, we need to make sure that it is valid for the revision we're at. If it is: great! It can be reused, and we don't need to recompute it. Otherwise, we need to recursively go into this query. Obviously, we also record a dependency on this query.

During the execution, we'll collect all the inputs and all the dependency queries, and ultimately we'll finally compute the result of our query. And when we do, we can fill out the memo: record the revision and the output.

And... done! Next time you request an output, we will look at this query object memo. If inputs did not change, we can just hand out the result. If they changed, we go down the query line, and do the same thing. So naturally only the things that actually might have changed will be recomputed.

In a recent development, oh, but there is one more crucial detail here, that makes everything even better. If revision changed, it does not automatically mean that we need to recompute this query. We might recompute dependencies, and compare them to the old values. If all the outputs are the equal to the old ones (imagine that word_count(a) changed from 67 to 69, but is_haha_number still returns true true: the query that depends on is_haha_number might not get invalidated), we can just mark the current version as verified and return the old result. And it can matter a lot when the expensive query has a lot of cheap dependencies.

It has been revealed that obviously, it's an overly simplified explanation. In practice, there are many, many caveats, tricky parts, and optimizations that make the experience work well. But my job here is to give you an idea; if you've become interested in the topic, I'd recommend looking to Salsa source code, it's very interesting.

And Salsa is awesome! With one caveat. It works in memory only. Well, there is ongoing work on persistency there, but AFAIU it is mostly focused on storing the computations on filesystem so that they can be reloaded later (snapshot-like). It is very valuable, but we still have to store stuff in the memory. For the project like Rust Glancer we want to offload stuff to occupy less RAM.

And in practice, there are several projects that do implement various kinds of persistence:.

So there are solutions for this problem, but none of them seem to be "Salsa but everything is on the filesystem".

I guess then it would be fine to build one?

Industry observers note that as you probably guessed, I did build one. And I called it Ajika. And I'm very proud of myself for coming up with this name, yes.

In a recent development, the library is here, it uses stable Rust, and is generally a complete project (but I'm working on improvements!). The post, however, is not meant to promote it; obviously it's a very young library, and while so far it works really well for me, probably sticking to Salsa if it works for you is a safe choice. Not gonna sell it, do your own research :).

What I want to share is how Ajika works under the hood and what makes it different from Salsa.

But (spoiler) in general it's just two things:.

And we'll get to it and see how it works, but to make everything clear, we'll need to start from something very basic.

Here's the same program we had for Salsa, but migrated to Ajika:.

It looks pretty similar, with API changes mostly being a taste difference, and on a first run it has the same output.

However, the key part here is that we can add the following to the end:.

And print_result will just print False. Nothing will be executed after restart! Persistency in action!

On a serious note, the main difference is the focus. When you start working on a project like that, choosing your priority can influence the design a lot. And the choice made here is being persistent-first. While Ajika provides an in-memory backend, it's mostly meant for tests. The intended use case is to use your disk.

And it starts with a very basic question that in-memory database does not have: what happens if I restart the application?

If you already have a cache locally, many things can make this cache invalid:.

And similarly, given that we cache computations, it's basically an optimization. If cache gets corrupted or removed while the application is running, user would most likely prefer the cache to be discarded and computations to be repeated one more time, rather than the app crashing with "cache is not available, what do I do???".

As a result, the cache must be throw-away. Both Ajika and application supply schema versions to identify the revision, and if the stored cache doesn't match it, we reset it. If cache gets corrupted, Ajika will attempt recovery over hard failing, even if it means re-computing data from scratch.

Recent findings suggest that the next most noticeable change is that most operations are fallible. Since IO is the basic property for us, and IO can fail, we need to think about it. Failed operation does not mean that cache is corrupted, but it does mean that the current query might not be computed. Typically, it can be retried, though.

Finally, the persistence is, unfortunately, a leaky abstraction. You cannot really hide from the fact that the data is outside of memory, because everything you persist must be serializable. And your interim query data might be reusable but not serializable (imagine an AST that borrows the source text: making it own the data likely will be worse), so some of the queries might be transient: we compute them once and retain while the current operation runs, but drop instead of persisting once operation ends.

Industry observers note that together, these properties start working rather nicely, however: your application has to be aware of persistence, but not in an annoying way. If something fails, you know about it, but you don't have to worry, since Ajika will repair things for you. If something is not serializable and it doesn't matter, it can be turned into a transient query. If you don't want your tests to rely on persistence, you just plug a memory backend in.

So let's take a look at how it works under the hood.

LLM usage disclaimer: The library discussed here is developed with use of LLMs, same as Rust Glancer. Hopefully, from this post it is evident that I'm using LLMs as a tool and have full control. It's not vibe coded.

There are three parts to Ajika: ajika itself, ajika_macros, and ajika_storage.

According to recent reports, we'll take a look at ajika and then at ajika_storage. Macros are left as an exercise to a reader, but they're generally pretty straightforward.

Ajika itself is very easy, just check out this diagram:.

Industry observers note that ...just kidding. But we'll fix that very swiftly.

The core idea is very similar to Salsa:.

Still, I think it might be useful to skim through the high level details.

Sources indicate that side note: Ajika has its own book which does a much deeper dive on many concepts than this blog post. I'll be referring to it in some places. The con is that, unlike this handwritten blog post, the text there is mostly LLM-generated, and even if I did a lot of polishing, it indicates. Eventually I'll do a full manual rewrite, but for now I figured that human-filtered-llm-guide is better than no guide at all.

Recent findings suggest that database is an entrypoint. You choose either an in-memory or persistent backend, supply Inputs and then run your operation.

It has been revealed that queries are the actual logic we want to execute. They are defined via ajika::query macro and in general pretty straightforward. More details on queries themselves are in the book, and we'll look at how queries are executed and what this Db object is a bit later in this post.

Inputs are somewhat more interesting. Your input type is defined through the ajika::input procedural macro, which would do some wrapping for you. And your input structure is basically a mapping: you specify a key, for example, String, and then you can use database to get an input value (or lack thereof) for whatever key you have, be it "foo" or even "bar". If you have a singleton value, like a config, you can use () as a key. Again, more on inputs can be found in the book, also might check out lazy inputs.

Outputs are probably the first part of the system that gets interesting because of persistence.

The outputs need to be stored on the filesystem, so they need to be serializable. For outputs that you don't want to serialize, you can use transient queries which will keep the value in memory only for the duration of a single operation. But even then, there is a problem: how substantial of an output do you want?

In a recent development, if you will have a 1000 very granular queries, it will mean that we need a lot of filesystem roundtrips. If you will have just a bunch of queries that compute a ton of data, you will need to deserialize a major value just to look at the part of it.

In a recent development, thus, outputs offer a solution that lies in between: you can choose to return a value directly, or return a handle to this value. If you return a handle, query can use this handle to retrieve the value from the database on demand. Directly returned values are fully deserialized. This offers you a nice granularity option: you have a query that encapsulates a meaningful unit of work, but it returns you an object that contains handles for particular results. Handle is cheap to obtain and deserialize, and you only query the data you actually need. Doing is most convenient through an ajika::output macro.

As usual, more details on how to use outputs are in the book.

And now we're getting to the interesting stuff.

To perform a single run we need three things:.

And there are two related concepts that make things work:.

Record contains information like values metadata for a query and dependencies for it (note: values are stored separately!). Thus, Memos are released on the end of the run and then later can be reconstructed from Record on demand.

In a recent development, and this is an key bit: released memos don't occupy RAM. This is the key part of Ajika! During the query execution, the values can be loaded, but if you don't run any operations, you don't have to pay for it. Outputs will just wait for you inside of the filesystem! Moreover, whenever we run queries, we only load what we need, not everything.

Each time a query logic actually runs (either from run or from another query), a new Db with a new Frame is created, sharing the same Operation.

When you ask Db to execute a query, here's a typical (overly simplified) workflow:.

And if during execution query receives another query result, it records it in its own Frame for reuse.

Obviously, there is a lot of bookkeeping, support for parallelism, and other things that make it complex, but in general the algorithm is pretty straightforward.

Once the operation finishes, we need to actually apply the changes. run works as a transaction, so everything that was done inside is immediately visible, but after run depending on whether run failed or succeeded, the results will either be discarded or persisted.

Checkpoint write is generally pretty straightforward:.

So checkpoint on the Ajika level is pretty straightforward. What is more interesting is how Ajika storage works in general.

Finally, we've got to the persistence!

Industry observers note that it's probably the most interesting part of Ajika. How do we store data in a way that is efficient?

According to recent reports, the first version of Ajika used redb for everything. It worked, but it did not work very well. Since we don't really have a "database" per se, and more of a storage for many blobs, redb added too much overhead. However, it provides much needed features like transactions.

So, Ajika uses redb as a metadata storage: it's an index which mostly contains pointers to the values.

In a recent development, the values are written in "pack files": basically, just binary files to which we can append new entries. And inside of redb we can just store a pointer: (file name, offset). Each stored entry has a header with information such as length and compression algorithm. For efficiency, if the value is very small, we can keep it inline inside of redb instead of writing it to a file.

Sources indicate that if you want to access a value, you will go to redb, check the corresponding key, and then either read it inline or read the specified pack at the specified access. Pretty simple.

Obviously, there is some more data stored there (we'll talk about identities soon, briefly), but in general it's a pretty "stupid" (hopefully in a good way) format of data storage.

However, there is one caveat: if we do it naively, the storage can grow without limits. Packs can end up with very low utilization factor, consisting mostly of "dead" values, and some of them might not be observable at all. So the storage supports maintenance: whenever you do an operation, Ajika might do a sweep that would re-pack values and revision pointers, and at the end of operation Ajika will try to signal to the storage which values can be removed now. There are a few knobs you can tune here: you can specify the retention limit time (so that the very old and unused queries are cleaned up) or target storage size (which acts as a soft limit, and will affect the cleanup policy).

But ultimately, this design makes value storing and retrieval pretty efficient, and it integrates with the overall Ajika design very well.

OK, we're almost done, I promise! The last small bit: interning.

Interning values is an optimization that gives you a way to turn any object into an ID. Imagine that you have file paths. They can work as IDs, but it would probably be more efficient if you used FileId(0) / FileId(1) instead. Not only in terms of performance, but often also in terms of memory: you'd rather not have a ton of strings in memory if you don't really need them. Sometimes, interning strings on its own can be a very useful memory optimization, which is why crates like string_cache exist.

But for us, having IDs for objects can be valuable in general, because your computations results might often be linked to some other objects, and it's useful to be able to use IDs for that.

Salsa supports interning for that purpose, and Ajika does it too. However, there is one caveat for Ajika: what happens if we have our IDs allocated, they become a part of the cache, and then we restart the application?

To avoid this problem, IDs in Ajika are persisted in addition to being stored in memory, and on restart this interner state is reloaded.

Industry observers note that ajika development itself was an experiment: I did not create it in vacuum, I was actually porting Rust Glancer to it at the same time. And the experiment was very successful. I was able to remove a lot of complexity from Rust Glancer, and Ajika unblocked many optimizations that were not realistic with hand-rolled caches (starting with lazy body evaluation).

At the end of the experiment, Rust Glancer got performance comparable to rust-analyzer (sometimes even better!). Ajika is obviously slower than salsa, but inside of IDE the difference between 1 and 30ms is negligible, both feel instant. What matters is the low RAM usage: Rust Glancer still stays well under 100MB RAM idle on pretty major projects.

Remark: exact comparison between two will be posted in the release notes for Rust Glancer 0.5.0, so stay tuned.

Recent findings suggest that as the experiments go, the branch of Rust Glancer where all of that happened is in a half-assembled state, and it's way too rushed and "prototyped" to just merge it, so I'm doing a clean reimplementation using extracted (and published) version of Ajika. It will take a while, but I'm very excited: Rust Glancer without compromises that feels instant and does not eat memory.

Thanks for reading, it turned out to be a long post. A lot of effort went into it, so I hope that it was useful, at least somewhat.

My next goal is to prepare an Ajika-based release of Rust Glancer, and after that I have a lot of ideas on how to make Ajika even faster/better/stronger. Who knows, maybe it will eventually grow into a product of its own, not merely a part of Rust Glancer ecosystem.

As usual, the best way to support if you like the project is to check out Rust Glancer, star Ajika (but only if you like it!) and/or follow me on twitter.

In a recent development, the $30,000 average wedding figure you see everywhere is misleading. That number is skewed upward by luxury weddings in expensive metros like Upcoming York, San Francisco, and Los Angeles. The national median — the number where half of weddings cost more and half cost less — sits closer to $10,000 to $15,000. That distinction matters because it means a beautiful, memorable wedding is absolutely possible without spending five figures you do not have.

The FI perspective adds another layer: every dollar spent on a wedding is a dollar that cannot compound for decades. A $30,000 wedding invested for 30 years at a 7% average annual return grows to roughly $228,000. That does not mean you should elope in a courthouse (unless you want to), but it does mean you should spend intentionally on the categories that matter most to you and cut ruthlessly everywhere else.

Here is where the typical wedding dollar goes:.

The biggest takeaway from this table: venue and catering are 60-70% of the total. If you can reduce those two categories, you change the entire math.

According to recent reports, ready to unlock a world of free travel? Start with the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card.

$95 annual fee | Earn 75,000 bonus points.

Side hustlers! With the Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card you can earn free travel from your business expenses.

In a recent development, chooseFI has partnered with CardRatings for our coverage of credit card products. ChooseFI and CardRatings may receive a commission from card issuers.

Not all wedding spending creates equal memories. Research consistently shows that couples remember three things most vividly years later: the ceremony itself, the food and drinks, and the photographs. Almost nobody remembers the chair covers, the napkin folds, or the custom monogram on the cocktail napkins.

That insight creates a clear FI-aligned strategy: splurge on what creates lasting memories (photographer, food, music) and minimize everything else.

In a recent development, the golden rule of wedding budgeting: if you cannot remember whether a detail was present at the last three weddings you attended, your guests will not notice either. Cut it without guilt.

According to recent reports, the biggest financial mistake couples make is not setting a firm budget before visiting any vendors. Venues and vendors are skilled at upselling, and without a hard number in mind, costs spiral quickly. Start with a number you can pay in cash — wedding debt is one of the worst ways to begin a marriage and a direct threat to your FI timeline.

Follow this payment timeline to manage cash flow without credit card debt:.

Sources indicate that A practical savings strategy: divide your total budget by the number of months until the wedding and automate that transfer to a dedicated savings account. If your budget is $15,000 and your wedding is 15 months away, that is $1,000 per month. Treat it like any other savings goal on your FI path — automate, do not touch, and watch it grow.

For couples on the FI path, consider this reframe: every dollar you shave from the wedding budget is a dollar that starts compounding immediately. Cutting $5,000 from a $20,000 wedding and investing that savings at 7% for 25 years creates roughly $27,000 in future wealth. You can have a wonderful wedding and build wealth simultaneously — but only if you strategy intentionally from the start.

Curious about your financial independence number?
