Before finalizing your wedding budget, run the compound interest math on any amount you are considering spending. A $30,000 wedding invested at 7% for 30 years becomes roughly $228,000. A $15,000 wedding invested at 7% for 30 years becomes roughly $114,000. This is not an argument against celebrating — it is an argument for spending intentionally on what matters to you and cutting everything else. The couple who spends $15,000 on a joyful celebration and invests the other $15,000 gets both the wedding and a significant head start on financial independence.

Sources indicate that there is no single right number, but the median US wedding cost of $10,000 to $15,000 is achievable for most couples without going into debt. Focus on what matters most to you and cut everything else. A $10,000 wedding with great food, a good photographer, and people you love is better than a $30,000 wedding that starts your marriage with financial stress.

No. Wedding debt is one of the worst forms of consumer debt because it funds a single day with no residual asset value. The average couple who finances their wedding on credit cards at 22% interest turns a $20,000 wedding into a $28,000 expense over 4 years of payments. Set a cash budget and stick to it.

Any contribution from parents is a gift, not an obligation. If parents offer to contribute, have an honest conversation about the total amount and whether it comes with expectations about the guest list or style. Budget based on what you can afford independently, then treat any parental contribution as a bonus.

Sources indicate that yes. Friday and Sunday weddings typically cost 20-30% less than Saturday weddings for the same venue and vendors. Some venues offer discounts of 40% or more for weekday weddings (Monday through Thursday). Off-season months like January, February, March, and November also offer significant savings.

Tips for vendors (plan 15-20% for catering staff, bartenders, and drivers), alterations for wedding attire ($200-$500), marriage license fees ($30-$100), and overtime charges if the reception runs past the contracted time. Build a 10% contingency buffer into your total budget for these surprises.

Set your budget privately as a couple before discussing with family. Present it as a decision, not a discussion. If family members want upgrades, they are welcome to fund those specific additions. Protect your financial foundation — the marriage matters more than the wedding, and starting debt-free sets up your partnership for success.

A meaningful wedding does not require $30,000 or any specific dollar amount. Set a cash budget based on what you can afford without debt, allocate spending toward what creates lasting memories (food, photography, people), and cut everything else. Every dollar you save on the wedding is a dollar that starts compounding toward your financial independence. The couples with the strongest financial futures are the ones who celebrate joyfully within their means and invest the difference.

We get it, Dario - you don't want people calling out sick to play.

Well, it’s official: Anthropic will become the first publicly-traded frontier AI lab in history come the opening of markets on Thursday.

The company kicked off its IPO roadshow last week, announcing looks to offer 825 million shares with an IPO price between $70 and $78 a share when sales begin Thursday.

The manufacturer's most recent SEC filing cites that price range but allows for the possibility of a higher price, which should be determined Wednesday night.

In a recent development, late on Wednesday, Bloomberg reported that Anthropic would price at $83, citing people familiar. Whatever the case, Anthropic is likely to be valued at more than $1 trillion.

Anthropic’s debutante ball has been on the horizon for a while, and documents leaked in late September made it all the more inevitable as the firm’s finances revved up and it sought to capture the momentum of its best quarter to date before things start to tail off.

The manufacturer revised its IPO documents on November 2, warning that the 12x growth it was touting was unlikely to continue in the long term due to compute infrastructure investments to the tune of nearly $900 billion it was on the hook for over the next few years.

"In the nine months ended September 30, 2026, our revenue was $33.2 billion, representing a year-over-year growth rate of 1,206%," the revised prospectus reads. "We do not expect our revenue will continue to grow at comparable rates, and we cannot assure you that it will continue to grow at all.".

It’s possible, in other words, that Anthropic may never be a money maker despite the hype and its position as the first mover. The IPO prospectus is short on answers to critical questions and leaves a lot unanswered - like, for example, whether it’s going to actually be able to pay its bills.

"Our ability to meet the substantial and growing financial obligations of these requirements to secure compute depends on our ability to generate significant revenue growth," the updated prospectus admits.

Investors don’t seem to care right now, though.

Sources indicate that anthropic already has compute commitments amounting to roughly $70.7 billion in the next 12 months. That’s just shy of its $81 billion run-rate as of October 31.

Expect more hot air to be injected tomorrow, adding additional surface tension and the possibility of even more losses if, and when, this monster pops. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that put a web server online and everyone starts trying to hack it. Why? A basic rule of economics. Short supply, significant demand - there arenât enough web servers for everyone. Letâs run a web server for every human on the planet, all 8 billion of them. I couldnât get funding, so weâre bootstrapping. The goal is to run 15 million web servers on one VM with 10GB of RAM and 1 CPU core. If we succeed, Iâll find some RAM from old microwaves around the house and weâll scale it up so everyone can have their own web server. Demand will drop to zero and cybersecurity will be solved once and for all.Web serverInstead of vibe coding it all, letâs use an ancient technique called learning. First of all, what is a web server? There are a few essential syscalls.listen - syscall, asks kernel to listen for connections on a socketaccept - syscall, accepts a connection on a socketrecv - receives data from a socketsend - sends dataclose - closesWhat is a syscall? A function that is executed by the OS kernel. Whatever fancy language or library you use for HTTP, it all comes down to those syscalls (well, yes, but actually no). Letâs use C to make it all explicit. We start listening, then read from the socket in a loop and always reply with OK.int main(void) { // We use port 0 which makes OS return any available port int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); if (listen(server, 128) < 0) return 1; const char reply[] = "HTTP/1.0 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 2\r\n\r\nOK"; for (int client; (client = accept(server, NULL, NULL)) >= 0;) { if (recv(client, NULL, 4096, MSG_TRUNC) > 0) send(client, reply, sizeof reply - 1, MSG_NOSIGNAL); close(client); } }It couldnât be simpler: listen on a socket, accept a connection, read the data, send a reply, close the client connection, and repeat. It gives us around 65k RPS. Now that weâve learned everything, letâs finish the article and call it a day:$ for i in $(seq 1 15_000_000); do echo $i; ./server &; done ... ... 28232 program exited with error 1Hm, why did listen fail? Ah, weâve run out of ports! Weâre using port=0, so the kernel picks an available port from ip_local_port_range.$ sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 32768 60999Why are so many ports skipped? Historically, port 0 was created for outbound connections. When you call connect('example.com', 80), Linux connects to the remote server (the sending part) and then allocates a random port on the host from ip_local_port_range to receive data (the receiving part). There are a few reasons the default range is small.Port 0 is special. You cannot listen on it (actually, you can - https://acid.vegas/blog/the-port-that-does-not-exist/).Ports 1-1024 require root.Ports 1024-32768 are skipped to keep dynamically allocated ports from conflicting with existing apps. You donât want to call connect('example.com') and end up allocating port 3306 to receive incoming data. mysql cannot start because you have example.com open in your Firefox would make for a confusing UX.Ports 60999 - 65535 are excluded for historical reasons dating back to IP Masquerading.Nothing prevents us from overriding the range and using 1-65535, but thatâs still a bit short of 15 million. A UDP server and a TCP server can use the same port, so we can double that to 128k. We could run a proxy in front to forward requests to the right process (virtual hosting, yay), but these are all ancient techniques - in the AI era, whenever you have a software problem, you just throw money at the hardware. Letâs simply connect 15M/32k=450 new network cards to the server.The 65k limit comes from the TCP standard. A port is a u16, so even if we hack the kernel with find '*.c' -exec sed -i 's/u16/u32/' \; to support bigger port numbers, normal clients still wouldnât be able to connect. Each listening server is identified by a (protocol, IP, port) tuple. That explains how we can use the same port for UDP and TCP. It also means we can use a bunch of different IPs for our web servers. If we connect 450 network cards to the server, weâll get 450 unique IP addresses and be able to listen on 15 million unique addresses!UPD. Iâve heard from readers that the network card is the ONLY hardware component that didnât get 100 times more expensive in the last year. Canât we avoid ruining that too and solve this in software?Letâs use a beautiful technology called AnyIP, which lets us listen on a whole subnet. Many VPS and dedicated server providers routinely give you a whole TCPv6 subnet. We can simply run sudo ip -6 route add local 2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 dev lo to get 18 quintillion addresses (plus or minus one) to listen on. You can do the same for IPv4 - acquiring a subnet with 15M addresses would cost around $250 million, so adjust the command for your environment. Weâll change our server to pick the nth IP from our range:// Read IP index from CLI, shift base IP by it int i = read_cli_param(argv[1]); const uint32_t base_ip = 0x0a400001; // ex. 10.64.0.1 addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(first_ip + i); // shift, ex. 10.64.0.2And now we can finally finish the article.$ for i in $(seq 1 15_000_000); do echo $i; ./server $i &; done ... ... Out of memoryHm, one server consumes 1.5MB of RAM, so running that many would takeâ¦ 20TB of RAM, which is a few bytes more than our 10GB budget.RuntimeBy pure coincidence (what are the odds?), I explained in Running 10 million Codex CLIs on one server - LFI processes why running millions of processes creates too much overhead. The answer is to run them all in one process inside a custom runtime, much as V8 can run millions of guests in a single process. In Userland Linux scheduler in Rust, I revealed how to build a specialised userland scheduler and switch between tasks with the absolute minimum amount of RAM per task.TLDR: Weâre using LFI for sandboxing. It gives us memory isolation and replaces all syscalls with calls to our host handler, which lets us implement I/O however we like. To schedule multiple guests, we load them all into our main processâs memory and make the CPU constantly switch between guests - we become our own micro OS.Since we need to save every byte and CPU cycle we can, weâre doomed to build another specialised runtime. Letâs get started. How much is 10GB divided by 15M, exactly?Ten Great Britains divided by 15 million gives around half of kilo britain. Not much. If we run all our guests in our runtime, our custom scheduler needs to switch between them. Whatâs the absolute minimum state we need to preserve for each guest? We can ignore server initialisation and assume switches only happen within the main loop. Letâs take another look at the loop.for (int client; (client = accept(server, NULL, NULL)) >= 0;) { if (recv(client, NULL, 4096, MSG_TRUNC) > 0) send(client, reply, sizeof reply - 1, MSG_NOSIGNAL); close(client); }This code has only two state variables, server and client. Both are simple file descriptors. If our scheduler had to suspend a guest at any syscall point in this loop, weâd need to save the following state:struct Context { pc: u64, // Instruction address to return to fd_server: i32, // server file descriptor fd_client: i32, // client file descriptor }We only need 16 bytes per guest, so to run 15M guests in our runtime and be able to suspend them and switch between them, we would need 220MB of RAM. Weâre playing it safe here - we donât need the full u64 or i32, and with bit packing, we could probably get down to 8 bytes per guest. What else do we need?$ codex "How much TCP connection takes?" Idle connection takes zero, while active connection consumes around 5kbHereâs what we get if we assume that only 1M of connections are active at any given moment.14M idle connections - 0 bytesScheduling state for 15M guests - 220MB1M active connections at 5kb each = 5GBOnly half of our RAM budget, yay! I donât often exceed my own expectations. Letâs validate it:int main(void) { // Run 14M of idle connections - just listen and do nothing // SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY! for (int i = 0; i < 14_000_000; i++) { int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); listen(server, 1) } }$ ./run_15m_idle_servers Out Of Memory $ dmesg | tail -n 1 'SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY' - what are you, stupid?Looks like the kernel still has some leftover comments from Linus. Iâm not stupid, but I have to admit I was below average here. While an LLM is a significant boost for learning, itâs too easy to accept its answers without thinking critically and feel ashamed later on. But hey, embarrassment is a cost of entry - letâs dive into networking in the kernel.Networking in the kernelRemember when I said that our simple server uses only 5 syscalls? I missed one that was right in front of me. Let me highlight it:int main(void) { for (int i = 0; i < 10_000_000; ++i) { socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); } }That code will OOM in a 10GB VM. The socket syscall allocates around 3300 bytes, whether the socket is active, listening, or doing nothing. Linux was clearly written at a time when RAM was big and cheap, sigh. Letâs ask AI where all the memory goes:StructsizeofDescriptionstruct tcp_sock2240BTCP state, queues, timers, sequence numbers, congestion control, retransmit and delivery bookkeepingstruct socket_alloc768BA 128-byte struct socket with an embedded wait queue, plus a 608-byte sockfs inode and paddingstruct file184BOpen-file operations, flags, credentials, reference count, and the pointer back to the socketstruct dentry192BThe sockfs pseudo-name, inode pointer, and VFS lookup and lifetime bookkeepingTotal3384BPotato-potato, TLDR, the kernel uses that memory for many things. I was hoping to see some buffer: [u8; 3300], but it doesnât look like we can optimise much without rewriting half the kernel. Itâs Sunday and I have few tokens left, so weâll have to think instead - how can we bypass the kernel?What are our options? Engineering wisdom tells us that if we canât solve a task, weâre working at the wrong level of abstraction. Hmâ¦ level, level, layer. Wait a minute! We started with HTTP and went level down to TCP/IP. That reminds me of something! Mom! Mom! Where are all my university books? I NEED THEM NOW!The OSI model isâ¦ umâ¦ something I studied at university. Yeah, thatâs a good definition. We started with our app and HTTP at the application layer, then went down to TCP/IP at the transport layer. There are three more layers below that. Can we go lower to get full control and solve our RAM problem? Oh yes, thatâs exactly what operating at the network and data link layers lets us do. What about going to the lowest?Clear.Each layer wraps the data from the layer above it.HTTPApplication Â· L7TCPTransport Â· L4IPNetwork Â· L3EthernetData link Â· L2PhysicalL1GET /PayloadPayloadPayloadâ¡ð©Src port50123Dst port80Seq1001ACK7001FlagsACKSrc IP192.0.2.10Dst IP198.51.100.20TTL64Protocol6 (TCP)Dst MAC02:00:00:00:00:feSrc MAC02:00:00:00:00:01EtherType0x0800 (IPv4)FCSCRCTCP/IP is stateful, but everything below is stateless. None of the lower layers know or care about the payload, so nothing prevents us from sending new IP packets or even Ethernet frames with our own handcrafted binary data. We just need to reimplement the TCP and IP stack ourselves. Are there any examples? Embedded folks have solved this millions of times. The most extreme case is Adam Dunkelsâs Miniweb - it combines a custom TCP/IP implementation and an HTTP server that together need only 28 bytes (B-Y-T-E-S) to work.There are plenty of less extreme, more mature implementations, though:gVisor essentially reimplements the whole OS, including the network stackSeastar is a whole runtime with its own network stack from the amazing team behind ScyllaDBlwIP is a popular C implementation of TCP/IPF-Stack uses FreeBSDâs TCP/IP stackGo, C++, and C are nice languages (well, kinda), but theyâre nowhere near as nice as our beloved Rust. So weâll take smoltcp, which is purely amazing:>smoltcp is a standalone, event-driven TCP/IP stack that is designed for >bare-metal, real-time systems. smoltcp does not need heap allocation at allSo, cargo add smoltcp and call it a day? Not so fast. smoltcp is essentially a smart parser and canât do I/O. How does it communicate with your network card? There are 3 ways:TUN is a virtual network interface that the kernel provides. It operates at the IP layerTAP is another kernel feature that operates one layer down, at the Ethernet layerDPDK lets you communicate directly with the network card using Ethernet frames, completely bypassing the kernelsmoltcp is kind enough to provide the first two options out of the box, and theyâre easy to use.fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let (mut device, config) = match std::env::args().nth(1).as_deref() { Some("tun") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltun", Medium::Ip)?, Config::new(HardwareAddress::Ip), ), Some("tap") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltap", Medium::Ethernet)?, Config::new(EthernetAddress([0x02, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2]).into()), ), _ => panic!("pass tun or tap"), }; let mut iface = Interface::new(config, &mut device, Instant::now()); iface.update_ip_addrs(|addrs| { addrs.push(IpCidr::new(IpAddress::v4(192, 0, 2, 2), 24)).unwrap(); }); let mut sockets = SocketSet::new(Vec::new()); // Main network loop loop { let now = Instant::now(); iface.poll(now, &mut device, &mut sockets); wait(device.as_raw_fd(), iface.poll_delay(now, &sockets))?; } }But what about the third option, DPDK? When you care about latency A LOT, every syscall is a bloody wound. The syscall itself might take 500ns, and copying data from the kernel to userspace might take another 1000ns, depending on the buffer size. That sounds tiny, but for perspective: itâs common for high-frequency trading firms to saturate 400Gbs network interfaces. That means processing up to 600 million packets per second, or roughly 1.7ns per packet.DPDK lets your program communicate directly with the hardware network card using Ethernet frames, bypassing the entire kernel network stack. You read from and write to a memory-mapped buffer without syscalls: when you want to send data - you simply write it to the buffer and youâre done; when you want to read what youâve received - itâs already there.Thereâs another, less obvious advantage - what happens when a new packet arrives at your network device? An interrupt fires, the CPU core stops executing your app, switches to the kernel, processes the interrupt, and then goes back to your app. Now imagine A LOT of incoming packets, so many that your app gets interrupted all the time. It has a beautiful name, livelock, and I guess debugging it in production is its own level of hell. DPDK lets you avoid all that, but thereâs a cost.DPDK works by running a busy loop that takes up an entire CPU core. It constantly moves data between memory and the network device in both directions, kinda like that:loop { send_from_app_memory_to_network(); receive_from_network_to_app_memory(); }Thereâs another, less obvious nuance. DPDK requires exclusive access to the network device because it uses a driver that operates at the hardware level - two drivers canât work with the same device at the same time. Once you enable the DPDK driver for your network interfaceâ¦ it disappears from the OS. Yep, nothing in ifconfig, if you enable it over SSH, youâll lose SSH access too. I can imagine a lot of funny stories coming out of that.Actually, thereâs a fourth option now - Linux now has an AF_XDP subsystem that does something similar. It lets you bypass the kernel network stack and uses the same idea of memory-mapped buffers to get zero-copy I/O in your app. The kernel still owns the device and interrupts still happen as usual. When a new packet arrives, the kernel runs a simple eBPF filter that decides whether to send it directly to the userspace buffer, bypassing the network stack, or process it normally. That means SSH still works. AF_XDP supports an alternative mode, SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL, which is even closer to DPDK: you get a busy loop with no interrupts at the cost of a CPU core. DPDK still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but AF_XDP is very close (and simply easier to manage).To support DPDK and AF_XDP in smoltcp, we only need to implement the Device trait with 3 methods if we want full control. Alternatively, we can use the existing crates rust-dpdk-net for DPDK and xsk-rs for AF_XDP to help us.Now the final flow is:The runtime loads 15M web server guests into its memoryThe runtime scheduler starts executing guests one by oneGuest syscalls are intercepted by the runtime and replaced by the smoltcp network stack and its adaptersAll 15M guests start listening, each on its own addressThe scheduler polls for incoming data from smoltcp adapters, wakes up a guest, makes it process the data, and switches to the nextAnd now we can finally finish the article. The kernel network stack uses up all the RAM at around 2.5M web servers, and RPS drops as we run more servers. With smoltcp, RAM usage grows slower - 620 bytes per idle server and around a kilobyte for an active one, we got to 16M of servers. DPDK is clearly the beast in this benchmark, with AF_XDP just behind it:Why is this so exciting? It means that by moving the network stack to userland, you can get full control on RAM usage and improve performance. And with custom runtime, you can simply run guests faster.Simply is a bit of a stretch - building a proof of concept is easy. Building a compatible Linux runtime and reimplementing all the syscalls with 100% POSIX compatibility take a bit more thought. And another article.Referenceshttps://github.com/artemyarulin/AI10M/tree/main/poc/ten-million-webservers sourcehttps://medium.com/beyond-localhost/how-we-handle-15M-websocket-connections-on-a-single-server-8917c3952f59 great overview of DPDKhttps://doc.dpdk.org/guides/index.html DPDK main documentation sitehttps://docs.kernel.org/networking/af_xdp.html AF_XDP overview.

What about going to the lowest?Clear.Each layer wraps the data from the layer above it.HTTPApplication Â· L7TCPTransport Â· L4IPNetwork Â· L3EthernetData link Â· L2PhysicalL1GET /PayloadPayloadPayloadâ¡ð©Src port50123Dst port80Seq1001ACK7001FlagsACKSrc IP192.0.2.10Dst IP198.51.100.20TTL64Protocol6 (TCP)Dst MAC02:00:00:00:00:feSrc MAC02:00:00:00:00:01EtherType0x0800 (IPv4)FCSCRCTCP/IP is stateful, but everything below is stateless. None of the lower layers know or care about the payload, so nothing prevents us from sending new IP packets or even Ethernet frames with our own handcrafted binary data. We just need to reimplement the TCP and IP stack ourselves. Are there any examples? Embedded folks have solved this millions of times. The most extreme case is Adam Dunkelsâs Miniweb - it combines a custom TCP/IP implementation and an HTTP server that together need only 28 bytes (B-Y-T-E-S) to work.There are plenty of less extreme, more mature implementations, though:gVisor essentially reimplements the whole OS, including the network stackSeastar is a whole runtime with its own network stack from the amazing team behind ScyllaDBlwIP is a popular C implementation of TCP/IPF-Stack uses FreeBSDâs TCP/IP stackGo, C++, and C are nice languages (well, kinda), but theyâre nowhere near as nice as our beloved Rust. So weâll take smoltcp, which is purely amazing:>smoltcp is a standalone, event-driven TCP/IP stack that is designed for >bare-metal, real-time systems. smoltcp does not need heap allocation at allSo, cargo add smoltcp and call it a day? Not so fast. smoltcp is essentially a smart parser and canât do I/O. How does it communicate with your network card? There are 3 ways:TUN is a virtual network interface that the kernel provides. It operates at the IP layerTAP is another kernel feature that operates one layer down, at the Ethernet layerDPDK lets you communicate directly with the network card using Ethernet frames, completely bypassing the kernelsmoltcp is kind enough to provide the first two options out of the box, and theyâre easy to use.fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let (mut device, config) = match std::env::args().nth(1).as_deref() { Some("tun") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltun", Medium::Ip)?, Config::new(HardwareAddress::Ip), ), Some("tap") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltap", Medium::Ethernet)?, Config::new(EthernetAddress([0x02, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2]).into()), ), _ => panic!("pass tun or tap"), }; let mut iface = Interface::new(config, &mut device, Instant::now()); iface.update_ip_addrs(|addrs| { addrs.push(IpCidr::new(IpAddress::v4(192, 0, 2, 2), 24)).unwrap(); }); let mut sockets = SocketSet::new(Vec::new()); // Main network loop loop { let now = Instant::now(); iface.poll(now, &mut device, &mut sockets); wait(device.as_raw_fd(), iface.poll_delay(now, &sockets))?; } }But what about the third option, DPDK? When you care about latency A LOT, every syscall is a bloody wound. The syscall itself might take 500ns, and copying data from the kernel to userspace might take another 1000ns, depending on the buffer size. That sounds tiny, but for perspective: itâs common for high-frequency trading firms to saturate 400Gbs network interfaces. That means processing up to 600 million packets per second, or roughly 1.7ns per packet.DPDK lets your program communicate directly with the hardware network card using Ethernet frames, bypassing the entire kernel network stack. You read from and write to a memory-mapped buffer without syscalls: when you want to send data - you simply write it to the buffer and youâre done; when you want to read what youâve received - itâs already there.Thereâs another, less obvious advantage - what happens when a new packet arrives at your network device? An interrupt fires, the CPU core stops executing your app, switches to the kernel, processes the interrupt, and then goes back to your app. Now imagine A LOT of incoming packets, so many that your app gets interrupted all the time. It has a beautiful name, livelock, and I guess debugging it in production is its own level of hell. DPDK lets you avoid all that, but thereâs a cost.DPDK works by running a busy loop that takes up an entire CPU core. It constantly moves data between memory and the network device in both directions, kinda like that:loop { send_from_app_memory_to_network(); receive_from_network_to_app_memory(); }Thereâs another, less obvious nuance. DPDK requires exclusive access to the network device because it uses a driver that operates at the hardware level - two drivers canât work with the same device at the same time. Once you enable the DPDK driver for your network interfaceâ¦ it disappears from the OS. Yep, nothing in ifconfig, if you enable it over SSH, youâll lose SSH access too. I can imagine a lot of funny stories coming out of that.Actually, thereâs a fourth option now - Linux now has an AF_XDP subsystem that does something similar. It lets you bypass the kernel network stack and uses the same idea of memory-mapped buffers to get zero-copy I/O in your app. The kernel still owns the device and interrupts still happen as usual. When a new packet arrives, the kernel runs a simple eBPF filter that decides whether to send it directly to the userspace buffer, bypassing the network stack, or process it normally. That means SSH still works. AF_XDP supports an alternative mode, SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL, which is even closer to DPDK: you get a busy loop with no interrupts at the cost of a CPU core. DPDK still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but AF_XDP is very close (and simply easier to manage).To support DPDK and AF_XDP in smoltcp, we only need to implement the Device trait with 3 methods if we want full control. Alternatively, we can use the existing crates rust-dpdk-net for DPDK and xsk-rs for AF_XDP to help us.Now the final flow is:The runtime loads 15M web server guests into its memoryThe runtime scheduler starts executing guests one by oneGuest syscalls are intercepted by the runtime and replaced by the smoltcp network stack and its adaptersAll 15M guests start listening, each on its own addressThe scheduler polls for incoming data from smoltcp adapters, wakes up a guest, makes it process the data, and switches to the nextAnd now we can finally finish the article. The kernel network stack uses up all the RAM at around 2.5M web servers, and RPS drops as we run more servers. With smoltcp, RAM usage grows slower - 620 bytes per idle server and around a kilobyte for an active one, we got to 16M of servers. DPDK is clearly the beast in this benchmark, with AF_XDP just behind it:Why is this so exciting? It means that by moving the network stack to userland, you can get full control on RAM usage and improve performance. And with custom runtime, you can simply run guests faster.Simply is a bit of a stretch - building a proof of concept is easy. Building a compatible Linux runtime and reimplementing all the syscalls with 100% POSIX compatibility take a bit more thought. And another article.Referenceshttps://github.com/artemyarulin/AI10M/tree/main/poc/ten-million-webservers sourcehttps://medium.com/beyond-localhost/how-we-handle-15M-websocket-connections-on-a-single-server-8917c3952f59 great overview of DPDKhttps://doc.dpdk.org/guides/index.html DPDK main documentation sitehttps://docs.kernel.org/networking/af_xdp.html AF_XDP overview.

What is a syscall? A function that is executed by the OS kernel. Whatever fancy language or library you use for HTTP, it all comes down to those syscalls (well, yes, but actually no). Letâs use C to make it all explicit. We start listening, then read from the socket in a loop and always reply with OK.int main(void) { // We use port 0 which makes OS return any available port int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); if (listen(server, 128) < 0) return 1; const char reply[] = "HTTP/1.0 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 2\r\n\r\nOK"; for (int client; (client = accept(server, NULL, NULL)) >= 0;) { if (recv(client, NULL, 4096, MSG_TRUNC) > 0) send(client, reply, sizeof reply - 1, MSG_NOSIGNAL); close(client); } }It couldnât be simpler: listen on a socket, accept a connection, read the data, send a reply, close the client connection, and repeat. It gives us around 65k RPS. Now that weâve learned everything, letâs finish the article and call it a day:$ for i in $(seq 1 15_000_000); do echo $i; ./server &; done ... ... 28232 program exited with error 1Hm, why did listen fail? Ah, weâve run out of ports! Weâre using port=0, so the kernel picks an available port from ip_local_port_range.$ sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 32768 60999Why are so many ports skipped? Historically, port 0 was created for outbound connections. When you call connect('example.com', 80), Linux connects to the remote server (the sending part) and then allocates a random port on the host from ip_local_port_range to receive data (the receiving part). There are a few reasons the default range is small.Port 0 is special. You cannot listen on it (actually, you can - https://acid.vegas/blog/the-port-that-does-not-exist/).Ports 1-1024 require root.Ports 1024-32768 are skipped to keep dynamically allocated ports from conflicting with existing apps. You donât want to call connect('example.com') and end up allocating port 3306 to receive incoming data. mysql cannot start because you have example.com open in your Firefox would make for a confusing UX.Ports 60999 - 65535 are excluded for historical reasons dating back to IP Masquerading.Nothing prevents us from overriding the range and using 1-65535, but thatâs still a bit short of 15 million. A UDP server and a TCP server can use the same port, so we can double that to 128k. We could run a proxy in front to forward requests to the right process (virtual hosting, yay), but these are all ancient techniques - in the AI era, whenever you have a software problem, you just throw money at the hardware. Letâs simply connect 15M/32k=450 upcoming network cards to the server.The 65k limit comes from the TCP standard. A port is a u16, so even if we hack the kernel with find '*.c' -exec sed -i 's/u16/u32/' \; to support bigger port numbers, normal clients still wouldnât be able to connect. Each listening server is identified by a (protocol, IP, port) tuple. That explains how we can use the same port for UDP and TCP. It also means we can use a bunch of different IPs for our web servers. If we connect 450 network cards to the server, weâll get 450 unique IP addresses and be able to listen on 15 million unique addresses!UPD. Iâve heard from readers that the network card is the ONLY hardware component that didnât get 100 times more expensive in the last year. Canât we avoid ruining that too and solve this in software?Letâs use a beautiful technology called AnyIP, which lets us listen on a whole subnet. Many VPS and dedicated server providers routinely give you a whole TCPv6 subnet. We can simply run sudo ip -6 route add local 2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 dev lo to get 18 quintillion addresses (plus or minus one) to listen on. You can do the same for IPv4 - acquiring a subnet with 15M addresses would cost around $250 million, so adjust the command for your environment. Weâll change our server to pick the nth IP from our range:// Read IP index from CLI, shift base IP by it int i = read_cli_param(argv[1]); const uint32_t base_ip = 0x0a400001; // ex. 10.64.0.1 addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(first_ip + i); // shift, ex. 10.64.0.2And now we can finally finish the article.$ for i in $(seq 1 15_000_000); do echo $i; ./server $i &; done ... ... Out of memoryHm, one server consumes 1.5MB of RAM, so running that many would takeâ¦ 20TB of RAM, which is a few bytes more than our 10GB budget.RuntimeBy pure coincidence (what are the odds?), I explained in Running 10 million Codex CLIs on one server - LFI processes why running millions of processes creates too much overhead. The answer is to run them all in one process inside a custom runtime, much as V8 can run millions of guests in a single process. In Userland Linux scheduler in Rust, I revealed how to build a specialised userland scheduler and switch between tasks with the absolute minimum amount of RAM per task.TLDR: Weâre using LFI for sandboxing. It gives us memory isolation and replaces all syscalls with calls to our host handler, which lets us implement I/O however we like. To schedule multiple guests, we load them all into our main processâs memory and make the CPU constantly switch between guests - we become our own micro OS.Since we need to save every byte and CPU cycle we can, weâre doomed to build another specialised runtime. Letâs get started. How much is 10GB divided by 15M, exactly?Ten Great Britains divided by 15 million gives around half of kilo britain. Not much. If we run all our guests in our runtime, our custom scheduler needs to switch between them. Whatâs the absolute minimum state we need to preserve for each guest? We can ignore server initialisation and assume switches only happen within the main loop. Letâs take another look at the loop.for (int client; (client = accept(server, NULL, NULL)) >= 0;) { if (recv(client, NULL, 4096, MSG_TRUNC) > 0) send(client, reply, sizeof reply - 1, MSG_NOSIGNAL); close(client); }This code has only two state variables, server and client. Both are simple file descriptors. If our scheduler had to suspend a guest at any syscall point in this loop, weâd need to save the following state:struct Context { pc: u64, // Instruction address to return to fd_server: i32, // server file descriptor fd_client: i32, // client file descriptor }We only need 16 bytes per guest, so to run 15M guests in our runtime and be able to suspend them and switch between them, we would need 220MB of RAM. Weâre playing it safe here - we donât need the full u64 or i32, and with bit packing, we could probably get down to 8 bytes per guest. What else do we need?$ codex "How much TCP connection takes?" Idle connection takes zero, while active connection consumes around 5kbHereâs what we get if we assume that only 1M of connections are active at any given moment.14M idle connections - 0 bytesScheduling state for 15M guests - 220MB1M active connections at 5kb each = 5GBOnly half of our RAM budget, yay! I donât often exceed my own expectations. Letâs validate it:int main(void) { // Run 14M of idle connections - just listen and do nothing // SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY! for (int i = 0; i < 14_000_000; i++) { int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); listen(server, 1) } }$ ./run_15m_idle_servers Out Of Memory $ dmesg | tail -n 1 'SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY' - what are you, stupid?Looks like the kernel still has some leftover comments from Linus. Iâm not stupid, but I have to admit I was below average here. While an LLM is a significant boost for learning, itâs too easy to accept its answers without thinking critically and feel ashamed later on. But hey, embarrassment is a cost of entry - letâs dive into networking in the kernel.Networking in the kernelRemember when I mentioned that our simple server uses only 5 syscalls? I missed one that was right in front of me. Let me highlight it:int main(void) { for (int i = 0; i < 10_000_000; ++i) { socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); } }That code will OOM in a 10GB VM. The socket syscall allocates around 3300 bytes, whether the socket is active, listening, or doing nothing. Linux was clearly written at a time when RAM was big and cheap, sigh. Letâs ask AI where all the memory goes:StructsizeofDescriptionstruct tcp_sock2240BTCP state, queues, timers, sequence numbers, congestion control, retransmit and delivery bookkeepingstruct socket_alloc768BA 128-byte struct socket with an embedded wait queue, plus a 608-byte sockfs inode and paddingstruct file184BOpen-file operations, flags, credentials, reference count, and the pointer back to the socketstruct dentry192BThe sockfs pseudo-name, inode pointer, and VFS lookup and lifetime bookkeepingTotal3384BPotato-potato, TLDR, the kernel uses that memory for many things. I was hoping to see some buffer: [u8; 3300], but it doesnât look like we can optimise much without rewriting half the kernel. Letâs take another look at the loop.for (int client; (client = accept(server, NULL, NULL)) >= 0;) { if (recv(client, NULL, 4096, MSG_TRUNC) > 0) send(client, reply, sizeof reply - 1, MSG_NOSIGNAL); close(client); }This code has only two state variables, server and client. Both are simple file descriptors. If our scheduler had to suspend a guest at any syscall point in this loop, weâd need to save the following state:struct Context { pc: u64, // Instruction address to return to fd_server: i32, // server file descriptor fd_client: i32, // client file descriptor }We only need 16 bytes per guest, so to run 15M guests in our runtime and be able to suspend them and switch between them, we would need 220MB of RAM. Weâre playing it safe here - we donât need the full u64 or i32, and with bit packing, we could probably get down to 8 bytes per guest. What else do we need?$ codex "How much TCP connection takes?" Idle connection takes zero, while active connection consumes around 5kbHereâs what we get if we assume that only 1M of connections are active at any given moment.14M idle connections - 0 bytesScheduling state for 15M guests - 220MB1M active connections at 5kb each = 5GBOnly half of our RAM budget, yay! I donât often exceed my own expectations. Letâs validate it:int main(void) { // Run 14M of idle connections - just listen and do nothing // SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY! for (int i = 0; i < 14_000_000; i++) { int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); listen(server, 1) } }$ ./run_15m_idle_servers Out Of Memory $ dmesg | tail -n 1 'SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY' - what are you, stupid?Looks like the kernel still has some leftover comments from Linus. Iâm not stupid, but I have to admit I was below average here. While an LLM is a significant boost for learning, itâs too easy to accept its answers without thinking critically and feel ashamed later on. But hey, embarrassment is a cost of entry - letâs dive into networking in the kernel.Networking in the kernelRemember when I said that our simple server uses only 5 syscalls? I missed one that was right in front of me. Let me highlight it:int main(void) { for (int i = 0; i < 10_000_000; ++i) { socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); } }That code will OOM in a 10GB VM. The socket syscall allocates around 3300 bytes, whether the socket is active, listening, or doing nothing. Linux was clearly written at a time when RAM was substantial and cheap, sigh. Letâs ask AI where all the memory goes:StructsizeofDescriptionstruct tcp_sock2240BTCP state, queues, timers, sequence numbers, congestion control, retransmit and delivery bookkeepingstruct socket_alloc768BA 128-byte struct socket with an embedded wait queue, plus a 608-byte sockfs inode and paddingstruct file184BOpen-file operations, flags, credentials, reference count, and the pointer back to the socketstruct dentry192BThe sockfs pseudo-name, inode pointer, and VFS lookup and lifetime bookkeepingTotal3384BPotato-potato, TLDR, the kernel uses that memory for many things. I was hoping to see some buffer: [u8; 3300], but it doesnât look like we can optimise much without rewriting half the kernel. Itâs Sunday and I have few tokens left, so weâll have to think instead - how can we bypass the kernel?What are our options? Engineering wisdom tells us that if we canât solve a task, weâre working at the wrong level of abstraction. Hmâ¦ level, level, layer. Wait a minute! We started with HTTP and went level down to TCP/IP. That reminds me of something! Mom! Mom! Where are all my university books? I NEED THEM NOW!The OSI model isâ¦ umâ¦ something I studied at university. Yeah, thatâs a good definition. We started with our app and HTTP at the application layer, then went down to TCP/IP at the transport layer. There are three more layers below that. Can we go lower to get full control and solve our RAM problem? Oh yes, thatâs exactly what operating at the network and data link layers lets us do. What about going to the lowest?Clear.Each layer wraps the data from the layer above it.HTTPApplication Â· L7TCPTransport Â· L4IPNetwork Â· L3EthernetData link Â· L2PhysicalL1GET /PayloadPayloadPayloadâ¡ð©Src port50123Dst port80Seq1001ACK7001FlagsACKSrc IP192.0.2.10Dst IP198.51.100.20TTL64Protocol6 (TCP)Dst MAC02:00:00:00:00:feSrc MAC02:00:00:00:00:01EtherType0x0800 (IPv4)FCSCRCTCP/IP is stateful, but everything below is stateless. None of the lower layers know or care about the payload, so nothing prevents us from sending new IP packets or even Ethernet frames with our own handcrafted binary data. We just need to reimplement the TCP and IP stack ourselves. Are there any examples? Embedded folks have solved this millions of times. The most extreme case is Adam Dunkelsâs Miniweb - it combines a custom TCP/IP implementation and an HTTP server that together need only 28 bytes (B-Y-T-E-S) to work.There are plenty of less extreme, more mature implementations, though:gVisor essentially reimplements the whole OS, including the network stackSeastar is a whole runtime with its own network stack from the amazing team behind ScyllaDBlwIP is a popular C implementation of TCP/IPF-Stack uses FreeBSDâs TCP/IP stackGo, C++, and C are nice languages (well, kinda), but theyâre nowhere near as nice as our beloved Rust. So weâll take smoltcp, which is purely amazing:>smoltcp is a standalone, event-driven TCP/IP stack that is designed for >bare-metal, real-time systems. smoltcp does not need heap allocation at allSo, cargo add smoltcp and call it a day? Not so fast. smoltcp is essentially a smart parser and canât do I/O. How does it communicate with your network card? There are 3 ways:TUN is a virtual network interface that the kernel provides. It operates at the IP layerTAP is another kernel feature that operates one layer down, at the Ethernet layerDPDK lets you communicate directly with the network card using Ethernet frames, completely bypassing the kernelsmoltcp is kind enough to provide the first two options out of the box, and theyâre easy to use.fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let (mut device, config) = match std::env::args().nth(1).as_deref() { Some("tun") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltun", Medium::Ip)?, Config::new(HardwareAddress::Ip), ), Some("tap") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltap", Medium::Ethernet)?, Config::new(EthernetAddress([0x02, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2]).into()), ), _ => panic!("pass tun or tap"), }; let mut iface = Interface::new(config, &mut device, Instant::now()); iface.update_ip_addrs(|addrs| { addrs.push(IpCidr::new(IpAddress::v4(192, 0, 2, 2), 24)).unwrap(); }); let mut sockets = SocketSet::new(Vec::new()); // Main network loop loop { let now = Instant::now(); iface.poll(now, &mut device, &mut sockets); wait(device.as_raw_fd(), iface.poll_delay(now, &sockets))?; } }But what about the third option, DPDK? When you care about latency A LOT, every syscall is a bloody wound. The syscall itself might take 500ns, and copying data from the kernel to userspace might take another 1000ns, depending on the buffer size. That sounds tiny, but for perspective: itâs common for high-frequency trading firms to saturate 400Gbs network interfaces. That means processing up to 600 million packets per second, or roughly 1.7ns per packet.DPDK lets your program communicate directly with the hardware network card using Ethernet frames, bypassing the entire kernel network stack. You read from and write to a memory-mapped buffer without syscalls: when you want to send data - you simply write it to the buffer and youâre done; when you want to read what youâve received - itâs already there.Thereâs another, less obvious advantage - what happens when a new packet arrives at your network device? An interrupt fires, the CPU core stops executing your app, switches to the kernel, processes the interrupt, and then goes back to your app. Now imagine A LOT of incoming packets, so many that your app gets interrupted all the time. It has a beautiful name, livelock, and I guess debugging it in production is its own level of hell. DPDK lets you avoid all that, but thereâs a cost.DPDK works by running a busy loop that takes up an entire CPU core. It constantly moves data between memory and the network device in both directions, kinda like that:loop { send_from_app_memory_to_network(); receive_from_network_to_app_memory(); }Thereâs another, less obvious nuance. DPDK requires exclusive access to the network device because it uses a driver that operates at the hardware level - two drivers canât work with the same device at the same time. Once you enable the DPDK driver for your network interfaceâ¦ it disappears from the OS. Yep, nothing in ifconfig, if you enable it over SSH, youâll lose SSH access too. I can imagine a lot of funny stories coming out of that.Actually, thereâs a fourth option now - Linux now has an AF_XDP subsystem that does something similar. It lets you bypass the kernel network stack and uses the same idea of memory-mapped buffers to get zero-copy I/O in your app. The kernel still owns the device and interrupts still happen as usual. When a new packet arrives, the kernel runs a simple eBPF filter that decides whether to send it directly to the userspace buffer, bypassing the network stack, or process it normally. That means SSH still works. AF_XDP supports an alternative mode, SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL, which is even closer to DPDK: you get a busy loop with no interrupts at the cost of a CPU core. DPDK still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but AF_XDP is very close (and simply easier to manage).To support DPDK and AF_XDP in smoltcp, we only need to implement the Device trait with 3 methods if we want full control. Alternatively, we can use the existing crates rust-dpdk-net for DPDK and xsk-rs for AF_XDP to help us.Now the final flow is:The runtime loads 15M web server guests into its memoryThe runtime scheduler starts executing guests one by oneGuest syscalls are intercepted by the runtime and replaced by the smoltcp network stack and its adaptersAll 15M guests start listening, each on its own addressThe scheduler polls for incoming data from smoltcp adapters, wakes up a guest, makes it process the data, and switches to the nextAnd now we can finally finish the article. The kernel network stack uses up all the RAM at around 2.5M web servers, and RPS drops as we run more servers. With smoltcp, RAM usage grows slower - 620 bytes per idle server and around a kilobyte for an active one, we got to 16M of servers. DPDK is clearly the beast in this benchmark, with AF_XDP just behind it:Why is this so exciting? It means that by moving the network stack to userland, you can get full control on RAM usage and improve performance. And with custom runtime, you can simply run guests faster.Simply is a bit of a stretch - building a proof of concept is easy. Building a compatible Linux runtime and reimplementing all the syscalls with 100% POSIX compatibility take a bit more thought. And another article.Referenceshttps://github.com/artemyarulin/AI10M/tree/main/poc/ten-million-webservers sourcehttps://medium.com/beyond-localhost/how-we-handle-15M-websocket-connections-on-a-single-server-8917c3952f59 great overview of DPDKhttps://doc.dpdk.org/guides/index.html DPDK main documentation sitehttps://docs.kernel.org/networking/af_xdp.html AF_XDP overview.

Sources indicate that hm, why did listen fail? Ah, weâve run out of ports! Weâre using port=0, so the kernel picks an available port from ip_local_port_range.$ sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 32768 60999Why are so many ports skipped? Historically, port 0 was created for outbound connections. When you call connect('example.com', 80), Linux connects to the remote server (the sending part) and then allocates a random port on the host from ip_local_port_range to receive data (the receiving part). There are a few reasons the default range is small.Port 0 is special. You cannot listen on it (actually, you can - https://acid.vegas/blog/the-port-that-does-not-exist/).Ports 1-1024 require root.Ports 1024-32768 are skipped to keep dynamically allocated ports from conflicting with existing apps. You donât want to call connect('example.com') and end up allocating port 3306 to receive incoming data. mysql cannot start because you have example.com open in your Firefox would make for a confusing UX.Ports 60999 - 65535 are excluded for historical reasons dating back to IP Masquerading.Nothing prevents us from overriding the range and using 1-65535, but thatâs still a bit short of 15 million. A UDP server and a TCP server can use the same port, so we can double that to 128k. We could run a proxy in front to forward requests to the right process (virtual hosting, yay), but these are all ancient techniques - in the AI era, whenever you have a software problem, you just throw money at the hardware. Letâs simply connect 15M/32k=450 upcoming network cards to the server.The 65k limit comes from the TCP standard. A port is a u16, so even if we hack the kernel with find '*.c' -exec sed -i 's/u16/u32/' \; to support bigger port numbers, normal clients still wouldnât be able to connect. Each listening server is identified by a (protocol, IP, port) tuple. That explains how we can use the same port for UDP and TCP. It also means we can use a bunch of different IPs for our web servers. If we connect 450 network cards to the server, weâll get 450 unique IP addresses and be able to listen on 15 million unique addresses!UPD. Iâve heard from readers that the network card is the ONLY hardware component that didnât get 100 times more expensive in the last year. Many VPS and dedicated server providers routinely give you a whole TCPv6 subnet. We can simply run sudo ip -6 route add local 2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 dev lo to get 18 quintillion addresses (plus or minus one) to listen on. You can do the same for IPv4 - acquiring a subnet with 15M addresses would cost around $250 million, so adjust the command for your environment. You can do the same for IPv4 - acquiring a subnet with 15M addresses would cost around $250 million, so adjust the command for your environment. Weâll change our server to pick the nth IP from our range:// Read IP index from CLI, shift base IP by it int i = read_cli_param(argv[1]); const uint32_t base_ip = 0x0a400001; // ex. 10.64.0.1 addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(first_ip + i); // shift, ex. 10.64.0.2And now we can finally finish the article.$ for i in $(seq 1 15_000_000); do echo $i; ./server $i &; done ... ... Out of memoryHm, one server consumes 1.5MB of RAM, so running that many would takeâ¦ 20TB of RAM, which is a few bytes more than our 10GB budget.RuntimeBy pure coincidence (what are the odds?), I explained in Running 10 million Codex CLIs on one server - LFI processes why running millions of processes creates too much overhead. The answer is to run them all in one process inside a custom runtime, much as V8 can run millions of guests in a single process. In Userland Linux scheduler in Rust, I revealed how to build a specialised userland scheduler and switch between tasks with the absolute minimum amount of RAM per task.TLDR: Weâre using LFI for sandboxing. It gives us memory isolation and replaces all syscalls with calls to our host handler, which lets us implement I/O however we like. To schedule multiple guests, we load them all into our main processâs memory and make the CPU constantly switch between guests - we become our own micro OS.Since we need to save every byte and CPU cycle we can, weâre doomed to build another specialised runtime. Letâs get started. How much is 10GB divided by 15M, exactly?Ten Great Britains divided by 15 million gives around half of kilo britain. Not much. If we run all our guests in our runtime, our custom scheduler needs to switch between them. Whatâs the absolute minimum state we need to preserve for each guest? We can ignore server initialisation and assume switches only happen within the main loop. Letâs take another look at the loop.for (int client; (client = accept(server, NULL, NULL)) >= 0;) { if (recv(client, NULL, 4096, MSG_TRUNC) > 0) send(client, reply, sizeof reply - 1, MSG_NOSIGNAL); close(client); }This code has only two state variables, server and client. Both are simple file descriptors. If our scheduler had to suspend a guest at any syscall point in this loop, weâd need to save the following state:struct Context { pc: u64, // Instruction address to return to fd_server: i32, // server file descriptor fd_client: i32, // client file descriptor }We only need 16 bytes per guest, so to run 15M guests in our runtime and be able to suspend them and switch between them, we would need 220MB of RAM. Weâre playing it safe here - we donât need the full u64 or i32, and with bit packing, we could probably get down to 8 bytes per guest. What else do we need?$ codex "How much TCP connection takes?" Idle connection takes zero, while active connection consumes around 5kbHereâs what we get if we assume that only 1M of connections are active at any given moment.14M idle connections - 0 bytesScheduling state for 15M guests - 220MB1M active connections at 5kb each = 5GBOnly half of our RAM budget, yay! I donât often exceed my own expectations. Letâs validate it:int main(void) { // Run 14M of idle connections - just listen and do nothing // SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY! for (int i = 0; i < 14_000_000; i++) { int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); listen(server, 1) } }$ ./run_15m_idle_servers Out Of Memory $ dmesg | tail -n 1 'SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY' - what are you, stupid?Looks like the kernel still has some leftover comments from Linus. Iâm not stupid, but I have to admit I was below average here. While an LLM is a significant boost for learning, itâs too easy to accept its answers without thinking critically and feel ashamed later on. But hey, embarrassment is a cost of entry - letâs dive into networking in the kernel.Networking in the kernelRemember when I mentioned that our simple server uses only 5 syscalls? I missed one that was right in front of me. Let me highlight it:int main(void) { for (int i = 0; i < 10_000_000; ++i) { socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); } }That code will OOM in a 10GB VM. The socket syscall allocates around 3300 bytes, whether the socket is active, listening, or doing nothing. Linux was clearly written at a time when RAM was big and cheap, sigh. Letâs ask AI where all the memory goes:StructsizeofDescriptionstruct tcp_sock2240BTCP state, queues, timers, sequence numbers, congestion control, retransmit and delivery bookkeepingstruct socket_alloc768BA 128-byte struct socket with an embedded wait queue, plus a 608-byte sockfs inode and paddingstruct file184BOpen-file operations, flags, credentials, reference count, and the pointer back to the socketstruct dentry192BThe sockfs pseudo-name, inode pointer, and VFS lookup and lifetime bookkeepingTotal3384BPotato-potato, TLDR, the kernel uses that memory for many things. I was hoping to see some buffer: [u8; 3300], but it doesnât look like we can optimise much without rewriting half the kernel. Itâs Sunday and I have few tokens left, so weâll have to think instead - how can we bypass the kernel?What are our options? Engineering wisdom tells us that if we canât solve a task, weâre working at the wrong level of abstraction. Hmâ¦ level, level, layer. Wait a minute! We started with HTTP and went level down to TCP/IP. That reminds me of something! Mom! Mom! Where are all my university books? I NEED THEM NOW!The OSI model isâ¦ umâ¦ something I studied at university. Yeah, thatâs a good definition. We started with our app and HTTP at the application layer, then went down to TCP/IP at the transport layer. There are three more layers below that. Can we go lower to get full control and solve our RAM problem? Oh yes, thatâs exactly what operating at the network and data link layers lets us do. What about going to the lowest?Clear.Each layer wraps the data from the layer above it.HTTPApplication Â· L7TCPTransport Â· L4IPNetwork Â· L3EthernetData link Â· L2PhysicalL1GET /PayloadPayloadPayloadâ¡ð©Src port50123Dst port80Seq1001ACK7001FlagsACKSrc IP192.0.2.10Dst IP198.51.100.20TTL64Protocol6 (TCP)Dst MAC02:00:00:00:00:feSrc MAC02:00:00:00:00:01EtherType0x0800 (IPv4)FCSCRCTCP/IP is stateful, but everything below is stateless. None of the lower layers know or care about the payload, so nothing prevents us from sending new IP packets or even Ethernet frames with our own handcrafted binary data. We just need to reimplement the TCP and IP stack ourselves. Are there any examples? Embedded folks have solved this millions of times. The most extreme case is Adam Dunkelsâs Miniweb - it combines a custom TCP/IP implementation and an HTTP server that together need only 28 bytes (B-Y-T-E-S) to work.There are plenty of less extreme, more mature implementations, though:gVisor essentially reimplements the whole OS, including the network stackSeastar is a whole runtime with its own network stack from the amazing team behind ScyllaDBlwIP is a popular C implementation of TCP/IPF-Stack uses FreeBSDâs TCP/IP stackGo, C++, and C are nice languages (well, kinda), but theyâre nowhere near as nice as our beloved Rust. So weâll take smoltcp, which is purely amazing:>smoltcp is a standalone, event-driven TCP/IP stack that is designed for >bare-metal, real-time systems. smoltcp does not need heap allocation at allSo, cargo add smoltcp and call it a day? Not so fast. smoltcp is essentially a smart parser and canât do I/O. How does it communicate with your network card? There are 3 ways:TUN is a virtual network interface that the kernel provides. It operates at the IP layerTAP is another kernel feature that operates one layer down, at the Ethernet layerDPDK lets you communicate directly with the network card using Ethernet frames, completely bypassing the kernelsmoltcp is kind enough to provide the first two options out of the box, and theyâre easy to use.fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let (mut device, config) = match std::env::args().nth(1).as_deref() { Some("tun") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltun", Medium::Ip)?, Config::new(HardwareAddress::Ip), ), Some("tap") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltap", Medium::Ethernet)?, Config::new(EthernetAddress([0x02, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2]).into()), ), _ => panic!("pass tun or tap"), }; let mut iface = Interface::new(config, &mut device, Instant::now()); iface.update_ip_addrs(|addrs| { addrs.push(IpCidr::new(IpAddress::v4(192, 0, 2, 2), 24)).unwrap(); }); let mut sockets = SocketSet::new(Vec::new()); // Main network loop loop { let now = Instant::now(); iface.poll(now, &mut device, &mut sockets); wait(device.as_raw_fd(), iface.poll_delay(now, &sockets))?; } }But what about the third option, DPDK? When you care about latency A LOT, every syscall is a bloody wound. The syscall itself might take 500ns, and copying data from the kernel to userspace might take another 1000ns, depending on the buffer size. That sounds tiny, but for perspective: itâs common for high-frequency trading firms to saturate 400Gbs network interfaces. That means processing up to 600 million packets per second, or roughly 1.7ns per packet.DPDK lets your program communicate directly with the hardware network card using Ethernet frames, bypassing the entire kernel network stack. You read from and write to a memory-mapped buffer without syscalls: when you want to send data - you simply write it to the buffer and youâre done; when you want to read what youâve received - itâs already there.Thereâs another, less obvious advantage - what happens when a new packet arrives at your network device? An interrupt fires, the CPU core stops executing your app, switches to the kernel, processes the interrupt, and then goes back to your app. Now imagine A LOT of incoming packets, so many that your app gets interrupted all the time. It has a beautiful name, livelock, and I guess debugging it in production is its own level of hell. DPDK lets you avoid all that, but thereâs a cost.DPDK works by running a busy loop that takes up an entire CPU core. It constantly moves data between memory and the network device in both directions, kinda like that:loop { send_from_app_memory_to_network(); receive_from_network_to_app_memory(); }Thereâs another, less obvious nuance. DPDK requires exclusive access to the network device because it uses a driver that operates at the hardware level - two drivers canât work with the same device at the same time. Once you enable the DPDK driver for your network interfaceâ¦ it disappears from the OS. Yep, nothing in ifconfig, if you enable it over SSH, youâll lose SSH access too. I can imagine a lot of funny stories coming out of that.Actually, thereâs a fourth option now - Linux now has an AF_XDP subsystem that does something similar. It lets you bypass the kernel network stack and uses the same idea of memory-mapped buffers to get zero-copy I/O in your app. The kernel still owns the device and interrupts still happen as usual. When a new packet arrives, the kernel runs a simple eBPF filter that decides whether to send it directly to the userspace buffer, bypassing the network stack, or process it normally. That means SSH still works. AF_XDP supports an alternative mode, SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL, which is even closer to DPDK: you get a busy loop with no interrupts at the cost of a CPU core. DPDK still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but AF_XDP is very close (and simply easier to manage).To support DPDK and AF_XDP in smoltcp, we only need to implement the Device trait with 3 methods if we want full control. Alternatively, we can use the existing crates rust-dpdk-net for DPDK and xsk-rs for AF_XDP to help us.Now the final flow is:The runtime loads 15M web server guests into its memoryThe runtime scheduler starts executing guests one by oneGuest syscalls are intercepted by the runtime and replaced by the smoltcp network stack and its adaptersAll 15M guests start listening, each on its own addressThe scheduler polls for incoming data from smoltcp adapters, wakes up a guest, makes it process the data, and switches to the nextAnd now we can finally finish the article. The kernel network stack uses up all the RAM at around 2.5M web servers, and RPS drops as we run more servers. With smoltcp, RAM usage grows slower - 620 bytes per idle server and around a kilobyte for an active one, we got to 16M of servers. DPDK is clearly the beast in this benchmark, with AF_XDP just behind it:Why is this so exciting? It means that by moving the network stack to userland, you can get full control on RAM usage and improve performance. And with custom runtime, you can simply run guests faster.Simply is a bit of a stretch - building a proof of concept is easy. Building a compatible Linux runtime and reimplementing all the syscalls with 100% POSIX compatibility take a bit more thought. And another article.Referenceshttps://github.com/artemyarulin/AI10M/tree/main/poc/ten-million-webservers sourcehttps://medium.com/beyond-localhost/how-we-handle-15M-websocket-connections-on-a-single-server-8917c3952f59 great overview of DPDKhttps://doc.dpdk.org/guides/index.html DPDK main documentation sitehttps://docs.kernel.org/networking/af_xdp.html AF_XDP overview.
