Breaking: Sticky note on monitor provided keys to the company’s kingdom

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (578 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Don't leave your credentials out in public, where any visitor can see them.
  • Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we talk smack about organizations that have smacked themselves down by practicing poor security hygiene.
  • In a recent development, our terrifying tale comes courtesy of Christian Espinosa, a certified penetration tester with over 30 years of experience and the CEO of Blue Goat Cyber, a security company.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Don't leave your credentials out in public, where any visitor can see them.

Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we talk smack about organizations that have smacked themselves down by practicing poor security hygiene. This week's story involves everyone's favorite low-tech password manager: the sticky note.

In a recent development, our terrifying tale comes courtesy of Christian Espinosa, a certified penetration tester with over 30 years of experience and the CEO of Blue Goat Cyber, a security company. Espinosa shared an experience where critical credentials were right out in the open for any person in the office to see.

According to recent reports, during a walkthrough of a client's office, he noticed a password written on a sticky note that was taped to an employee's monitor. While writing down your password and placing it in a physically secure paper notebook might be ok, taping it to the computer is definitely not.

"Before I get my fingers on any system, I first walk the physical area that the system is located in — attackers do that when they're looking at a target too," Espinosa explained. “Physical security vulnerabilities are neglected much more often than technical security vulnerabilities and firms invest in firewalls where a sticky note is placed 3 feet from the front door.".

Recent findings suggest that espinosa took a photo of the sticky note and immediately tried logging into that employee's account. Success. Then, he tried the very same password on the VPN, which apparently had been maintained by that employee.

Once he connected to the VPN, Espinosa had full access to the company network and all of its shared drives. He opened a shared drive that this employee had access to and there was an HR folder with all kinds of personally identifiable information (PII) about employees, including home addresses, driver's licenses, and scanned W-4 forms. There were even spreadsheets that listed everyone's salaries.

The accounting server was a particular treasure trove of client information. On that server, Espinosa found a folder with vendor banking information, invoices, and payment records.

In a recent development, have a story about someone leaving a gaping hole in their network? Share it with us at pwned@sitpub.com. Anonymity is available upon request.

"At that point, a password I had read from a sticky note during a walk-through had taken me from one desk to information that could have been used for payroll fraud, identity theft, or vendor-payment fraud," Espinosa mentioned.

After getting access to all this information, the pen tester presented his findings to the client. They rapidly disabled the rogue account and started reviewing VPN access logs to see who else might have gotten into the network. They then searched the office to see if anyone else was exposing a password on a sticky note. Finally, they tightened permissions on the HR and accounting shares so that only people who really needed access to that data could get in.

In a recent development, the lessons here are pretty obvious. Don't expose your passwords and, perhaps even more importantly, limit who has access to file shares that contain mission-critical data such as employee or client information.

"The part that really got the client's attention was how easily the attack could have continued after I left the building," Espinosa posited. "Someone could have photographed that sticky note, walked out, connected to the VPN later that night, and started going through employee and financial records from somewhere else." ®.

Real-world AI agents, however, rarely finish their job in a single turn. They have to reason over partial observations, invoke tools, observe environment feedback, and adapt their strategy across multiple steps. So in this post, we will walk through how to train a multi-turn, tool-using LLM agent using Tunix's agentic reinforcement learning pipeline on Cloud TPU v6e-8. You can find the complete code in this GitHub repository.

It has been revealed that we will revisit the Plane Strike board game from an earlier TensorFlow/JAX reinforcement learning blog, replacing the custom MLP policy with Gemma 4 E2B in thinking mode on a single Cloud TPU v6e-8 host. Plane Strike is played on a 6x6 grid (A1 to F6) where one 8-cell plane is hidden in one of 4 orientations. Each turn, the agent sees the result of its previous strike and the raw visible board (. untried, X hit, O miss), thinks through candidate placements, and calls the strike(cell="...") tool to strike one cell. The game ends when all 8 plane cells are hit, or after 23 strikes.

Industry News: Announcing AWS Lambda Web Functions

📅 12 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1020 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, today, we’re announcing AWS Lambda Web Functions, a new form factor that lets you run standard HTTP web applications on Lambda without rewriting your code into an event handler.
  • With this launch, AWS Lambda now offers three distinct form factors, each built on the same Firecracker isolation technology and designed for a different programming model.
  • Sources indicate that lambda Event Functions are what you already know as Lambda functions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, today, we’re announcing AWS Lambda Web Functions, a new form factor that lets you run standard HTTP web applications on Lambda without rewriting your code into an event handler. You can take a standard port-listening server built with Express, Hono, Fastify, Next.js, or any Node.js framework, deploy it with a single command, and Lambda automatically handles scaling, multi-region distribution, and active CPU billing. No adapters, no infrastructure to manage, and no framework lock-in.

With this launch, AWS Lambda now offers three distinct form factors, each built on the same Firecracker isolation technology and designed for a different programming model.

Sources indicate that lambda Event Functions are what you already know as Lambda functions. They use the event-driven, single-concurrent handler model with wall-clock billing. We’re introducing the “Event Functions” name to highlight that programming model: your function receives an event, processes it, and returns a response. The event-driven programming model is ideal for event processing, queue consumers, and invocations triggered by other AWS services.

Industry observers note that lambda Web Functions use an HTTP-native programming model with multi-concurrent execution and active CPU billing. Your code listens on a port and handles standard HTTP requests. That programming model is ideal for web applications, API backends, and interactive HTTP workloads where multiple concurrent requests and I/O-heavy processing are the norm.

Lambda MicroVMs provide isolated, stateful sandbox environments with customer-managed lifecycles for running untrusted or user-generated code.

It has been revealed that the three complement each other. An application might use Event Functions for asynchronous backend processing, Web Functions for the user-facing API and server-side rendering layer, and MicroVMs for interactive code execution features, all within the same AWS account and sharing the same operational model.

It has been revealed that why Web FunctionsModern web applications need to serve global audiences with fast, consistent response times while giving developers the freedom to use standard frameworks and iterate swiftly. Building this today typically requires assembling multiple infrastructure components, configuring multi-region deployments, setting up latency-based routing, and tuning billing models to avoid paying for I/O wait. Developers often find themselves adapting their application code to fit a specific compute model rather than deploying the HTTP server they already have.

Lambda Web Functions removes this complexity. Each execution environment handles multiple requests simultaneously (up to 128 concurrent requests per environment), which means a burst of incoming traffic can share warm environments instead of mapping each request to a new one. Web Functions meter the CPU time your code uses, so time spent waiting on a database query or an API call consumes little CPU. Memory is metered for as long as the execution environment exists. For I/O-heavy web workloads like server-side rendering, API backends, and AI inference endpoints streaming token responses, this can reduce compute costs.

It has been revealed that let’s try it outTo get started, I wrote a simple Express.js server. This is the same code I run locally with node index.js, no Lambda-specific adapters or wrappers required.

Recent findings suggest that the only difference from running locally is the AWS_LAMBDA_HTTP_ENDPOINT environment variable, which Lambda sets to the host and port your server must listen on. To run locally, set it yourself, for example AWS_LAMBDA_HTTP_ENDPOINT=127.0.0.1:3000 node index.js.

With my code ready, I deployed using the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI):.

According to recent reports, one command. No prior resource setup. The CLI bundled my source, created the Web Function, published its first revision, attached a Web Function endpoint, and returned a live HTTPS URL in under a minute.

In a recent development, A revision is an immutable snapshot of the code I deployed. The endpoint is the HTTPS URL that routes traffic to a revision, or splits traffic across revisions. Those are the resources I use to iterate and to control how traffic moves to newly introduced code.

In a recent development, next, I wanted my application to serve people in Europe and Asia with lower latency. I redeployed with multiple regions:.

Sources indicate that lambda Web Functions replicated my code to all three regions and configured latency-based routing automatically. Each request now routes to the Region with the lowest latency for the caller, on a best-effort basis, through one global URL (.lambda-web.global.on.aws).

Industry observers note that when I updated my code and ran the same deploy command again, the CLI detected the existing function, uploaded the new revision, and pointed the endpoint at it. Total turnaround from code change to live: seconds.

For production workflows that require a more gradual rollout, I can shift traffic between revisions with a single API call:.

This sends 90% of endpoint traffic to the current revision and 10% to the new one, giving me a canary deployment without additional tooling.

In a recent development, better together with Amazon CloudFrontFor applications that combine static and dynamic content, Web Functions works well alongside Amazon CloudFront. You can select a Web Function endpoint as the origin for your CloudFront distribution. Static assets are served from the cache while dynamic requests route to your Web Function, giving you CDN performance for static content with serverless compute for the dynamic parts.

Industry observers note that web Functions improves the private-origin experience with CloudFront. With this launch, you attach CloudFront origin access control (OAC) to a Web Function endpoint instead. CloudFront signs requests to the origin, and the endpoint allows only your distribution to invoke it. You get the same private-origin pattern CloudFront already provides for Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), without exposing the endpoint or adding custom authorization to your app.

Industry observers note that now availableAWS Lambda Web Functions is available today in US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland). Web Functions run Node.js 24 (nodejs24.x) on Arm64 at launch and support Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) connectivity, allowing your function to access resources that exist within a VPC.

To get started, deploy your first Web Function in under a minute:.

Recent findings suggest that for pricing details, visit the AWS Lambda pricing page. To learn more, see the Lambda Web Functions documentation.

In a recent development, the gap between average and median retirement savings is one of the most crucial distinctions in personal finance. The average gets pulled upward by high-balance accounts — a single person with $5 million in their 401(k) dramatically inflates the average for their age group. But "better than average" and "on track for a secure retirement" are very different standards.

Fidelity's guideline of 1x salary by 30 and 10x salary by 67 is a reasonable starting point for traditional retirement planning. But for FI seekers, these benchmarks are the floor, not the ceiling. The ChooseFI community consistently demonstrates that saving 40-60% of income — rather than the national average of 4.6% — compresses the timeline from 40 working years down to 10-17.

If your balance is below the median for your age group, you are not alone — and you are not stuck. The math of compound growth means that aggressive action in your 40s and 50s can still produce a secure retirement or even an early one.

The IRS provides additional contribution room for savers age 50 and older. In 2027, the 401(k) catch-up contribution is $7,500 on top of the standard $25,500 limit, for a total of $31,000. IRA catch-up contributions add $1,000 to the standard $7,000 limit. HSA catch-up for those 55+ adds another $1,000. Combined with employer matching, a 50-year-old couple can potentially shelter $80,000 or more per year in tax-advantaged accounts.

It has been revealed that most financial advice focuses on investment returns, but the variable you control most directly is your savings rate. Moving from a 10% savings rate to a 30% savings rate has a dramatically larger impact on your retirement timeline than chasing an extra 2% of investment return. A household earning $120,000 that increases from 10% to 30% savings — a shift of $24,000 per year — adds roughly $600,000 to their retirement balance over 15 years (assuming 7% average returns).

The FI community's core insight is that savings rate is the primary driver of financial independence. At a 50% savings rate, you can reach FI in roughly 17 years regardless of income level. At 60%, it compresses to about 12 years. At 70%, you are looking at under 10 years. These numbers are independent of salary — they depend only on the ratio of savings to spending.

In a recent development, the average American contributes 4.6% of salary to their 401(k), receives a 3-4% employer match, and saves little outside of that. FIRE-path savers typically max every available tax-advantaged account, maintain savings rates of 40-60%, invest in low-cost index funds, and direct overflow savings into taxable brokerage accounts. The result: FIRE savers in their 40s commonly have $500,000 to $1.5 million in total investable assets — 5 to 10 times the national median for their age group. The difference is not income; many FIRE success stories come from median-income households that simply saved aggressively and avoided lifestyle inflation.

Always compare yourself to the median, not the average.

Yes — employer matching contributions are part of your retirement savings balance. In a typical arrangement, an employer matches 50% of your contributions up to 6% of salary. On a $75,000 salary, that adds $2,250 per year in free money. Over a 30-year career at 7% returns, that match alone grows to roughly $213,000.

Generally no. While your home is part of your net worth, it is not liquid retirement savings you can draw from to cover living expenses. You would need to sell or reverse-mortgage your home to access that equity. Retirement planning should focus on investable assets — accounts you can convert to income without selling your primary residence.

According to recent reports, A common guideline is 10-12x your pre-retirement income. For a household earning $100,000, that means $1,000,000 to $1,200,000 in retirement savings. The 4% rule suggests you can withdraw 4% of your portfolio annually with a high probability of not running out over 30 years — so $1 million supports roughly $40,000 per year in withdrawals.

Sources indicate that it is never too late, but the urgency increases with age. A 40-year-old saving $20,000 per year at 7% returns will accumulate roughly $1 million by age 65. A 50-year-old has access to catch-up contributions ($7,500 extra in a 401(k)) and can still build $400,000 to $600,000 in 15 years with aggressive saving. The key is maximizing savings rate immediately rather than trying to make up ground through risky investments.

Industry observers note that the average retirement savings benchmarks are useful directional guides, but they should not define your target. Most Americans are dramatically undersaved — the median 401(k) balance at retirement age is under $75,000, which supports only about $2,860 per year in withdrawals using the 4% rule. That is not a retirement initiative; it is a supplement to Social Security at best. The FI community takes a fundamentally different approach: define your actual annual spending, multiply by 25, and work backward to a savings rate that gets you there. Whether your number is $750,000 or $3 million, the path is the same — maximize tax-advantaged accounts, invest in low-cost index funds, maintain a high savings rate, and let compound growth do the heavy lifting. If you are behind the benchmarks, the single most impactful action is increasing your savings rate, not chasing higher returns.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Around 265,000 customers potentially affected as London transport operator grapples with another security breach.
  • Transport for London (TfL) has copped to another cybersecurity breach, this time involving the account details of around 265,000 Oyster photocard customers.
  • The capital's transport operator told The Register it first became aware something was amiss on November 16, when Oyster photocard customers started receiving emails asking them to create accounts they already had.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Around 265,000 customers potentially affected as London transport operator grapples with another security breach.

Transport for London (TfL) has copped to another cybersecurity breach, this time involving the account details of around 265,000 Oyster photocard customers.

The capital's transport operator told The Register it first became aware something was amiss on November 16, when Oyster photocard customers started receiving emails asking them to create accounts they already had. The emails came from TfL's own systems, the transport body confirmed, but were generated as a result of the compromise.

Sources indicate that "We immediately took the TfL photocard website down while this was being investigated," noted Shashi Verma, TfL's director of technology strategy and revenue. "The protection of personal information is a priority for us, and I apologize to our customers affected by this incident.".

It has been revealed that tfL reckons its speedy response spared a considerable number of customers from having their details compromised. The transport operator says it has since contained the incident and contacted those potentially affected, though it is rather more forthcoming about what the hackers didn't get their hands on than what they did.

Recent findings suggest that tfL says no passwords, bank or payment card details, or customer journey information were compromised. It also believes the names and dates of birth of children with Zip Oyster cards were unaffected.

Among those whose accounts may have been compromised are holders of Zip Oyster cards – issued to children as young as five – as well as students, apprentices, care leavers, veterans, and Londoners aged 60 and over.

According to recent reports, despite the assurances about passwords, TfL notes it will ask all photocard customers to change theirs, along with their security questions and answers. Those in the habit of recycling passwords across multiple websites are being advised to change them elsewhere, too.

Recent findings suggest that tfL says it has yet to find any evidence that the compromised data has been used and has notified the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO). The transport operator hasn't disclosed how the perpetrators got into its systems.

In a recent development, existing photocards will still let holders through the ticket barriers, though anyone needing to renew one or check their journey history will have to contact TfL's customer services team while the website is out of action. There's no word yet on when it'll be back.

"We hope to restore the affected website services as rapidly as possible," Verma noted.

TfL should be well versed in dealing with data breaches by now. In March, the transport operator told The Register it had notified more than 7 million customers following its September 2024 cyberattack. The hackers had accessed systems holding customers' names, email addresses, and home addresses, while around 5,000 customers were contacted as a priority because their bank account details may also have been compromised.

Industry observers note that two teenagers were subsequently charged in connection with the attack, which authorities linked to the notorious Scattered Spider cybercrime crew. The ICO looked into that incident but opted not to take enforcement action against TfL, having deemed its response proportionate. There's nothing at present to suggest the two incidents are related.

Londoners can at least rest assured that their Oyster photocards still work. Whether the information they handed over to obtain them is in someone else's hands is another matter. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some numbers are hard to picture until you sit with them for a moment.
  • The rest of the week pulled in a different direction: smaller, cheaper, and more constrained.
  • According to recent reports, headlinesAll the numbers: Amazon Prime Day 2026 powered by AWS is the latest entry in a tradition that goes back to 2016, and the scale is still difficult to hold in your head.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some numbers are hard to picture until you sit with them for a moment. Last week we published the Prime Day 2026 metrics, and the one that stuck with me is 2.3 quadrillion: the daily requests Amazon ElastiCache peaked at during the event. Prime Day ran back in June, so this post always lands as a retrospective, and that gap is part of what makes it worth reading. By the time the numbers reach you, the only evidence that any of it happened is that nothing went wrong.

The rest of the week pulled in a different direction: smaller, cheaper, and more constrained. Claude Haiku 5.5 arrived on Amazon Bedrock at roughly 75 percent less than Haiku 4.5, Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic made voice agents quicker on their feet, and Strands Box showed up to put real boundaries around what an agent is allowed to do. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news….

According to recent reports, headlinesAll the numbers: Amazon Prime Day 2026 powered by AWS is the latest entry in a tradition that goes back to 2016, and the scale is still difficult to hold in your head. Over the four days of Prime Day, Amazon DynamoDB processed more than 59 trillion requests while peaking at 192 million requests per second, and kept single-digit millisecond responses throughout. AWS Lambda handled over 2.3 trillion invocations per day. Amazon EBS peaked above 24.8 trillion I/O operations, moving more than an exabyte of data daily. Amazon ECS rolled out an average of 158.3 million tasks per day on AWS Fargate, a 47.7 percent jump over last year, and AWS Graviton powered up to 49 percent of the Amazon EC2 compute that Amazon.com used.

In a recent development, the number I keep coming back to, though, isn’t a throughput record. The team ran more than 44,000 AWS Fault Injection Service experiments ahead of the event, more than six times what they ran in 2025. Those are deliberate failures injected on purpose, months in advance, so that the trillions of requests above turn into an ordinary shopping afternoon. If you’re preparing for your own peak moment, AWS Countdown Premium is built for exactly that kind of planning.

#23828. Lisp Game Jam devlog: Polydraw

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1965 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Spritely ↗ Open Full Page

Lisp Game Jam devlog: Polydraw

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1965 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spritely

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this year's Autumn Lisp Game Jam has just wrapped up!
  • The rest of this post is a daily devlog of how we made Polydraw so you can see what the process look likes to make a game with Goblins and Hoot under a tight deadline.
  • In a recent development, it's go time!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this year's Autumn Lisp Game Jam has just wrapped up! Spritely's contribution to the jam was Polydraw, a peer-to-peer party game that is easy to pick up and play with friends. In Polydraw, players take turns being the artist who draws an image based on a prompt. The catch is that the artist only has 60 seconds and can only draw using triangles. All of the other players are guessers who try to correctly guess the prompt. We're quite pleased with how the game turned out!

The rest of this post is a daily devlog of how we made Polydraw so you can see what the process look likes to make a game with Goblins and Hoot under a tight deadline.

In a recent development, it's go time! First, we created a Git repository on Codeberg and copied the Hoot game jam template into it.

Since the core activity in Polydraw is drawing triangles, the first thing Dave implemented was an interface for doing that on a canvas. This first version was crude and didn't include a color picker.

We took the weekend off to prepare for a busy week ahead.

This is the day that we really got to work on the game jam.

The first version of the triangle editor stored pixel coordinates of the local canvas, but that wasn't going to be good enough to display on other machines with different sized canvases. So, Dave simply normalized triangle vertices into the [0,1] range so each peer could scale them as needed.

Dave also implemented a basic scene system, a common game programming pattern, to encapsulate the coarse game states such as the title screen, the lobby, and the main game.

A color palette was added along with some additional mockup UI around the canvas.

With a good enough game engine in place, we turned our attention to the game protocol. Since we are using Goblins, all interactions are modeled using actors. Dave came up with the following actors:.

Player: Used for player identity within the game and contains the player's self-proposed name.

Lobby: The place where players gather before the game starts. The player that creates the lobby is the host and all other players are guests.

Game: Holds all of the game state like the player list, whose turn it is, and the scoreboard.

Recent findings suggest that controller: A player's virtual game controller. Used to speak to the game actor, but all actions are scoped to the individual player.

A test script was written to simulate creating a game, joining the lobby, and playing a round. At this stage, everything was happening in a single process. Goblins makes it easy to start with a single process and then distribute the actors to multiple machines later.

In a recent development, now it was time to get the actors onto the network and hook them up to the game UI. For networking we used OCapN, naturally. Jessica started up an instance of our new end-to-end encrypted relay netlayer that we set as the default relay so the game would "just work" when we uploaded it to itch.io. In fact, dogfooding the relay was a large part of the motivation behind participating in the game jam in the first place!

It has been revealed that dave got the actors online with OCapN and connected the game UI to the actors, then confirmed that a three player game works. Three players is the minimum number of players needed to trigger OCapN's third-party handoff feature. Handoffs are what enable distributed networking in OCapN: Alice can give Bob a reference to Carol, which causes Bob and Carol to establish a new OCapN session with each other. This is the first application we've made that does handoffs over the relay netlayer and it was nice to see them working as intended.

Unfortunately, we discovered an issue with how Goblins handles two peers connecting to each other concurrently, a problem known as "crossed hellos". OCapN mandates that only one connection may be open between any two peers, so we have to pick which connection wins. The bug is that any promises that were created over the losing connection never resolve. This was observed in the game as an empty lobby player list that should be populated. It didn't prevent the rest of the game from working, though, so we didn't try to fix it (yet).

On this day, Dave discovered that, despite his best efforts, he fell victim to the "identity footgun". We could write a whole blog post series about the many subtle issues of object identity (in the sense of Scheme's eq?) in object capability systems, but instead we'll refer you to the The Grant Matcher Puzzle and just mention that using object references as keys in associative data structures is error-prone. A promise that eventually resolves to a reference to Alice is not identical (again, in the eq? sense) to a reference to Alice. So, if you accidentally use a promise as a key somewhere or use eq? directly you will probably have a bad time, which is exactly what happened to us.

To deal with this identity crisis, Dave first detected it at runtime by writing a wrapper around eq? called geq?. This new predicate throws an error when comparing a promise to a non-promise. Then he used the resulting backtraces to find the offending code and change it to resolve all necessary promises before doing identity comparisons.

Christine finally cleared enough other things off her plate where she could start contributing to the game. We thought it would be nice to have the game start with a splash screen of triangle'y animations that would resemble the kinds of art players would make in the game. We decided to use the Blender add-on by Ursula Kurdali named Stop Motion since it gives a great amount of freedom to animate by creating and destroying as much geometry as you like. Christine made the first mockup of a splash screen animation of a "death" type character swinging a scythe.

According to recent reports, however, the animation hadn't left Blender yet. We're gonna have to figure out how to get those polygons out and into the game engine!

In a recent development, this was the day to finish implementing the core game loop. We wanted the weekend to be all about fixing bugs and making it look and feel as good as we can. At last, the points awarded at the end of each round were displayed in the UI. The player list on the left side of the screen was transformed into a leaderboard that sorted players by score.

Recent findings suggest that while creating the leaderboard it was discovered that Goblins was not correctly parsing pairs received over OCapN. Christine swooped in with a quick fix and Jessica folowed up with a regression test.

It has been revealed that we also added a small set of emoji reactions underneath the leaderboard. Reactions were not critical to the core gameplay but they were planned from the very beginning of the project. It's good that we had time to add them because it was a lot of fun to spam emojis at the artist to give them an indication of how good or bad they were doing.

With two days left and the core gameplay loop complete, the focus shifted to bug fixing and adding juice. Up until this point the HTML was mostly unstyled (as you can see in the videos above), so Dave added a little CSS to improve the look and feel.

Industry observers note that A playtest revealed that the simple PRNG we were using was implemented incorrectly. We noticed because the artist prompt was always "bus" no matter how many rounds you played. Oops! This was fixed.

In a recent development, remember that crossed hellos bug from day 7? Dave finally implemented a workaround, which was to simply throw out the first pancake and try again, as suggested by Christine. A simple race against a timeout was all that was needed. We'll be thinking about how to fix this in Goblins so this situation cannot happen in the future.

Industry observers note that christine started work on making more animations for the game's intro. The "death" animation was a good "hello world" for testing the exporter, but being all black it was too simple to make sure everything worked right; draw order, etc, didn't matter. Christine made a "square guys" animation as a kind of Acid2 test equivalent. This file had several tricky properties to it, most especially that draw order would matter, colors would be vital, et cetera.

Christine also made this triangle'y duck themed piece:.

In a recent development, christine wrote a Python script to export the animations from Blender into a custom format encoded using Syrup. The encoded data was then embedded into the Scheme program as bytevector literals using a little script. Dave then started work on a renderer for these animations, but it wasn't working quite well enough by the end of the day to commit and push it.

Up until this point we only had a small number of frequently-repeated words. Morgan Lemmer-Webber curated a word list for us, starting with an existing public domain word list of 5000 words, and curated down to a 621 words, selecting for words that were more feasible to draw (ranging from easy to challenging, but all trying to be feasible).

The game name was changed from the placeholder "Twenty Triangles" to "Polydraw".

Recent findings suggest that the code to render animations was finished. Some final minor bug fixes were made. Some CSS was tweaked. Original music and sound effects by encrypted.whispers were added. Additionally, we used a few CC0-licensed sound effects by Kenney.

According to recent reports, A few gameplay improvements were made, such as showing guessers what the prompt was when the round ends and how many triangles the artist had remaining. Little improvements can make a big difference and both of these changes were very helpful for players and made the game feel more polished.

There wasn't enough time remaining to do as much work on resiliency in the face of network partitions as we would have liked, but Dave did squeeze in a commit that allowed the game to survive if a guest leaves. Unfortunately, the experience for the disconnected guest isn't very good as they don't see any message that their connection dropped.

It has been revealed that we did a final playtest to confirm that there weren't any showstopper bugs. Christine added final splash animations.

Finally, Christine added some code (fixed up by Dave) and animations which would overlay over the drawings indicating that drawing was starting, it was time to guess, or the results.

We submitted the game two hours before the deadline! Now it was time to catch our breath and show off the game to everyone we could. Dave even played it live with a couple other people on a stream! Here's a screenshot which gives you a good look of the final result:.

According to recent reports, the response was quite positive! The feedback we received closely matched the things we wanted to improve upon if we had more time: better disconnect handling, a way for the host to skip to the next phase instead of being forced to wait for the timer to run out, and invite URLs (rather than URIs) that auto-join the game when visited.

Polydraw ranked 5th overall in the official game jam results.

Try playing it over on itch.io and leave us a comment!

In a recent development, your support makes our work possible! If you like what we do, please consider becoming a Spritely supporter today!

Latest Update: Cyberattack on service provider exposes payee data at 40 Irish credit unions

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (615 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Minister calls notification delay 'not acceptable' after October attack on Irish banking player Wellington IT came to light in November.
  • An attack on software provider Wellington IT exposed saved payee details held by around 40 Irish credit unions, prompting a minister to criticize the firm's delay in notifying them.
  • Robert Troy, Ireland's minister of state with responsibility for credit unions, mentioned the breach happened in October but many affected institutions only learned of it in recent days.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Minister calls notification delay 'not acceptable' after October attack on Irish banking player Wellington IT came to light in November.

An attack on software provider Wellington IT exposed saved payee details held by around 40 Irish credit unions, prompting a minister to criticize the firm's delay in notifying them.

Robert Troy, Ireland's minister of state with responsibility for credit unions, mentioned the breach happened in October but many affected institutions only learned of it in recent days.

Troy told Irish broadcaster RTÉ that the breach occurred "sometime in October," and Wellington IT's delay in providing details to its credit union customers was "not acceptable.".

News of the concerns affecting Irish credit unions broke on Tuesday, although the government said at the time it was only investigating a "possible cybersecurity incident" in the first instance, and did not name Wellington IT until Wednesday.

Recent findings suggest that affected credit unions said attackers exploited a vulnerability in their provider's online banking platform between October 2 and 4. The flaw was closed on October 6.

Troy mentioned the affected credit unions were only informed for the first time in recent days.

The exposed records concern payees saved in members' online banking accounts. Those records can also be linked to the members who created them.

The information exposed varies between institutions and individual records, but disclosures list the following data types:.

Names on payee bank accounts and saved nicknames.

Business Identifier Codes (BICs).

International Bank Account Numbers (IBANs).

Internal reference numbers that do not identify customers.

Industry observers note that credit unions including St. Canice's said online banking passwords, PINs, and login credentials were unaffected, and that the exposed payee details did not provide access to members' accounts or funds.

Sources indicate that st. Canice's warned members not to transfer money in response to anyone claiming it needed to be moved to safety because of the breach.

The CEO of Belfast-based Wellington IT, Colin Mitchell, said in a statement that the firm notified the affected organizations "as soon as we confirmed the potential risk to customer data.".

He said Wellington IT has engaged outside cybersecurity experts to help investigate the breach, and reported the matter to the relevant authorities.

Mitchell added: "We are directly supporting our customers in their assessment of the potential impact on affected individuals and to help them meet any applicable regulatory obligations.

Industry observers note that "We recognize the importance of this matter to our customers and their members and are treating it with the utmost seriousness. We remain focused on completing a thorough investigation and communicating directly with our customers as the investigation progresses.".

Owned by Canadian company Vencora, Wellington IT has offices in Belfast and Dublin, and provides credit unions with software, mobile apps, private cloud infrastructure, and fully managed services.

Around 40 credit unions in Ireland were affected, roughly a quarter of the national total, Troy mentioned.

Credit unions operate similarly to traditional banks, offering savings accounts and loans, but are owned by their members and are not-for-profit organizations.

Troy told RTÉ that cybersecurity is a constant challenge for financial institutions, as technology and threats evolve over time.

"What's most vital is that financial institutions take all the right measures to mitigate against these threats and that is what is happening," he remarked.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that developers building web and AI applications on Vercel can now add Amazon S3 storage resources directly from the Vercel Marketplace and v0, combining the durability, scalability, and performance of S3 with the convenience of Vercel’s provisioning workflow.
  • Sources indicate that why this matters Millions of developers build, deploy, and scale web and AI applications on Vercel.
  • According to recent reports, getting started From the Vercel dashboard, go to the Storage tab and choose Create.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that developers building web and AI applications on Vercel can now add Amazon S3 storage resources directly from the Vercel Marketplace and v0, combining the durability, scalability, and performance of S3 with the convenience of Vercel’s provisioning workflow. Starting today, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), including Amazon S3 Tables and Amazon S3 Vectors, is natively available on the Vercel Marketplace and v0 by Vercel, covering three distinct workloads: everyday storage, analytics, and AI.

Sources indicate that why this matters Millions of developers build, deploy, and scale web and AI applications on Vercel. Storage is essential to performant applications, but provisioning it previously required navigating to the AWS Management Console to configure policies and credentials. Now, S3 storage integrates directly into the Vercel developer experience, with resource provisioning and connection configuration handled automatically. Together with existing integrations for Amazon Aurora, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, you get a complete application stack inside Vercel (from your database layer through to object, vector, and open table storage), all on one AWS account with one bill.

Figure 1 – The AWS page on the Vercel Marketplace.

According to recent reports, getting started From the Vercel dashboard, go to the Storage tab and choose Create. Select AWS, pick your S3 bucket type, choose a Region, and create the bucket. Provisioning takes a few seconds.

Figure 2 – Creating an Amazon S3 general purpose bucket in Vercel by choosing a Region and a name.

Connect the bucket to a project, then pull the environment variables with the Vercel CLI:.

The integration injects AWS_REGION, AWS_ROLE_ARN, AWS_RESOURCE_ARN, and a bucket name such as S3_BUCKET_NAME, S3_TABLE_BUCKET_NAME, or S3_VECTOR_BUCKET_NAME. At runtime, the awsCredentialsProvider from @vercel/functions/oidc exchanges a short-lived OIDC token with AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) for temporary credentials scoped to your resource. No static keys are stored anywhere.

Object storage with S3 This Next.js route uploads a file to a general purpose bucket:.

Use ListObjectsV2Command and GetObjectCommand with the same client to list and read objects.

It has been revealed that analytics with S3 Tables S3 Tables offer S3 storage purpose-built for analytics and are designed to automatically optimize query performance as data volumes grow. They provide fully managed Apache Iceberg tables with automated table maintenance and compaction, and they work with any Apache Iceberg REST Catalog-compliant engine. You can use DuckDB inside a Vercel Function for lightweight queries. This example attaches the table bucket by its ARN and runs an aggregate query:.

If you run DuckDB inside a Next.js route, add @duckdb/node-api to serverExternalPackages in next.config.mjs so the native bindings are not bundled.

It has been revealed that vector search with S3 Vectors S3 Vectors deliver purpose-built, cost-optimized vector storage for AI agents, AI inference, and semantic search of your content stored in Amazon S3. S3 Vectors provides native support for storing and querying vectors without a separate vector database, but it does not generate them. Create the embeddings with your model of choice, then query the index for the closest matches:.

Industry observers note that building with v0 by Vercel From v0, describe what you want to build and it provisions the right resource. Ask for “a photo gallery where users upload images using AWS” to get a general purpose bucket, “a support bot that answers questions from my PDFs” to get S3 Vectors, or “an analytics dashboard for my clickstream data” to get S3 Tables. v0 then configures the connection and generates working code.

Figure 3 – v0 generating a PDF support bot from a natural language prompt, with Amazon S3 Vectors connected and the application in the Preview panel.

Combining S3 with AWS databases Every AWS service on Vercel shares the same account and authentication model, so you can combine them with no extra setup. For example, store file metadata in Aurora with the files in S3, or store document text in DynamoDB with embeddings in S3 Vectors for RAG retrieval.

It has been revealed that using Vercel with your AWS account You can create a fresh AWS account through the integration, which supports S3 features for building and testing. You can also link an existing AWS account to use your full set of S3 and AWS capabilities and keep your current billing. If you link an existing AWS account, Vercel works only with new buckets that you create through the platform. Because every S3 resource lives in your own AWS account, you keep AWS-native tooling and a single place to manage storage.

In a recent development, pricing and availability There is no charge for the integration, and you pay standard Amazon S3 pricing for the resources you use. New AWS accounts created through Vercel receive $100 in credits valid for six months. Amazon S3, including S3 Tables and S3 Vectors, is available from v0 and the Vercel Marketplace in all commercial AWS Regions supported by Vercel. To get started, visit v0 or the AWS page on the Vercel Marketplace.

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (648 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that nothing last week added a newly introduced kind of compute.
  • In a recent development, the counterweight arrived on Thursday.
  • HeadlinesAWS Lambda Web Functions is a latest form factor that runs a standard HTTP web application on Lambda without rewriting it into an event handler.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that nothing last week added a newly introduced kind of compute. What it did instead was shorten the distance between the code you already have and that code being live. AWS Lambda learned to run a plain HTTP server with no adapter in front of it, and Amazon S3 became something you can provision from inside the tool you were already using, without opening the AWS Management Console. Different services, same direction.

In a recent development, the counterweight arrived on Thursday. As it gets easier to put things into production, it matters more that you can say what those things are allowed to do, and this week’s most interesting read is about exactly that. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news….

HeadlinesAWS Lambda Web Functions is a latest form factor that runs a standard HTTP web application on Lambda without rewriting it into an event handler. You take a port-listening server built with Express, Hono, Fastify, or Next.js, run aws lambda-web deploy, and get back a live HTTPS URL in under a minute. No adapters, no infrastructure to set up first, no framework lock-in. Lambda now has three form factors on the same Firecracker isolation, which compose inside one application: Event Functions (the model you already know) for async work, Web Functions for the user-facing layer, and MicroVMs for stateful sandboxes running untrusted code.

Recent findings suggest that two details make this more than repackaging. Each execution environment handles up to 128 concurrent requests, so a burst of traffic shares warm environments instead of mapping one request to one environment, and billing meters the CPU time your code actually uses rather than wall-clock time. For server-side rendering, API backends, and inference endpoints streaming tokens, where most of the elapsed time is spent waiting, that changes the arithmetic. Adding --regions to the same deploy command replicates your code and configures latency-based routing behind a single global URL, and you can split traffic across revisions by weight for a canary rollout. It’s available in five Regions, running Node.js 24 on Arm64 with VPC connectivity. The AWS Compute Blog has a longer walkthrough, and Amazon CloudFront can now use a Web Function endpoint as an origin with origin access control.

The week’s other headline isn’t a launch. Trust in Depth: giving agents more autonomy without losing control makes an argument I keep running into in practice: putting a person in the loop for every agent action works at small scale and then quietly stops working, because people asked to check everything stop catching what matters. The alternative is four questions answered at four moments, which AWS calls scope, know, bound, and observe. The part worth sitting with is that an agent’s limits belong outside its own reasoning, in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore policies enforced at the gateway, because an agent cannot turn off a control it does not run. AWS has run automated reasoning in production for more than a decade, including AWS Identity and Access Management at more than 2.1 billion requests per second, and the case here is for pointing it at the rules you write for agents.

Microsoft To Do will soon become Microsoft Done

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (444 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apps retire in June 2027, with no automatic task migration and no Planner replacement for personal accounts.
  • Microsoft has slipped some bad news into this week's Ignite AI puffery: the To Do apps are retiring on June 30, 2027, ending a journey that began with its acquisition of Wunderlist more than a decade ago.
  • It has been revealed that the confirmation came in an announcement about unified tasks and looks for Copilot and Microsoft 365.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apps retire in June 2027, with no automatic task migration and no Planner replacement for personal accounts.

Microsoft has slipped some bad news into this week's Ignite AI puffery: the To Do apps are retiring on June 30, 2027, ending a journey that began with its acquisition of Wunderlist more than a decade ago.

It has been revealed that the confirmation came in an announcement about unified tasks and looks for Copilot and Microsoft 365. Until now, there was To Do or Planner (in basic or premium guise). The idea is "a single system for tracking your work as an individual, as a team, and as an organization." To Do contributes features to that future, but its apps don't get to join it.

It has been revealed that the problem is that Planner doesn't do everything To Do does. Microsoft would like customers to migrate to Planner but, by the firm's own admission, there are plenty of gaps. No native Windows or Mac desktop apps are planned to replace To Do; file attachments aren't supported on tasks in the Planner private blueprint, and there's no equivalent to To Do list groups in Planner. "Equivalent To Do printing and email-list capabilities are not right now planned for the replacement experience," and so on.

In a recent development, existing To Do tasks and lists won't migrate to Planner either. They'll remain accessible through Planner until June 30, 2027, but that access ends with the apps. Microsoft says the date does not itself trigger deletion of the underlying data.

Very much a case of "don't let the door hit you on the way out.".

Unifying tasks and looks is a good idea – the current situation does create confusion, as Microsoft acknowledged. However, taking an axe to To Do, which was developed to be a successor to Wunderlist (acquired in 2015 for a figure between $100 million and $200 million, an early action under Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella), seems extreme.

Microsoft calls the replacement "a unified platform for people and agents across Microsoft 365" and stated: "This unified platform makes accessing Planner through Copilot, Cowork and Autopilot easier.".

Some owners responding to the announcement were unimpressed, with one declaring "What a mess," and another asking if To Do might be spun off into an open source project: "Not everything needs to be put into an AI/Copilot agent.".

According to recent reports, indeed, it doesn't. But a useful service that doesn't ram Copilot and AI integration down customers' throats at every opportunity? That would never do.

The message for To Do consumers appears to be: Get with the Plan(ner) or just get out. ®.

#23819. Tech Report: Design for Understandability
