Tech Report: Design for Understandability

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 28 min read (5651 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jschuster

⏱️ ~28 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this is a talk I gave at Google’s internal Code Health Summit in November of 2025.
  • In a world where LLMs generate much of our code, understanding that code is more crucial than ever.
  • In a recent development, there’s a better way to go about this.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is a talk I gave at Google’s internal Code Health Summit in November of 2025. I’m sharing it here in the hopes that it sparks further learning and discussion.

In a world where LLMs generate much of our code, understanding that code is more crucial than ever. But with a system as large and complex as Google’s codebase, SWEs can easily fall into a pattern of learned helplessness where the best you can do is tweak the code and pray that it passes the tests. Without understanding, LLMs are little more than complexity-generating machines running at top speed.

In a recent development, there’s a better way to go about this. Just as our industry has learned to design software for testability, we can also design it for understandability. We can use ideas like design by contract, class invariants, modularity, and more to create systems that we can understand one piece at a time, rather than piling more onto the big ball of mud and hoping it doesn’t all collapse.

Industry observers note that is it easy? No. But is it worthwhile? Absolutely. These ideas aren’t new, but they’re not nearly as widely taught or well understood as they deserve to be, and mastering them leads to a world where we can have more confidence in our code and increase velocity at the same time.

Hi everyone, thanks for having me! Let’s get started.

I’d like to start this talk with a question: If LLMs can code, then what is left for human SWEs?

The tech industry is promptly looking to large language models to write all of our code. But you might say: isn’t writing code our job as software engineers? Where does this leave the responsibility of SWEs? What is the essential human element that SWEs add on top of LLMs?

Sources indicate that every one of you is going to have a different answer to this question, and that’s fine. But here’s my take.

That necessary human element is judgment. Judgment of whether the code is maintainable. Judgment of whether it is healthy.

In a recent development, LLMs can follow patterns and generate code that looks like what it was trained on. Sometimes they can produce useful tips and critiques for a piece of code. But that critical piece of judgment, of deciding whether some code is suitable for the task it was designed for, is still up to you, the human.

Sources indicate that because here’s the thing: LLMs today are still a sloppy intern. Sometimes the code they produce is good, but sometimes it’s completely off-track and needs correcting. You wouldn’t incorporate a sloppy intern’s code into your system without a close review first, so you shouldn’t do so for an LLM’s code either.

YOU are responsible for the quality of your code, regardless of whether you had an LLM generate it for you or wrote it the old-fashioned way with fingers on a keyboard.

So where does that leave us? If LLMs are going to write a lot of the code for us, then we’re looking at a future where we humans are going to spend less time writing code, and more time reading code and understanding it, in order to make sure it passes our quality bar.

This means it’s more key than ever to get better at understanding code, and to speed up that reading and understanding process.

Industry observers note that now: if you want to get better at something, it’s helpful to set an aspirational goal for yourself. Something that’s above your current skill level, and drives you to get better and better every day.

Here’s the goal I propose: we should be able to predict the behavior of every line of code, without running a single test.

Let me say that again: We should be able to predict the behavior of every line of code, without running a single test.

Recent findings suggest that now, I know you may be thinking: “Understand every line of code? Without testing? Are you serious?! There’s way too much complexity and legacy code for me to ever be able to do that!”.

Sources indicate that you might think so. And if we take our hands off the wheel and relinquish all control, you might be right. But I’m here to tell you there’s a better way.

We can design our code to be understandable.

Sources indicate that consider that a decade or two ago, we used to think that writing multiple tests for every public method in an API would have been infeasible. It wasn’t because we didn’t want to, or that we weren’t trying. It was because we hadn’t designed our code to make testing possible at that level. But gradually, across the software industry, we changed our practices to design for testability. Today, designing our code for testability is so ingrained into our culture that doing anything else is practically unthinkable. We can do the same for understandability, so that our code enables us to understand it better.

Industry observers note that our own Code Health guide makes a strong case for understandability. It states “For code to be sustainable, it must be understood. Change cannot be made unless a developer knows what the system currently provides, and what needs to change to adapt to new circumstances. As a result, key components of code health include good documentation, easy to understand error messages, and clear, simple code”.

Not only is designing for understandability crucial, but it’s a learnable skill. It’s not some magical ability that you either have or you don’t. There are specific, concrete actions you can take to improve the understandability of your code.

Sources indicate that I’m going to introduce you to a few of those today. Think of it as a “starter kit” for designing for understandability. We’ll also talk more about a general theme that runs through all of these practices, so that at a certain point you can find even more ways to design your code for understandability.

It has been revealed that the ideas I’m going to show you today are not fresh. But they’re not taught as well as they should be, when they’re taught at all, and most of us have only a rough understanding of how to apply them. My goal today is to sharpen that understanding just a little bit, and make it just a little more practical, so we can kickstart a process of making our code more understandable over time.

So let’s get started on each of these Design for Understandability practices.

The first one is Design by Contract.

To motivate the idea, let’s ask the question: when calling a method, what behavior should you rely on?

Let’s say we have this binary search method, but its documentation is not terribly helpful (you’ve probably seen something like this before).

Binary search is reasonably well understood, but as a caller of the method, we have some questions we want to ask about this specific implementation. Such as:.

It has been revealed that the documentation doesn’t answer these questions. So what can we do?

According to recent reports, first, we could guess. But we’ll probably be wrong.

Sources indicate that second, we could read the code. But that might take a long time, especially if the particular behavior we care about is buried several levels deep.

According to recent reports, third, we could test the code on some examples and see what happens. But just because it works a certain way on some examples doesn’t necessarily mean it works that way for all such inputs. Furthermore, even if it works that way now, there’s no guarantee that it will continue to work that way in the future.

Recent findings suggest that the point is that without a clear statement of what this code is intended to do, there’s no distinction between implementation and intent. The SWE who wants to use this code has to guess at which behavior the method commits to, versus which behavior is an implementation detail that might change over time.

This is where contracts come in.

There are many ways to define a contract, but for the sake of this talk I’m going to define it as a formal-ish description of the observable behavior that each participant in an interaction commits to.

In the real world, a basic contract is something like “If I cook dinner, then you will wash the dishes”.

In programming, an example might be: “If the caller provides a non-negative integer n, then the square-root function returns the square root of n”.

Let’s see how contracts can help us with our binary-search example.

Sources indicate that here’s a possible contract for this function. It notes, “If the list is sorted, binarySearch returns the index of the first occurrence of t in the list, or -1 if not found. Behavior is undefined for unsorted lists.”.

We can see that this contract answers the questions we asked about it:.

It has been revealed that the power of a contract is that it defines a clear boundary between the author’s intent and the implementation. The caller doesn’t have to guess at the behavior anymore: they can just read the contract, and if a specific detail of the behavior isn’t there, they will know that it’s unspecified.

Industry observers note that in reality, this isn’t always perfect. Whether intentionally or accidentally, we still tend to end up with code that relies on implementation details rather than specified behavior. But contracts at least give us a way to minimize this behavior.

Now that we understand what a contract looks like, let’s talk about how contracts can help us reason about and understand our code better.

Suppose you just wrote a method. I’m going to draw that method as a little circle here.

You want to know if it’s correct.

I’m going to use a purple circle to stand for methods we’ve read the code for.

Now, our method doesn’t live in isolation: it calls some other code.

Sources indicate that so, you think “Okay, well, I need to understand what those do. I’m going to read the code for those methods.”.

In a recent development, well, those methods call other methods, and we start thinking about this, and figure out how we’re going to reason about those. And at this point you can maybe see where I’m going.

In a recent development, oh no. Now we have lots and lots of code we have to read across our entire code base.

Recent findings suggest that why do we need all this reasoning just to reason about one single method? That’s all we’re trying to do! How did we get so out of control?

So, let’s back up and try again, using Design by Contract this time.

Recent findings suggest that you still have to read your own code. We can’t get around this part; that’s the change we just made.

And we haven’t changed the code. It still calls those other methods.

But now, the trick is that we can read just the contract on those called methods, not the code.

And that’s it! We can stop here. We don’t need to worry about all of that other code. The contracts tell us all we need to know about calling these other two methods.

The rest of that code still exists, but we don’t have to think about it. The contract abstracts away all that other behavior that doesn’t matter to us as the caller of these two methods.

So that is the power that contracts give to us to reason about our code.

Finally, I’ll wrap up this section with a few tips for writing contracts:.

Recent findings suggest that first, document the behavior that you’re willing to commit to. This is usually the same as what you want your callers to rely on. For example, you probably want to document the return value of your method. But the exact human-readable text in your error messages? Not so much.

According to recent reports, second, describe your error handling in your contracts. A contract does not and should not be just about the happy path. If your method might go wrong in some way, tell the caller under what conditions it might go wrong, and how you’re going to signal that to the caller, whether it be through a special return value, or an exception, or something else.

Sources indicate that finally, keep in mind that the more callers your method has, the harder it is to change the contract. If it’s a private method used only by your team? Sure, that’s probably an easy case to change both the contract and change the callers to match. If it’s a public method on a popular framework used by hundreds of other projects? Then renegotiating the contract is a much more expensive effort, so you should evaluate the costs and benefits carefully before deciding to do that.

So that was the first element in our Design for Understandability starter kit.

The next one is data invariants.

Let me explain this idea with a little story.

Industry observers note that early in the COVID-19 pandemic, when my wife and I started working from home, we missed having free soda at work. So we got in the habit of keeping cans of Diet Coke in the fridge.

But there was a problem: we were great at taking cans out of the fridge, but not so great about putting new ones back in. So if you’re working hard and looking forward to taking a break with a nice cold beverage, it was a major disappointment to open a Coke-less fridge and resort to drinking room-temperature soda from the pantry instead.

The problem was that we hadn’t set any rules on how we retrieve Diet Coke and how we replenish the fridge. Without any rules governing access to the fridge, we eventually got into an unwanted state: in this case, an empty fridge.

In a recent development, this happens in code, too. For example, let’s say you have this proto to represent a customer’s order [Note: “proto” is Google jargon for a Protocol Buffers message, similar to a JSON object]. If you receive this proto, how much do you trust that the total actually indicates the total amount on the items?

In a recent development, probably not much, right? This proto could have come from any part of your code, so it’s easy to imagine that someone forgot to set that field appropriately.

Protos give you completely uncontrolled access to the underlying representation of your data. Protos are great for transferring data back and forth across the network, but they’re poorly suited to situations where you want to rule out certain states.

To solve these kinds of problems, we can use data invariants. A data invariant is a statement about a piece of data that is always true.

Recent findings suggest that data invariants are a principled way to enforce these kinds of valid states in your data. If you use them well, you can avoid a lot of bugs in your code.

Let’s see how we can use invariants to solve the Diet Coke problem, and similar problems you might come across in your own code.

First, identify the invariant you want to maintain.

Ask yourself: What’s the property you want to rely on for this piece of data? Where are the places in the code where you explicitly validate and return an error if invalid? Alternatively, where do you make the assumption that it’s invalid, but you’re not actually sure?

In this case, the invariant we want is “the fridge always contains a Diet Coke”.

Second, you need to document the invariant.

In a recent development, it’s important to note this is a separate step. It’s one thing to have an invariant in your own head. It’s another thing to write it down so that you communicate it to everyone else who might touch this code. Not to mention that if you come back to this code months or years later, you yourself might have forgotten which exact invariant you meant to maintain.

Write it down where people will see it: probably close to the relevant data members, or maybe in a class-level comment at the top.

Industry observers note that third, establish the invariant at creation time. Usually this will be done in a constructor or factory method. In this case, we’re constructing the fridge with a few drinks already added.

Fourth, every time you change your the data, make sure you maintain the invariant.

Recent findings suggest that this is the part my wife and I didn’t do for our fridge. What we should have done is established a rule where if you take a Diet Coke, you put another one back in the fridge to make sure there’s another for the next person.

It has been revealed that you can maintain the invariant many ways – that part is up to you. The important thing is that you always maintain it. Without that, you have to think to yourself “Wait, are there going to be Diet Cokes in the fridge? Did I already take them out earlier? Let me go back and check all my callers to see if they did that already”. With an invariant, though, you just know: If I have a Fridge object, then it definitely has Diet Cokes, regardless of the sequence of operations that led to this point.

Finally, one last step, and this might be the hardest one: you need to maintain the invariant as the code evolves. It’s relatively easy to maintain the invariant for a single version of code. But over the weeks, months, and years, complexity will creep in, fresh requirements will force you to change the code, and you might accidentally break the invariant or forget you even had one.

Sources indicate that establish the culture on your team that maintaining invariants is just a thing you do. If you have a mental checklist of things you look for in code review, make sure that maintaining the invariants is on that checklist.

In a recent development, so how do data invariants help us design for understandability? Let’s first consider what we have to do when we don’t have an invariant.

Recent findings suggest that recall this representation of all the methods in your codebase, calling each other in various ways. Suppose you have a proto-based version of the fridge, and you want to know if it has any Diet Cokes in it. Because it’s a proto, you don’t have a way of knowing what state it’s in.

So, you need to check all the callers of the current method.

And you do the check, crawling across the codebase, and you find that there’s one particular case where you didn’t enforce it.

Of course you can fix these issues one at a time as they crop up, but all that searching sounds like a lot of work, right? What do you think are the chances you’re always going to find that one particular buggy spot? What are the chances that latest methods added to this web of code are going to maintain that condition?

In contrast, let’s try the version with our Fridge class and its invariant.

Recent findings suggest that in this case, the class has an invariant: the Fridge always has at least one Diet Coke, no matter what operations have been done previously or where we came from. By maintaining that invariant, we’ve removed the need to check what every single caller does.

This is what data invariants do for you: they let you focus on the state you’re in now, and not how you got there.

That wraps up the section on data invariants.

The final practice I want to discuss today is isolating side effects and dependencies on global state.

Sources indicate that to motivate this idea with an example. Let’s say there’s a supermarket point-of-sales system with this method to compute sales tax. Now ask yourself: what are the inputs and outputs for this method?

Seems pretty obvious, right? It takes in a customer’s grocery order and returns the sales tax as an integer.

Industry observers note that but that’s not the whole story. If you dig into the implementation of this method, you’ll find that it reads in a set of sales tax rates from a separate file. That’s effectively a new input channel! The code depends on that data to compute the tax just as much as it depends on the content of the grocery order itself.

In a recent development, and if you look further, you’ll find that the method also records the computed tax in the store’s account database for bookkeeping purposes. That’s a fresh output, but it’s nowhere to be found in the type signature!

So functions have two kinds of input and output: the ones that are visible in the type signature, like the order and the computed sales tax, and the ones that are hidden, like the tax rates file and the entry in the accounting database.

The hidden outputs are more commonly known as side effects. Side effects generally come in two flavors: mutation, so modifying something like a global variable or one of your input arguments, and outputs outside of your process. That would be things like database writes, remote procedure calls, printing to the console, etc.

In a recent development, I don’t know a common term for the hidden inputs, but I would call these dependencies on global state. Again, there are two flavors: dependency on the state of some global variable, or a dependency on the state of the system your program is running in. That’s things like permissions to access the database, the existence of a given file on the file system, and even the ability to read the system clock.

Sources indicate that so why are these hidden inputs and outputs a problem? They make code hard to test, hard to reuse, and hard to reason about.

According to recent reports, hard to test because you have to make sure you have all the necessary dependencies are set up before you can even run the method in your test. And then once you do run the method, side effects often force the test to rely more on interaction verification than state verification, which can be brittle.

According to recent reports, hard to reuse because the code now makes assumptions about what kinds of resources you have available to you. If you need to reuse some method in another part of the codebase, but the input data needs to come from a different source, or you need to store the results in a different place, those side effects and global states are going to create a tight coupling between your computation code and the specific sources and destinations for that computation, which will make your life harder.

Hard to reason about because, by definition, these inputs and outputs are hidden! If you don’t even know that your method is making these kinds of assumptions on the system that it’s running in, then you’re going to make some faulty conclusions about how your code will behave.

According to recent reports, now I’m not saying all side effects or global state are bad. And I’m not saying we should all immediately switch to a pure functional programming language like Haskell.

Effects have to happen somewhere. Without side effects, computation is just the process of making a metal box hot for a little while(and even that heat is a side effect! although not usually one we care about).

In a recent development, but by default, we tend to sprinkle them everywhere throughout the code. Need some input? Just read the file at whatever point you happen to be at in the code. Need to store your result? Go ahead and do it 4 layers deep into your business logic.

Without a principled approach to side effects and global state, we’re constantly running into the kinds of problems we just described.

Industry observers note that there’s a better way, which is to isolate the side effects and the dependencies on global state. Much of our code is just logic on top of the data (once we get it) and creating upcoming data based on that. Divide your code into the computational parts on one hand, and the parts that deal with side effects and global state on the other.

There are a few common patterns for this.

Industry observers note that one of them is Command/Query Separation. It’s a pattern where each method is either a command, which performs some side effect, or a query, which is a pure function that returns its output as the return value. But you maintain a strict separation so that no function does both of those things.

Industry observers note that another pattern is called “Functional Core, Imperative Shell”. This is a pattern at the architectural level. You focus the inner modules of your system on the business logic and computation, not performing side effects – this is the “functional core”. The outer modules coordinate the effects of your system with that computation, so that the complexity of the side effects is isolated to just that outer layer, and the majority of your system is simpler due to the functional purity.

As with the other two practices, side effects and global state have a significant impact on how we think about code.

For example, you might be working on a method and need to delete a file. Your assumption is that it should be okay, you think no one is using it.

According to recent reports, but then it turns out, some other part of the codebase was relying on it, and you just broke them. The code was so far away and unrelated that you didn’t even think to check there.

On the other hand, if you isolate your side effects and global state such that they only happen in a known region of the code, then you can have confidence that you really aren’t going to break anyone else.

So, those are the three starter practices for Design for Understandability: Design by Contract, Data Invariants, and Isolating Side Effects and Dependencies on Global State.

Now, I’ve presented these as independent practices, but in fact they’re not so distinct. There’s a unifying theme to them. That theme is local reasoning.

What do I mean by local reasoning?

Local reasoning means you can come to conclusions about some chunk of code by looking only at that chunk of code, plus just a small amount of the neighboring code, like the specifications or contracts of the components that you directly interact with.

Sources indicate that this is as opposed to global reasoning. That’s the kind of reasoning where to answer even a simple question, you have to read a large chunk of the codebase, because the answer could be in any method, at any level of the call stack.

The benefit of local reasoning is that it puts a hard boundary on how far you have to look in order to figure something out about your system: there’s always a limit to how far you have to search.

Industry observers note that so let’s talk about how each of the practices we talked about enables local reasoning. You may have noticed we covered this already, but let’s review.

Design by Contract defines the expected behavior for a caller and a called method. That means that to understand what behavior a caller can rely on, or what behavior a called method is obligated to implement, the only place we need to look is the defined interface for that called method. Without that, we would revert to global reasoning to find all the parts of the code that might depend on some aspect of this method’s behavior.

Data invariants often go hand in hand with contracts, but they usually say something about an entire object rather than a single method on that object.

If you have a piece of data and you want to know something about its validity, like “does this fridge have any diet cokes?”, an invariant is what lets you immediately conclude yes, without looking at the callers that produced that data.

Finally, by isolating side effects and global state, you minimize the number of places in your code where a change in one part of the code can cause a problem in a completely unrelated part. So it lets you say things like “this is the only part of the code that’s allowed to touch this file, so I know for sure that it’s safe to delete”.

Another way of looking at local reasoning is to say that it minimizes the amount of context we need in order to reason about the system.

In a recent development, with global reasoning, you might need to know about any arbitrary part of your codebase, because the part that breaks your assumptions could be anywhere. You need to have the whole system loaded into your head in order to understand it.

Local reasoning keeps the amount of stuff you need loaded into your head to a reasonable size.

And guess what else benefits from small contexts: LLMs!

In a recent development, A key portion of making an LLM useful for your work is giving an LLM the right context to give good suggestions. But contexts costs tokens, and your tokens are limited. So LLMs give us another great motivation to use local reasoning and minimize our context.

It has been revealed that in other words, if you want your LLMs to be useful to you, then design your systems for understandability. Keep the necessary context small to make it easier for both you and your LLM to work with your code.

Sources indicate that at the beginning of this talk, I compared “Design for Understandability” to “Design for Testability”. I’d like to revisit that for a moment.

According to recent reports, before designing for testability was the norm, the default testing approach was application-level testing. Our code wasn’t set up for practices like dependency injection, so there was no way to run your code without setting up a huge set of dependencies as well. It wasn’t until we started designing and building our systems with testability in mind that we were able to make unit testing practical.

According to recent reports, that’s how it is with understandability and local reasoning, as well. If you don’t design for it ahead of time, it’s somewhere between hard and impossible to use local reasoning. But if you design for it along the way, you can make it work.

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve never heard of unit testing, then application-level testing seems obvious, and straightforward. But it’s not sufficient for modern software engineering. The same is true for global reasoning. I say it’s time we made designing for understandability a required part of our work, just like we did for testability.

So you may be thinking: that all sounds good, and these practices sound good on paper, but is designing for understandability feasible in practice? You’re probably not working in a brand-newly introduced greenfield project. You’re probably working on old code, with lots of old warts and complexity, and the situation may seem hopeless. Can you really do this?

It has been revealed that I’m here to say yes, this is feasible, if you take it one small step at a time. I’ll share some tips for getting started.

It has been revealed that first off, take little bits at a time. Don’t try to boil the ocean. Don’t say “We’re going to take two weeks off from our normal work, make all of our code perfectly understandable, and then we’re done!”. That’s not going to work; you’re going to have a bad time.

According to recent reports, instead, try applying some of these practices to just new methods that you write. You might have some old code out there that’s hard to change. So be it. Start with just the new methods and build some momentum.

Sources indicate that teach your teammates, as well. Maybe share this talk, or find other ways to help your teammates design for understandability.

Recent findings suggest that and finally, you might consider group programming sessions where you all get together and discuss: what does designing for understandability mean in your context? The Monarch team at Google did this with their Design by Contract practice and it worked well for them.

According to recent reports, here are some further resources to learn more about Design for Understandability. I’m not going to go into them in detail, but please feel free to go revisit the slides after the talk and check these out.

[Public links reproduced here for the blog post:].

In a recent development, in conclusion: design your code for understandability. Whenever you’re working on some code and realize that you’re falling back to global reasoning, pause for a moment. Ask yourself: can I do this with local reasoning instead? Would a contract or an invariant help here? Or what if I moved the side effects and global state somewhere else? Or, maybe you’ll think of some other practice that fits here – you probably know a lot of local-reasoning practices, even if you didn’t have the terminology to call it that until today.

It has been revealed that it’s time to make design for understandability just as much a part of software engineering as designing for testability is today. Understandability is not just helpful – it’s crucial, especially with Google-size systems. And not just that, but making your code understandable is doable if you design for it along the way.

Trust me: you’ll be glad you did.

Industry News: Voyager 1 celebrates one light-day with a nice lie-down

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Carrier signal still reaches Earth, but science and engineering data have gone AWOL.
  • Voyager 1 marked its milestone of one light-day from Earth in time-honored fashion: by giving controllers the silent treatment.
  • On November 14, the mission team noticed that the veteran spacecraft had stopped returning science and engineering data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Carrier signal still reaches Earth, but science and engineering data have gone AWOL.

Voyager 1 marked its milestone of one light-day from Earth in time-honored fashion: by giving controllers the silent treatment.

On November 14, the mission team noticed that the veteran spacecraft had stopped returning science and engineering data. A Deep Space Network antenna in Canberra, Australia, picked up its carrier signal, but no data.

The carrier signal indicates that Voyager 1 can still keep its antenna pointed at Earth and operate its transmitting equipment. However, something could be amiss with the system responsible for collecting and collating data from the spacecraft.

Something similar happened in 2023. After a few months of troubleshooting, engineers managed to coax a response from the probe, and by June 2024, NASA was delighted to announce that the spacecraft was back in action.

The problem was traced to a faulty computer chip, and engineers devised a software update to work around the defective hardware. That experience will stand the team in good stead this time around.

There was also a brief interruption in communications with Voyager 1 in October, which could have been caused by the spacecraft dropping into safe mode after a thruster failover occurred. Engineers are investigating whether the two incidents are connected.

Recent findings suggest that the Voyagers have an impressive amount of fault protection built in, which has contributed to their extraordinary longevity. It will be half a century in 2027 since the spacecraft were debuted, so glitches are understandable and likely.

NASA expects to confirm on November 19 that Voyager 1 was still operating when it reached one light-day from Earth on November 18, using its carrier signal and trajectory calculations. The day's delay neatly illustrates a major headache for engineers: communication latency.

Industry observers note that it now takes more than 24 hours for commands to reach the spacecraft, and the same amount of time for a response to be received. Diagnosing the fault could therefore take weeks or longer. ®.

Industry News: Introducing Amazon ECS Gateway: A fully-managed ingress solution for ECS services

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (874 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when platform teams manage containerized applications at scale on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), configuring ingress networking for each service often becomes a bottleneck.
  • Today, we’re announcing Amazon ECS Gateway, a latest account-level resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized workloads by dynamically provisioning and managing the necessary infrastructure on your behalf, with all resources created directly in your account.
  • ECS Gateway introduces a clear separation of responsibilities between platform teams and application teams.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when platform teams manage containerized applications at scale on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), configuring ingress networking for each service often becomes a bottleneck. For every new service, teams must provision and connect Application Load Balancers (ALBs), AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificates, AWS WAF web ACLs, and security groups, then keep those resources in sync as services scale, patch, or operate. This per-service overhead slows down deployment velocity and increases the risk of configuration drift across an organization.

Today, we’re announcing Amazon ECS Gateway, a latest account-level resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized workloads by dynamically provisioning and managing the necessary infrastructure on your behalf, with all resources created directly in your account.

ECS Gateway introduces a clear separation of responsibilities between platform teams and application teams.

ECS Gateway offers host-based routing using ALBs and enables up to 25 services to share a single ALB, optimizing infrastructure costs. ECS manages the full lifecycle of the underlying infrastructure, provisioning the first ALB when your first service connects, adding more ALBs as capacity is reached, and removing them when no longer needed. Each service receives a unique DNS hostname, giving your teams a ready-to-use endpoint the moment provisioning completes.

Industry observers note that A first look at ECS Gateway In the ECS console, platform team can create a gateway and sets its configuration. The infrastructure role is an IAM role that ECS assumes to provision and manage networking resources such as ALBs, security groups, and certificates in your account. To create a gateway, provide a gateway name and select an infrastructure role. You can optionally associate the gateway with ECS clusters during creation or later.

Recent findings suggest that choose a load balancing scheme, either public or VPC-internal traffic routing. Under Additional Settings, you can also set up a listener, port, maximum count of load balancers the gateway can scale to, and a web ACL lets you protect your web applications. Some settings, including the name, scheme, VPC, subnets, IP address type, listener protocol and port cannot be changed after gateway creation.

In a recent development, using AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), call CreateGateway with a name (unique per account), an infrastructure role, and a configuration object. No infrastructure is provisioned until a service connects with a gateway connector.

Once the gateway is created, you can take a look at the detailed configuration, gateway routes, load balancers, and associated clusters.

Now associate the gateway with one or more clusters (many-to-many), to make it available to ECS services on those clusters.

Use AssociateGatewayWithCluster to make the gateway available to services on a cluster:.

Industry observers note that to create and manage the ECS Gateway programmatically, including calling APIs and searching documentation, try the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI coding tool. To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS Gateway documentation.

ECS Gateway:Behind the scenesA gateway can be associated with up to 10,000 clusters, and a single cluster supports up to five gateway associations. This many-to-many relationship gives platform teams the flexibility to share a gateway across environments or assign multiple gateways (for example, public and private) to a single cluster.

It has been revealed that platform teams can control access by choosing which gateways to associate with which clusters. For additional control, use IAM policies to restrict who can deploy services to specific clusters.

Application teams add the gateway connector to each service definition in CreateService or UpdateService. If you have an existing ECS service with its own load balancer, you can adopt ECS Gateway incrementally by calling UpdateService to add a gateway connector. Both ingress paths remain available, allowing you to validate the gateway connection before removing the existing load balancer configuration.

At deployment time, Amazon ECS evaluates the gateways associated with the cluster and connects the service to every compatible gateway. A gateway is compatible when its access type matches the service’s connector filter, it is in the same VPC as the service, and it covers all Availability Zones used by the service’s configured subnets.

For each connection, Amazon ECS assigns the service to an ALB with available capacity and provisions the per-service resources: an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, a listener rule routing traffic for that hostname to the service target group, and a service security group allowing inbound traffic only from the ALB security group. If no existing ALB has capacity, ECS creates a newly introduced one (up to maxAlbCount referring to quota limit). Once provisioning completes, the gateway route becomes ACTIVE, and the service URL is ready to receive traffic.

ECS Gateway handles common operational scenarios automatically:.

Things to Know Here are a few important details to keep in mind:.

Now available Amazon ECS Gateway is available now in all commercial AWS Regions where ECS is available at no additional charge. You pay only for the underlying infrastructure provisioned in your account when services connect to a gateway, including applicable ALB charges, CloudWatch logs and metrics, ACM certificates, and data transfer charges. To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS Pricing page.

To get started, create your first gateway today in the ECS console, and send feedback to AWS re:Post for ECS or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

LeRobot v0.6.0: Imagine, Evaluate, Improve

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This upcoming release is about closing the robot learning loop: policies that imagine the future before acting, reward models that tell you when your robot succeeds, a deployment CLI that turns failures into training data, and six new simulation benchmarks to measure it all.
  • LeRobot v0.6.0 introduces world model policies (VLA-JEPA, FastWAM, LingBot-VA) that learn to imagine the future, a wave of upcoming VLAs (GR00T N1.7, MolmoAct2, EO-1, EVO1, Multitask DiT), and a new reward models API (Robometer, TOPReward).
  • In a recent development, the robotics world is asking a major question: do world models actually help robot policies?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This upcoming release is about closing the robot learning loop: policies that imagine the future before acting, reward models that tell you when your robot succeeds, a deployment CLI that turns failures into training data, and six new simulation benchmarks to measure it all. It also brings depth sensing, VLM-powered dataset annotation, custom video encoding, cloud training on HF Jobs, and a much leaner install.

LeRobot v0.6.0 introduces world model policies (VLA-JEPA, FastWAM, LingBot-VA) that learn to imagine the future, a wave of upcoming VLAs (GR00T N1.7, MolmoAct2, EO-1, EVO1, Multitask DiT), and a new reward models API (Robometer, TOPReward). It ships six new simulation benchmarks unified under lerobot-eval, the lerobot-rollout CLI with DAgger-style human-in-the-loop corrections, FSDP training, and cloud training on HF Jobs. Datasets get depth support, an automatic language annotation pipeline, custom video encoding, and up to 2x faster data loading, all on top of a leaner installation.

In a recent development, the robotics world is asking a major question: do world models actually help robot policies? v0.6.0 brings three policies to LeRobot to help answer that question. Each one learns to imagine the future as part of its training, and each takes a different path to keep that imagination affordable.

VLA-JEPA teaches a compact VLA (built on Qwen3-VL-2B) to predict the future in latent space while it learns to act: during training, a JEPA world model has to anticipate upcoming frames from the model's own actions. The trick is that the world model then disappears at inference, so you get world-model supervision at zero extra inference cost. Three ready-to-use checkpoints are on the Hub, including a DROID-pretrained base for fine-tuning:.

Check out the VLA-JEPA documentation and the paper to learn more.

Industry observers note that lingBot-VA goes one step further: an autoregressive video-action model that predicts future video and actions together, chunk by chunk, and feeds real observations back in to keep its imagination grounded. You can even save what the robot imagined (--policy.save_predicted_video=true) and compare it with what actually happened. Inference runs on a single 24–32 GB GPU. Check out the documentation and the paper for the technical details.

FastWAM asks the question in its paper title: do world action models need test-time future imagination? It pairs a ~5B video-generation expert with a compact action expert in a single network, so the model literally learns to dream its own rollouts. At inference it skips the dreaming entirely and directly denoises action chunks. Fine-tune it from lerobot/fastwam_base, and read more in the documentation.

Industry observers note that we upgraded our NVIDIA GR00T integration to GR00T N1.7, the newest open generation of NVIDIA's cross-embodiment foundation model. N1.7 swaps the previous VLM for Cosmos-Reason2-2B (built on Qwen3-VL) feeding a flow-matching action head, and our integration is parity-tested against NVIDIA's original Isaac-GR00T implementation: same inputs, same outputs. Flash-attention is now optional, so pip install 'lerobot[groot]' just works, and you can load NVIDIA's published checkpoints directly.

It has been revealed that GR00T N1.7 replaces N1.5 in LeRobot. If you need N1.5, pin lerobot==0.5.1.

MolmoAct2, the Allen Institute for AI's vision-language-action model, is now ported into LeRobot with the full lifecycle covered: fine-tuning (full or LoRA), evaluation, and real-robot deployment. Ready-made checkpoints with calibration correction baked in mean you can run it zero-shot on an SO-100/101:.

According to recent reports, inference fits in ~12 GB at bf16, and LoRA fine-tuning fits on a single 24 GB GPU. See the MolmoAct2 documentation for the full deployment guide.

Industry observers note that EO-1, a VLA pretrained upstream on interleaved vision-text-action data, joins LeRobot: a Qwen2.5-VL-3B backbone with a flow-matching action head, contributed by one of the paper's own authors. Train it with the standard lerobot-train workflow using --policy.type=eo1. Details in the documentation and the paper.

Industry observers note that the Multitask Diffusion Transformer policy brings the TRI Large Behavior Models recipe to LeRobot: a ~450M-parameter diffusion transformer conditioned on CLIP vision and language embeddings, so one model learns many tasks selected via natural language. It supports both diffusion and flow-matching objectives, and it is small enough to train yourself. See the documentation.

VLAs don't have to be huge. EVO1 packs its policy into 0.77B parameters, an InternVL3-1B backbone with a flow-matching action head, small enough to fine-tune and run in real time on modest GPUs. It ships with two-stage fine-tuning and Real-Time Chunking support out of the box. See the EVO1 documentation and the paper.

Success detection and progress estimation are missing pieces in the robot learning loop, and v0.6.0 gives them a home. LeRobot now has a unified reward models API (lerobot.rewards), mirroring the policies API, with four reward models behind one interface - the HIL-SERL reward classifier, SARM, and two newly introduced additions:.

Robometer is a pretrained, general-purpose reward model: point lerobot/Robometer-4B at any LeRobot dataset and it scores task progress and success from raw video plus a language instruction, with no task-specific training required. It is built on Qwen3-VL-4B and trained via trajectory comparisons over a dataset of more than one million robot trajectories (RSS 2026 paper).

TOPReward goes fully zero-shot: no reward weights at all. It wraps an off-the-shelf VLM (Qwen3-VL) and reads the log-probability of the token "True" given the trajectory video and the task instruction. Any capable VLM becomes a reward function.

According to recent reports, both ship with labeling scripts that write per-frame progress curves into your dataset, ready for reward-aware behavior cloning (RA-BC), dataset quality inspection, and progress-overlay videos. Check the Robometer and TOPReward docs.

Recording is no longer stuck with one hard-coded codec. The new --dataset.rgb_encoder.* options expose the full encoding surface (codec, quality, pixel format, GOP, presets), and vcodec=auto probes for hardware encoders like NVENC, VideoToolbox, VAAPI, and QSV before falling back to the default software AV1 encoder. For existing datasets, one command re-encodes everything:.

Full details in the video encoding documentation.

Plug in an Intel RealSense, set use_depth: true, and LeRobot records depth maps end to end: captured in millimeters, compressed as compact 12-bit depth video streams alongside your RGB cameras, and decoded back to physical units at training time. Depth renders live during recording and in lerobot-dataset-viz, and it works across SO-100/101, Koch, OpenArm, reBot, Unitree G1 and more.

In a recent development, your dataset stops being one task string per episode. LeRobot datasets now natively store rich language annotations (timestamped subtasks, plans, memory, corrections, speech, and per-camera VQA pairs), and the fresh lerobot-annotate CLI fills them in automatically using a VLM that watches your episodes:.

It has been revealed that A YAML recipe layer then renders these annotations into chat-style training messages at sample time: exactly the data tomorrow's long-horizon, talking robot policies will train on. Scale it up with HF Jobs, and read the annotation pipeline docs to learn more.

Training on video datasets is now up to ~2x faster out of the box: multi-camera frames decode in parallel, dataloader workers ship compact uint8 frames (4x less memory between processes), and persistent workers keep decoder caches alive across epochs. Loading a subset of a large dataset (episodes=[...]) went from minutes to milliseconds (275 s down to 0.06 s in our benchmark). Sampling is also deterministic and resumable now, so interrupted trainings restart sample-exact.

v0.5.0 planted the flag on LeRobot as an evaluation hub for VLAs; v0.6.0 makes it the real deal with six new simulation benchmarks, all runnable through the same lerobot-eval CLI, each with a docs page, a Docker image, and a SmolVLA baseline checkpoint smoke-tested in CI:.

Simulator backends require specific system dependencies with their own install steps; each docs page has the exact recipe, and every benchmark ships a ready-made Docker image if you'd rather skip the setup.

It has been revealed that together with LIBERO, Meta-World, and NVIDIA IsaacLab-Arena, that makes nine benchmark families under one roof, and a upcoming Adding a New Benchmark guide documents exactly how to plug in yours. Evaluation also got faster: parallel eval now defaults to async vectorized environments, benchmarked at up to 2x faster.

Industry observers note that deploying a policy used to be a hack on top of lerobot-record. The new lerobot-rollout CLI makes deployment its own workflow, with pluggable strategies and inference backends (including Real-Time Chunking for slow compatible VLAs). The base strategy just runs the policy. sentry records continuously, rotating episodes and uploading to the Hub as it goes. highlight keeps a ring buffer and saves the last N seconds when you hit a key, so an interesting moment is never lost. episodic mirrors the classic episode/reset recording workflow. And dagger turns deployment into data collection.

With the DAgger strategy, you watch your policy run, hit a key (or a USB foot pedal) the moment it goes wrong, take over with your leader arm to record the correction, and hand control back. Actuated leaders are driven to the follower's pose before you take over, so the handover is jerk-free. Every correction frame is tagged with an intervention flag, and the resulting dataset is ready for the next fine-tune:.

Deploy, collect corrections, fine-tune, repeat: the robot learning flywheel is now a CLI flag. Read the deployment docs.

Recent findings suggest that robot foundation models are outgrowing single GPUs. LeRobot training now supports FSDP (fully sharded data parallel) through Accelerate: parameters, gradients, and optimizer state are sharded across GPUs, and checkpoints are gathered back into a plain single-file model.safetensors that loads like any other policy. You can even resume an FSDP run on a different number of GPUs. See the multi-GPU training docs.

It has been revealed that no GPU? No problem. The exact same lerobot-train command now runs in the cloud by adding one flag:.

In a recent development, leRobot pushes your local dataset to a private Hub repo if needed, submits the job, streams logs to your terminal, and pushes the trained policy to the Hub at the end. Pick anything from a T4 to 8x H200 with --job.target (compute is billed pay-as-you-go). Check out the documentation.

Check the release notes for the full list and migration pointers for the breaking changes.

Beyond these headline features, v0.6.0 includes hundreds of bug fixes, documentation improvements, and quality-of-life upgrades across the codebase, from smarter defaults to more reliable CI.

We want to extend a huge thank you to everyone in the community. This release includes work from academia, industry and hobbyists teams who chose LeRobot as the home for their models and benchmarks. Every PR and bug report pushes open-source robotics forward.

Industry observers note that stay tuned for more to come 🤗 Get started here! – The LeRobot team ❤️.

When using the out-of-the-box Gemini Enterprise web application, identity and access management happen behind the scenes. Employees sign in through Google Identity or Workforce Identity Federation (such as Microsoft Entra ID or Okta), search results automatically respect per-user access controls (ACLs), and third-party login prompts for Federated Connectors or custom agents appear automatically in the chat UI.

Sources indicate that in practice, however, many enterprises build their own Customer UI to embed Gemini Enterprise into an internal portal, intranet, or line-of-business application. To do this, Customer BE calls the Gemini Enterprise StreamAssist API.

The moment an application builds a custom UI and calls the StreamAssist API directly, the three authentication flows that the built-in web app handled automatically become the responsibility of Customer UI and Customer BE:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Selected customers can put Dragonfly AI200 through its paces on Cirrascale's cloud.

Qualcomm has opened cloud-based trials of its Dragonfly AI200 rack-scale inference system to selected customers through Cirrascale Cloud Services.

Dragonfly AI200 is Qualcomm's pitch for running large language, multimodal, and other AI models without Nvidia-sized power and operating bills.

According to recent reports, whether it delivers those savings is something customers can now put to the test on Cirrascale's AI Innovation Cloud, with a route into production deployments, Qualcomm indicates. Cirrascale also demonstrated the system at SC26 in Chicago on November 17-18.

Industry observers note that the AI200 is part of Qualcomm's Dragonfly datacenter lineup, which also includes the AI250 and AI300 accelerators and the C1000 server CPU. The tech giant set out its broader ambitions at its Investor Day in June.

In a recent development, each AI200 accelerator card carries 768 GB of LPDDR memory, with 56 cards providing about 43 TB in a liquid-cooled rack. Qualcomm notes the system supports models ranging from 7 billion to 10 trillion parameters, including long-context, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and agentic workloads.

As we previously explored, packing in memory doesn't necessarily mean matching Nvidia's performance. Its Blackwell-based NVL72 systems use fast – and costly – HBM3e stacks, while Qualcomm has opted for LPDDR, more commonly found in mobile devices.

"AI inference is becoming one of the largest and most important computing workloads in the datacenter, and the industry needs a more efficient approach," mentioned Tony Pialis, Qualcomm's executive vice president and general manager for datacenter.

He claimed that the AI200 brings the company's experience with high-performance, low-power computing to a rack-scale infrastructure, in an architecture designed around the performance, memory, and cost requirements of inference workloads.

"Our customers need efficient, scalable infrastructure that can support increasingly sophisticated models without allowing power and operating costs to become the limiting factor," mentioned Cirrascale CEO Dave Driggers.

"By working with Qualcomm, we can give customers evaluation access to a compelling newly introduced architecture purpose-built for the next generation of AI inference.".

In a recent development, the chip firm also has its own software stack, the Dragonfly AI Infrastructure Management Suite, for provisioning, monitoring, workload orchestration, and fault handling across rack-scale deployments. ®.

Breaking: AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1240 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, we’re announcing the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities.
  • Using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process.
  • According to recent reports, continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, we’re announcing the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities. AWS Continuum is a security service that finds and validates code vulnerabilities, then delivers fixes as patches you can automate or as pull requests in your repositories. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities confirms which findings are exploitable in your environment, ranks the resulting problems by business impact, and proposes a fix for each one. Every remediation starts in a mode where Continuum proposes the fix and a person approves it before it ships. In the future, you will be able to decide which actions Continuum can take on its own, within the guardrails you define.

Using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process. If your organization runs a large application estate, your scanners likely produce thousands of findings a day, and many of them need no action. A finding can be unreachable, unexploitable, or already mitigated by a runtime control. Generic severity scores don’t tell you which resources a threat actor can actually reach, so a critical score on a dev-only utility looks the same as a medium score on a service one step away from a payments database. Previously, confirming whether a finding was exploitable took hours of manual investigation, and shipping a fix with confidence took days of coordination across security, infrastructure, and application teams, because the blast radius of a change is hard to assess without business context. To close that gap, Continuum proves which findings are exploitable and bounds the risk of each fix it proposes.

According to recent reports, continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment. For AWS, you set up a collector in the account and Region where your code runs. The collector gathers resource details such as AWS Config resources and network configuration so Continuum can judge whether a vulnerability is reachable over the network and what a threat actor could reach from it. From this graph, Continuum learns which systems are business-critical, who owns them, how services depend on one another, and which data each one touches. It uses that picture to identify your highest-value systems, such as customer data stores, payment pipelines, and authentication services, and then ranks each resulting issue by how close its attack path runs to those systems.

Continuum analyzes each finding against your code and its environment context and assigns an evidence level, such as a verdict proven by static analysis of the vulnerable code path. For findings it can reproduce, Continuum runs the exploit in an isolated sandbox and attaches proof-of-concept code with the reproduction steps. It produces the attack path, the supporting source analysis, and a blast radius assessment instead of a risk score alone. It also evaluates whether your existing defenses would detect and stop the validated path.

In a recent development, for each confirmed issue, Continuum generates a fix (a code patch, a dependency upgrade, or a configuration change) and opens it as a pull request in your connected repository, ready to review. Every fix requires human approval: you review and merge the pull request, so the final decision stays with your team. In the future, you will be able to build confidence in specific remediation classes and let Continuum apply those fixes automatically once its confidence gates pass, such as test coverage, scope bounds, and historical success rate.

Industry observers note that AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities in actionTo show how this works, I open AWS Continuum in the console and go to Code vulnerabilities. Before I can review issues, I set up an environment. I connect a code source, either a GitHub integration or an Amazon S3 bucket, and then create an environment that scans it on a schedule I choose. An Amazon S3 source has a couple of prerequisites: the bucket sits in the same account and AWS Region where I turn on AWS Continuum, and I grant access through an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that AWS Continuum assumes. I can optionally add AWS infrastructure context by setting up an AWS Continuum collector in the account and Region where my code runs and authorizing my environment to use it. For the full requirements and steps, see the AWS Continuum User Guide.

The Overview page brings these pieces together in one place, showing my Code integrations, the Environments built on them, and the status of any AWS collector that supplies AWS resource context.

I open one of my environments. The Issues tab lists validated, prioritized issues rather than raw scanner output, each with a severity, a status, and the time it was created. I choose one of the issues.

In a recent development, the Overview rates it High severity, with the status Completed and the remediation already Delivered to GitHub. The Risk assessment explains why. Continuum rates its Exploitability as Exploitable, with an evidence level of Static proven and a validation run status of Completed. Likelihood is High, since the service is reachable from an attacker, requires no authentication, and needs no user interaction. Impact is Moderate, which means an attacker gains the ability to modify business data, with a blast radius reaching other owners in the same tenant. A Proof section includes the source analysis behind the verdict.

The Remediation section shows a fix already delivered as a pull request in GitHub, changing four files, with 50 lines added and 24 removed across the cart service. Continuum opens the fix as a pull request titled Continuum fix, and I choose View pull request to open it in GitHub. The console is explicit that a generated patch does not mean the issue is fixed. I still review and merge it, which keeps the final decision with my team. A Contributing findings section lists the specific scanner finding this issue was built from.

The pull request description carries the same risk assessment, remediation summary, and proof from the console, so whoever reviews it in GitHub sees the evidence without leaving their workflow.

The Findings tab lists the raw scanner findings across the environment, the evidence that concerns are built from.

The Scans tab demonstrates the history of each scan with its status, origin, and request and completion times, and I use Configure scan frequency to change the cadence or Queue scan to run one on demand. The Configuration tab is where I manage the environment: the code and context sources it reads from, its code integrations, environment settings such as whether Continuum creates remediation patches, and the AWS collectors it uses for AWS context.

Industry observers note that in a single workflow, I work through the validated complications in priority order with each scan, reviewing the evidence and scope behind each one before I approve and merge the fixes I trust. Every fix waits for my approval, so the backlog keeps shrinking while my team keeps control of what ships.

Sources indicate that now available AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is available today in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon) Regions. For pricing, visit the pricing page.

To learn more, visit the AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities product page and the User Guide. Give it a try in the AWS Continuum console today, and send us feedback through your usual AWS Support contacts.

#23811. Breaking: Run AI workloads on any cloud, store on Hugging Face: zero-egress storage with SkyPilot

📅 07 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1058 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Run AI workloads on any cloud, store on Hugging Face: zero-egress storage with SkyPilot

📅 07 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1058 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For most teams, models and datasets live in a bucket in one region of one cloud.
  • Industry observers note that together with Hugging Face, we've joined the two halves: your models and datasets stay on the Hub, and SkyPilot runs the compute (dev, training, or serving) on whatever cluster has the GPUs.
  • According to recent reports, skyPilot tasks already read and write cloud object stores (S3, GCS, Azure, R2, and many more) by mounting them at a local path.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For most teams, models and datasets live in a bucket in one region of one cloud. The GPUs you can get, whether for development, training, or serving, increasingly sit on a different cloud than your data. The moment those two come apart, you pay a cross-cloud transfer tax just to read your own data onto your own GPUs.

Industry observers note that together with Hugging Face, we've joined the two halves: your models and datasets stay on the Hub, and SkyPilot runs the compute (dev, training, or serving) on whatever cluster has the GPUs. Mount a Hugging Face Bucket or any Hub repo into a SkyPilot job with one hf:// URL and the HF_TOKEN you already have, then launch it wherever capacity is. Hugging Face charges no egress, so reading your data onto those GPUs costs nothing, on any cloud.

According to recent reports, skyPilot tasks already read and write cloud object stores (S3, GCS, Azure, R2, and many more) by mounting them at a local path. Hugging Face Storage now joins that list as store: hf, reached through the hf:// scheme:.

It has been revealed that that one hf:// scheme covers the whole lifecycle: read the model and dataset from their repos, write checkpoints to a Bucket while you train, publish the finished model back to a repo, and pull it onto inference servers when you serve. Most teams already keep their models and datasets on the Hub, so there is no migration step and no latest storage account to create.

MOUNT uses Hugging Face's hf-mount FUSE backend, so a bucket or repo indicates up as a local path next to SkyPilot's other FUSE mounts (gcsfuse, blobfuse2, rclone, goofys). The fetching happens at the filesystem layer: when your code issues a read(), the driver pulls just those bytes from the Xet backend, so only the data you actually touch crosses the network, and hf-mount keeps an on-disk cache so repeat reads stay local. That on-disk cache is the behavior SkyPilot gives its other backends under MOUNT_CACHED, where a plain MOUNT instead streams every read from the bucket with nothing kept locally. For the hf store, MOUNT and MOUNT_CACHED behave the same, so either mode keeps the cache.

Because reads are lazy, a process can start working through a large file before the whole file has downloaded, instead of blocking on a full copy first. That keeps the GPU busy almost immediately, training on data as it streams in rather than sitting idle (and billing) while a dataset or checkpoint copies down. It pays off most on the first epoch, when nothing is cached yet. COPY takes the other route and downloads through huggingface_hub up front, with no special requirements.

Authentication is the token you already have. Set HF_TOKEN in your environment and hand it to a run with --secret HF_TOKEN; SkyPilot uses it for the mount on whatever cloud the job lands. One token works whether the job lands on AWS, GCP, Azure, Nebius, Lambda, or your own Kubernetes cluster, so there are no per-cloud bucket keys to juggle.

GPU capacity rarely comes from one place anymore. To get enough H100s and H200s, teams hold reserved and committed capacity across several vendors at once (a block on a hyperscaler, a cluster on a neocloud, maybe an on-prem rack) and run wherever they have allocation. SkyPilot is built for this: one job spec, scheduled across 20+ clouds, Kubernetes, and on-prem, landing on whichever reserved cluster is free.

Object storage has been the catch. Object stores are regional and per-cloud, so feeding a GPU or an inference server that sits in a different vendor's data center means either keeping a copy of your data in every vendor's bucket or paying to pull it across. Most clouds charge egress (around $0.09/GB out of AWS) the moment data leaves their network, and often between regions inside one cloud. Pulling a base model onto every inference node, or iterating a dataset for several epochs from a cluster on another cloud, adds a hefty bill on top of GPUs you have already reserved. Teams end up pinning each run to whichever vendor holds the data and leaving the rest of their capacity idle.

Hugging Face Storage takes that cost off the table where it bites: the read side. With no egress or CDN fees and storage at $12-18/TB/month (versus AWS S3 at roughly $23/TB plus egress), the same bucket is reachable from every one of those clusters, and reading from it is free no matter where the GPUs run. Writing back still costs your compute cloud's usual egress, the same as it would to any off-cloud store, but for most AI work the reads dominate: a dataset streamed over many epochs, or model weights pulled onto every new training or inference node. So you stop pinning each run to whichever vendor holds a copy of the data.

To collect some benchmark numbers, we ran a small fine-tune: Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B on the HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking dataset with TRL's SFTTrainer, mounting the model read-only from its Hub repo and writing every checkpoint to a Hugging Face Bucket. The same SkyPilot YAML ran on AWS, GCP, and Lambda, changing only --infra. SkyPilot placed each job wherever GPUs were free, and all three read and wrote the same bucket.

Per cloud, checkpoints wrote to the bucket at:.

Hugging Face Buckets are built on Xet, which uses content-defined chunking to split files into ~64 KB chunks and store each unique chunk once. Because the boundaries follow the content, an edit changes only the chunks it touches and the rest are recognized as already stored. This pays off in a few places:.

How much you save depends on how much your artifacts overlap, but the deduplication is automatic: you write a checkpoint as usual, and only the new chunks leave the machine.

It has been revealed that add an hf:// mount to any SkyPilot task and launch. MOUNT needs a base image with glibc 2.34+ and /dev/fuse.

The initial store: hf support started as a contribution from Nikhil Jha. The Hugging Face team carried it forward and upstreamed the hf-mount FUSE fixes that let it mount in unprivileged containers, the default on many Kubernetes clusters. The SkyPilot team wired it into the storage backend. The whole path is open source: SkyPilot, Hugging Face's hf-mount, and the huggingface_hub client.
